Without keeping the source text, ALOUD doubles the accuracy of a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B on long documents compressed 5x and 10x, from 27.7% to 54.8% at 5x, near the original text's 58.5%.
AI.motivation: Visual-text compression renders long contexts as images and is designed around how much text a VLM can recover, but recovered text is not necessarily usable, since models can transcribe words and still fail to answer from them.
AI.method: The authors measure recognition and use separately, finding that Qwen3-VL-8B's recognition saturates at 15-pixel characters while use needs 24 pixels, and that scaling from 2B to 32B raises recognition without narrowing the gap. They then propose ALOUD, which allocates visual resolution to finding and recognizing evidence and language tokens to using it, and compare with methods that paste back the original text.
AI.result: ALOUD takes a frozen Qwen3-VL-8B from 27.7% to 54.8% at 5x compression, close to the original text's 58.5%, and at equal budget it leads every method that does without the source text at every compression level. It also beats AGAR and VERA, which paste the original text back, and at 5x beats LensVLM-9B, which is trained and keeps the original text. In a preregistered held-out test, the gap ranks how much eight VLMs gain from their own words over pixels (Spearman rho = 0.86).
AI.conclusion: Visual-text compression is limited by how much a model can use recovered text, not only by how much it can recover.

title: LLM-Enhanced Multimodal House Price Prediction using Structured, Textual, and Visual Features
comment: 35 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Accurate house price prediction is essential for real estate buyers, sellers, agents, and financial institutions. Traditional methods rely primarily on structured data, e.g., number of bedrooms, bathrooms, parkings, but they overlook rich contextual information embedded in textual descriptions and property photos. Previous deep learning approaches for house price prediction have fused multimodal data but they fall short to extract structured spatio-temporal and contextual features from texts and semantic visual information from images. In this paper, we introduce a novel multimodal framework that addresses these limitations by systematically integrating structured attributes, textual descriptions, and visual images of properties to achieve higher prediction accuracy while maintaining interpretability. We use a large language model to derive domain-specific spatio-temporal and contextual features from text, and an unsupervised vision-language approach to automatically group photos into meaningful classes like indoor, outdoor, mixed, or floorplan, that are commonly present in real-world house listings. These categories are created without manual labeling by aligning image clusters with carefully designed pseudo text prompts. We fuse all features into a unified representation and use an optimized regressor to predict prices. Experiments on a large real-world property dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms traditional methods and existing multimodal baselines. Ablation studies confirm that the novel textual feature extraction and categorized visual embeddings substantially contribute to more accurate and reliable price predictions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multimodal house price prediction framework that combines structured attributes, LLM-derived features from listing text and unsupervised vision-language grouping of photos into indoor, outdoor, mixed and floorplan classes. It reports better accuracy than traditional methods and existing multimodal baselines on a large real-world property dataset.
AI.motivation: Traditional house price models use mainly structured data and miss contextual information in listing descriptions and photos, while earlier multimodal fusion methods extract weak spatio-temporal and visual semantics.
AI.method: An LLM derives domain-specific spatio-temporal and contextual features from text. An unsupervised vision-language approach groups photos into classes such as indoor, outdoor, mixed or floorplan by aligning image clusters with designed pseudo text prompts, with no manual labels. All features are fused into one representation and an optimized regressor predicts prices.
AI.result: The method outperforms traditional methods and existing multimodal baselines on a large real-world property dataset. Ablations show the textual feature extraction and categorized visual embeddings each contribute substantially to accuracy and reliability.
AI.conclusion: Combining structured, textual and visual features gives more accurate and interpretable price predictions, and the gains come from the text and categorized-image components.

title: CREDO: Evidence-Conditioned Credit Assignment for Temporal Reasoning Agents
comment: Code available at this https URL
summary: Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) requires language model agents to retrieve evidence, select relevant facts, and perform multi-step temporal reasoning. However, the trajectory-level outcome signal in GRPO does not explicitly distinguish the quality of intermediate decisions: downstream failures can penalize useful evidence acquisition, while identical rewards in all-failed groups eliminate the relative outcome signal despite differences in intermediate progress. We propose Credit Redistribution with Evidence-Driven Opportunities (CREDO), which uses intermediate evidence to recover local supervision, including in all-failed groups, and determine where outcome supervision acts. CREDO assigns positive stage-level credit through comparisons among rollouts of the same question and uses retained answer overlap as an opportunity proxy to shift part of the outcome-policy weight toward reasoning and answering. The framework preserves terminal rewards and trajectory-level advantages, while redistribution conserves total outcome-policy weight per trajectory. Following the public evaluation protocol of prior work, CREDO raises Overall accuracy from 78.0% to 82.4% and Multiple accuracy from 55.0% to 65.6% on MultiTQ relative to the strongest published baseline in our comparison. On TimelineKGQA, it raises cross-KG accuracy from 30.9% to 36.4% relative to our reproduced baseline via direct transfer to ICEWS Actor under matched training and evaluation settings.

AI.tldr: CREDO is a credit-assignment method for GRPO-trained temporal knowledge graph question answering agents that uses intermediate evidence to give local supervision, including in all-failed groups, and redistributes outcome weight toward reasoning and answering. It raises Overall accuracy on MultiTQ from 78.0% to 82.4% and Multiple accuracy from 55.0% to 65.6% relative to the strongest published baseline in the comparison.
AI.motivation: In GRPO, the trajectory-level outcome signal does not distinguish the quality of intermediate decisions, so useful evidence acquisition can be penalized by downstream failure, and all-failed groups give identical rewards that remove the relative signal.
AI.method: CREDO assigns positive stage-level credit through comparisons among rollouts of the same question and uses retained answer overlap as an opportunity proxy to shift part of the outcome-policy weight toward reasoning and answering. It preserves terminal rewards and trajectory-level advantages, and conserves total outcome-policy weight per trajectory.
AI.result: On MultiTQ, CREDO raises Overall accuracy from 78.0% to 82.4% and Multiple accuracy from 55.0% to 65.6% relative to the strongest published baseline in the comparison. On TimelineKGQA it raises cross-KG accuracy on ICEWS Actor from 30.9% to 36.4% relative to the authors' reproduced baseline, under matched training and evaluation settings.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-conditioned credit redistribution gives useful learning signal in groups where all rollouts fail and improves temporal reasoning agents on TKGQA benchmarks.

title: MAC-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration via Interconnected Tasks
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) tackle challenging tasks by dividing work among agents and coordinating their contributions toward shared objectives. Evaluating these systems therefore requires benchmarks that assess not only task-solving performance but also the ability to handle interdependent work. However, existing benchmarks often emphasize task difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements or evaluate only a limited range of predefined collaboration patterns. In this paper, we introduce MAC-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaboration through interconnected tasks. Rather than imposing predefined agent roles or communication protocols, MAC-Bench embeds collaboration requirements directly into task dependencies and shared-resource constraints. Specifically, we mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, while global task structures characterize how these interactions contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition, these structures are recombined into task graphs combining different collaboration requirements. Tasks are instantiated in executable environments with automated verification of partial progress and complete task resolution.

AI.tldr: MAC-Bench is a benchmark for multi-agent collaboration that embeds collaboration requirements in task dependencies and shared-resource constraints rather than in predefined roles or protocols. It mines reusable local collaboration patterns and global task structures from selected tasks and composes them into executable task graphs with automated verification of partial and complete progress.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent benchmarks emphasize difficulty without substantial collaboration requirements, or evaluate only a limited set of predefined collaboration patterns.
AI.method: The authors mine reusable collaboration structures from selected benchmark tasks at two levels. Local collaboration patterns capture recurring interactions among subtasks, and global task structures characterize how these contribute to complete workflows. Through coarse-to-fine composition these are recombined into task graphs with different collaboration requirements, instantiated in executable environments with automated verification.
AI.result: The abstract does not report experimental results.
AI.conclusion: MAC-Bench offers a benchmark for evaluating interdependent multi-agent work through executable, verified task graphs, but the abstract does not report findings on any agent system.

title: Evolving Memory, Learning to Meta-Control: Test-Time Adaptation for Experience-augmented LLM Agents
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to ACL Rolling Review (October 2026)
summary: Self-evolving agents accumulate experience from task streams, but existing frameworks typically rely on fixed pipelines to retrieve and utilize this experience, neglecting when and how to deploy it. We introduce Online Meta-Control of Experience (OMCE), a framework that updates experience memory and learns a meta-control policy from task feedback during test-time adaptation. OMCE employs a lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller that uses compact retrieval signals to select among four cognitive actions: DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE, and DISTILL. This routing mechanism operationalizes three coupled decisions: whether to invoke experience, which memory format to utilize, and when to consolidate new guidance. OMCE evolves online, leveraging task feedback to update the memory bank and refine the routing policy via contextual bandit updates. Experiments on four online adaptation benchmarks across four backbones show that OMCE improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points over the strongest compared baseline, while reducing per-task token use by a factor of 5.7 to 62.5 relative to ACE with GPT-5.2. Controlled ablations further support the benefits of learned routing and continued routing policy adaptation.

AI.tldr: Online Meta-Control of Experience (OMCE) updates an agent's experience memory and learns a contextual-bandit meta-controller that chooses among four cognitive actions, DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE and DISTILL, during test-time adaptation. It improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 percentage points over the strongest compared baseline while using 5.7 to 62.5 times fewer tokens per task than ACE with GPT-5.2.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving agents accumulate experience, but existing frameworks use fixed pipelines to retrieve and use it, and do not decide when and how to deploy it.
AI.method: A lightweight contextual-bandit meta-controller uses compact retrieval signals to select among DIRECT, EPISODE, GUIDE and DISTILL. This routing covers whether to invoke experience, which memory format to use and when to consolidate new guidance. The memory bank and routing policy are updated online from task feedback through contextual bandit updates.
AI.result: Across four online adaptation benchmarks and four backbones, OMCE improves first-attempt success by up to 20.5 points over the strongest compared baseline, while reducing per-task token use by a factor of 5.7 to 62.5 relative to ACE with GPT-5.2. Ablations support the benefits of learned routing and continued routing-policy adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Learned, online meta-control over experience memory improves adaptation efficiency and success for experience-augmented LLM agents.

title: Rubric-Based Assessment of Student Reports Using Small Language Models
comment: Full paper accepted for the 58th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science (SIGCSE TS 2027)
summary: Language models can analyze and assess student texts using predefined rubrics and deliver structured feedback, reducing instructors' workload. However, existing solutions often rely on external services that are resource-intensive, costly, and raise privacy concerns, making them unsuitable for constrained environments. This study evaluates an automated assessment pipeline with three key aims: design for low-resource environments, privacy, and focus on a novel context in cybersecurity education. The pipeline integrates lightweight language models for textual evaluation and a vision-language model for image interpretation. Responses from 105 students were collected over two semesters of an undergraduate course during a cybersecurity exercise on incident response. Results across different hardware configurations show that small models in low-resource environments can achieve up to 97% accuracy in text-only and up to 94% in rich-text assessments. This rivals or even outperforms a large model while adding the benefits of locally hosted assessment. Our solution can help educators and practitioners who need grading assistance without replacing human oversight, especially in environments where cloud-based solutions may be impractical. This study contributes an open-source, locally deployable AI-assisted scoring pipeline that runs on affordable hardware and can be extended to various types of student reports in computing education. As a result, it makes automated assessment accessible to a broad range of educators and institutions.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates a locally deployable pipeline that uses small language models and a vision-language model to grade cybersecurity incident-response reports from 105 students against rubrics. Small models reach up to 97% accuracy on text-only and up to 94% on rich-text assessments, comparable to or better than a large model.
AI.motivation: Automated rubric-based assessment with cloud LLMs is costly and raises privacy concerns, and it is unsuitable for constrained environments, so the authors target low-resource, privacy-preserving grading in cybersecurity education.
AI.method: The pipeline integrates lightweight language models for text evaluation and a vision-language model for image interpretation. Responses from 105 undergraduate students over two semesters of an incident-response exercise were collected, and results are compared across hardware configurations.
AI.result: Small models in low-resource environments reach up to 97% accuracy on text-only assessments and up to 94% on rich-text assessments. This rivals or outperforms a large model while allowing local hosting.
AI.conclusion: The open-source, locally deployable scoring pipeline can support educators with grading assistance without replacing human oversight, and could extend to other computing-education reports.

title: The Scope Grammar of Natural-Language Rules: Counting and Enumerating Readings modulo Logical Equivalence
summary: A rule written for people fixes its atomic conditions and connectives but leaves open how the connectives are bracketed, and each bracketing is a different logical reading that an autoformalizer must resolve or expose. We study the scope grammar, a deliberately ambiguous context-free grammar whose derivation trees are the readings of a connective skeleton and whose quotient by logical equivalence is what matters downstream. A skeleton with $k$ binary connectives has $C_k$ derivation trees, the $k$-th Catalan number, but far fewer logically distinct readings. For the positive, repetition-free fragment we make the gap exact: through the uniqueness of the read-once normal form we characterize the realizable normal forms by lowest common ancestors and count them with a two-label recurrence over the operator word, verified against exhaustive enumeration up to eleven atoms. The count is invariant under reversal and $\wedge/\vee$ duality; a skeleton is ambiguous if and only if it uses both $\wedge$ and $\vee$, a one-pass test; and the number of classes is at least $2^{\lfloor n/3\rfloor}$. Up to fifteen atoms the alternating pattern is the worst case; its count has a cubic generating function, is the 3-Schröder sequence (OEIS A137842), and grows with base $\varphi^{5/2}\approx3.330$, below the Catalan base 4. We reduce maximality to an inequality on increments, verified to sixteen atoms, and explain why local exchange arguments cannot prove it. We also treat negation, exceptions, and background axioms, where normal-form uniqueness still decides equivalence but counting is open.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the scope grammar of natural-language rules, a deliberately ambiguous grammar whose derivation trees are bracketings of a connective skeleton, and counts the logically distinct readings after quotienting by equivalence. For the positive, repetition-free fragment, the count is characterized by lowest common ancestors and computed by a two-label recurrence, and the alternating pattern is the worst case up to fifteen atoms.
AI.motivation: A rule with fixed atomic conditions and connectives still has many bracketings, each a different logical reading that an autoformalizer must resolve or expose, and the number of distinct readings is smaller than the Catalan count of derivation trees.
AI.method: The authors verify the characterization of realizable normal forms and the recurrence against exhaustive enumeration up to eleven atoms. They prove the count is invariant under reversal and conjunction-disjunction duality, that a skeleton is ambiguous if and only if it uses both conjunction and disjunction, and that the number of classes is at least 2^floor(n/3). They reduce maximality to an inequality on increments, verified to sixteen atoms.
AI.result: The count of classes has a cubic generating function, is the 3-Schroder sequence (OEIS A137842), and grows with base phi^(5/2), about 3.330, below the Catalan base 4, for the alternating pattern up to fifteen atoms. The maximality inequality is verified to sixteen atoms but not proven, and local exchange arguments cannot prove it. Negation, exceptions and background axioms are treated, where normal-form uniqueness still decides equivalence but counting is open.
AI.conclusion: Scope ambiguity in rule formalization is quantified precisely for the positive fragment, with the maximality conjecture and the extended cases left open.

title: Self-Evolving Agentic Workflows via Semantic Decomposition of Complex Tasks
comment: Accepted as a Spotlight at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB), GLEE Competition Track; 1st place in the GLEE competition. 21 pages
summary: Agentic workflows organize complex tasks into reusable procedures. However, invoking an LLM at every step incurs repeated inference costs and delays. We propose a framework for self-evolving agentic workflows through semantic task decomposition. Each subtask has explicit applicability conditions and a procedure that executes code or invokes a model as needed. An agent uses execution feedback to refine the decomposition and update these procedures. Experiments in the GLEE competition show the framework on bargaining, negotiation and persuasion. Most observed final-decision procedures are implemented in code. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes self-evolving agentic workflows that decompose complex tasks semantically into subtasks, each with explicit applicability conditions and a procedure that runs code or invokes a model as needed. Execution feedback refines the decomposition and procedures, and in the GLEE competition on bargaining, negotiation and persuasion most final-decision procedures are implemented in code.
AI.motivation: Invoking an LLM at every step of an agentic workflow incurs repeated inference cost and delay.
AI.method: Each subtask has explicit applicability conditions and a procedure that executes code or invokes a model as needed. An agent uses execution feedback to refine the decomposition and update these procedures, and the framework is evaluated in the GLEE competition.
AI.result: Experiments in the GLEE competition cover bargaining, negotiation and persuasion. Most observed final-decision procedures are implemented in code.
AI.conclusion: Semantic decomposition with code-executed procedures is a route to reducing LLM calls in self-evolving workflows, with the abstract reporting no quantitative cost or accuracy figures.

title: Quantizing Recurrent Language Models Is Easier Than You Think
summary: Linear recurrences are becoming an increasingly common building block in large language models, replacing the growing KV cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state that enables efficient decoding. However, the quantization stack has largely been developed around softmax Transformers, whose numerical properties and inference state differ from those of recurrent models. Our goal is to understand these differences and study the design space of quantization methods for recurrent models. In our analysis, we differentiate between two targets. First, extra-state quantization concerns weights and activations outside the recurrent state, whose distributions are shaped indirectly by the sequence mixer during training. In controlled 1.3B parameter models, we find that decayed recurrences develop weaker residual outlier channels than softmax attention and are therefore easier to quantize without incoherence processing. Second, intra-state quantization concerns the recurrent state itself during decode, where repeated updates create a different numerical problem from KV cache quantization. We instantiate our findings as LoReS, a state quantization pipeline combining value-axis scale grouping to match output channel magnitude, decay-based mixed-precision to protect slowly decaying heads or channels, and stochastic rounding to limit error accumulation under repeated requantization. Across Qwen-3.5 9B, Nemotron-H 8B, and Kimi-Linear 48B-A3B, LoReS supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower effective precision on shorter decode horizons. We implement LoReS in vLLM and demonstrate end-to-end decode speedups.

AI.tldr: Shows that linear-recurrent language models are easier to quantize than softmax Transformers in their extra-state weights and activations, and proposes LoReS, a recurrent-state quantization pipeline that supports robust 8-bit state quantization with end-to-end decode speedups in vLLM.
AI.motivation: Quantization methods were developed around softmax Transformers, whose numerical properties and growing KV cache differ from fixed-size recurrent state, so the quantization design space for recurrent models was not well understood.
AI.method: The authors separate extra-state quantization (weights and activations outside the recurrent state) from intra-state quantization (the recurrent state during decoding). LoReS combines value-axis scale grouping to match output channel magnitude, decay-based mixed precision for slowly decaying heads or channels, and stochastic rounding to limit error accumulation under repeated requantization.
AI.result: In controlled 1.3B models, decayed recurrences develop weaker residual outlier channels than softmax attention and are easier to quantize without incoherence processing. Across Qwen-3.5 9B, Nemotron-H 8B and Kimi-Linear 48B-A3B, LoReS supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower effective precision on shorter decode horizons.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent models need their own quantization treatment for the recurrent state, and LoReS, implemented in vLLM, demonstrates practical end-to-end decode speedups.

title: To Align Long, Plan Short: Simulating Diverse Profile-Aligned Students by Realizing Short-Term Plans in Long-Horizon Learning Environments
summary: Simulated students offer a scalable way to test learning platforms and AI tutors before deployment with real students and to augment scarce data for studying learning at scale. Existing LLM-based simulators primarily target short, language-centered interactions. In open-ended learning environments, however, student behavior emerges from patterns across long-horizon interaction trajectories, where turn-level prompting can drift from an assigned behavior profile. We introduce ALPS (Align Long-term by Planning Short-term), a hierarchical simulated student conditioned on observable, environment-specific behavior profiles. Rather than selecting every action independently, ALPS alternates between planning profile-aligned task segments and generating the corresponding actions. We evaluate ALPS in both data-sufficient and data-scarce settings, where supervision comes either from real student trajectories or from a teacher LLM. Across both settings, we compare in-context learning (ICL), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reward-ranked fine-tuning (RAFT), and their sequential combination (SFT followed by RAFT). Experiments in an inquiry-based physics game and a pharmacy simulation evaluate behavioral density and coverage against held-out real data, and profile consistency using a human-aligned LLM judge. Across both settings, ALPS consistently outperforms turn-level generation, achieving comparable density and judge pass rates under scarce supervision, although coverage remains lower. These results show that hierarchical planning enables faithful, profile-aligned simulation over long interaction horizons, even with limited real student data.

AI.tldr: Introduces ALPS, a hierarchical simulated student that plans profile-aligned short task segments and then generates the actions for them, and reports that it consistently outperforms turn-level generation in long-horizon learning environments.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based student simulators target short, language-centered interactions, whereas in open-ended learning environments student behaviour emerges over long trajectories, where turn-level prompting can drift from the assigned behaviour profile.
AI.method: ALPS alternates between planning profile-aligned task segments and generating the corresponding actions, conditioned on observable, environment-specific behaviour profiles. It is compared with in-context learning, supervised fine-tuning, reward-ranked fine-tuning (RAFT) and SFT followed by RAFT, under data-sufficient and data-scarce settings with supervision from real trajectories or a teacher LLM.
AI.result: In an inquiry-based physics game and a pharmacy simulation, ALPS consistently outperforms turn-level generation and reaches comparable behavioural density and judge pass rates under scarce supervision, although its coverage remains lower. Profile consistency is measured with a human-aligned LLM judge.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical planning enables faithful, profile-aligned simulation over long interaction horizons, even with limited real student data.

title: ClickSight: An LLM Framework for Interpreting Student Clickstreams Through Learning Strategies
comment: 29 pages, 12 figures, 19 tables. Under review. Code: this https URL
summary: Digital learning environments produce rich clickstream data that can reveal how students approach learning tasks, yet interpreting these fine-grained traces often requires substantial expert effort. We introduce ClickSight, a framework for interpreting student clickstreams through learning strategies defined in the literature. Given a student clickstream and a predefined set of learning strategies, ClickSight uses a staged LLM-based pipeline to identify strategy-relevant evidence, assess adherence to each strategy, and generate an evidence-grounded interpretation of the student's behavior. We evaluate ClickSight across two learning environments, 365 students, and 12 model backbones using an expert-grounded quality rubric and an LLM judge calibrated with human-expert ratings. Our results show that ClickSight can generate high-quality strategy-based interpretations across different models and environments, with reasoning models performing more consistently than instruction-tuned counterparts. We further find that providing external clickstream-extracted guidance can improve interpretation quality for strategies that require precise quantitative information from the trace. By connecting fine-grained clickstreams with theoretically defined learning strategies and preserving the evidence underlying each judgment, ClickSight provides a flexible approach for studying student behavior in digital learning environments.

AI.tldr: Presents ClickSight, a staged LLM pipeline that interprets student clickstreams through predefined learning strategies and produces evidence-grounded interpretations that are rated high quality across models and environments.
AI.motivation: Clickstream data is rich, but interpreting fine-grained traces usually requires substantial expert effort.
AI.method: Given a student clickstream and a predefined set of learning strategies, a staged LLM pipeline identifies strategy-relevant evidence, assesses adherence to each strategy, and generates an evidence-grounded interpretation of the student's behaviour.
AI.result: Evaluated on two learning environments with 365 students and 12 model backbones, using an expert-grounded quality rubric and an LLM judge calibrated to human-expert ratings. Reasoning models perform more consistently than instruction-tuned counterparts, and external clickstream-extracted guidance improves interpretation for strategies that need precise quantitative information.
AI.conclusion: Linking clickstreams to theoretically defined learning strategies while preserving the supporting evidence gives a flexible way to study student behaviour in digital learning environments.

title: ParetoSaddler: Pareto-Guided Optimization of Agent Harnesses for Quality and Cost
comment: Project website and code will be available at this https URL
summary: Harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents without modifying model weights, but existing methods primarily optimize response quality. Extending them to joint quality--cost optimization introduces a challenge: applying the deployment preference during intermediate updates can prematurely reject candidates that are valuable for later improvements. We introduce ParetoSaddler, which addresses this mismatch by separating intermediate candidate promotion from final deployment selection. At each iteration, an optimizer updates a parent harness to produce a candidate, and then compares the two over repeated executions and uses Bayesian bootstrap Pareto support to promote candidates showing credible progress in either quality or cost. Promoted candidates receive broader development evaluation and remain available as parents for later optimization steps. We evaluate ParetoSaddler on ClawMark and GAIA2 using domain-disjoint splits. On ClawMark, ParetoSaddler improves quality from 70.86\% to 81.35\% while reducing cost from \$1.17 to \$1.01 per task; on GAIA2, it improves quality from 56.22\% to 62.89\% while reducing cost from \$0.78 to \$0.45 per task. The Pareto-selected harnesses also achieve higher quality at lower cost than quality-only harness optimization. Analysis shows that Pareto-aware optimization retains intermediate candidates that would be discarded by deployment preference but can support later improvements, while Bayesian bootstrap screening filters out candidates whose gains are weakly supported across runs.

AI.tldr: Proposes ParetoSaddler, which optimizes agent harnesses for joint quality and cost by separating intermediate candidate promotion from final deployment selection, and reports higher quality at lower cost on ClawMark and GAIA2.
AI.motivation: Harness optimization for LLM agents has mainly targeted response quality; applying the deployment cost preference during intermediate updates can prematurely reject candidates that would help later.
AI.method: At each iteration an optimizer updates a parent harness to produce a candidate, and the two are compared over repeated executions. Bayesian bootstrap Pareto support promotes candidates that show credible progress in quality or cost; promoted candidates get broader development evaluation and remain available as parents.
AI.result: On ClawMark, quality rises from 70.86% to 81.35% while cost falls from $1.17 to $1.01 per task. On GAIA2, quality rises from 56.22% to 62.89% while cost falls from $0.78 to $0.45 per task. The Pareto-selected harnesses achieve higher quality at lower cost than quality-only harness optimization.
AI.conclusion: Retaining intermediate candidates that deployment preference would discard, and screening them with bootstrap support, lets Pareto-aware harness optimization find better quality-cost trade-offs.

title: Order-Only On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own generations by matching the teacher's token probabilities. These probabilities entangle two kinds of information: which tokens the teacher prefers, and how confident it is. The latter reflects the teacher's own capacity and calibration, which a smaller student may be unable to reproduce. Because the teacher temperature changes these values without changing the ordering, OPD is also sensitive to the temperature choice. We ask whether the teacher's ordering of candidate tokens is enough, and propose Order-Only On-Policy Distillation (O$^{3}$PD). At each student-generated prefix, O$^{3}$PD trains the student to reproduce the order of the teacher's top-$K$ tokens, without fitting their probability values. The objective is therefore invariant to the teacher temperature and needs no temperature tuning. Across six teacher--student pairs, O$^{3}$PD outperforms OPD on the average over HMMT25, AIME24, and AIME25 in every pair, by up to 2.9 points, with gains of up to 5.6 points on AIME25. Other ranking losses yield similar gains, so the benefit comes from ordinal supervision itself. Analysis shows that O$^{3}$PD departs further from the teacher's probabilities than OPD, yet reproduces its ranking more faithfully and yields a stronger student. The ranking, not the probability values, thus carries the knowledge that on-policy distillation needs to transfer.

AI.tldr: Proposes Order-Only On-Policy Distillation (O$^{3}$PD), which trains the student to reproduce the ordering of the teacher's top-K tokens rather than their probability values, and outperforms OPD on the average over HMMT25, AIME24 and AIME25 in every one of six teacher-student pairs, by up to 2.9 points.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation matches teacher token probabilities, which mix ranking information with the teacher's confidence and calibration, a level a smaller student may be unable to reproduce; OPD is also sensitive to the teacher temperature.
AI.method: At each student-generated prefix, O$^{3}$PD trains the student to reproduce the order of the teacher's top-K tokens without fitting their probability values. The objective is therefore invariant to teacher temperature and needs no temperature tuning.
AI.result: Across six teacher-student pairs, O$^{3}$PD outperforms OPD on the average over HMMT25, AIME24 and AIME25 in every pair, with gains of up to 5.6 points on AIME25. Other ranking losses give similar gains, so the benefit comes from ordinal supervision itself.
AI.conclusion: The teacher's ranking of tokens, not their probability values, carries the knowledge that on-policy distillation needs to transfer.

title: Conditional Calibration Contracts under Coupled Load: A Branch-Aware Audit of Switched Inference
comment: 12 pages including references and appendices, ACM sigconf. Historical 40-cell campaign (10 training seeds x 4 coupling levels), with separate three-seed sweeps/ablations. Includes proofs, prospective FIFO mechanism checks, and limitations; prospective contract validation remains open
summary: Bursty serving changes both queue states and the population selected for each model. We study conditional calibration contracts as a specification to be validated, rather than a certified property of an existing router. CA-MHD combines load-coupled distillation, closed-loop replay and a cost-informed Schmitt router in a discrete-event simulator with a hardware service table. Across 40 cells (ten training seeds and four content-load coupling levels), we distinguish the original teacher, frozen wide heads on an adapted trunk, and the narrow student. A common teacher-trajectory audit has median absolute student-teacher deficit 0.06 percentage points, but does not certify the student-selected deployment support. Historical results use a kernel correctness gap, not the published SmoothECE; we separately prove selected-branch composition for a residual functional at a common fixed scale. The deployed wide branch has lower ordinal accuracy than the original teacher in all 40 cells. Same-checkpoint student-only serving has lower historical ordinal gap in 27/40 cells; routing also exposes violation tails up to 17.5 percent. Student p99 latency remains above the 1.5 ms target. Retrospective temporal recalibration improves the ordinal gap in 39/40 cells, but causal delayed-label availability is unverified and no incremental per-mode benefit is detected after multiplicity adjustment. An in-sample CUSUM detects 30/40 checkpoint changes at five historical false alarms, with no prospective false-alarm guarantee. These findings support a branch-aware audit and a scoped negative result, not demonstrated routing superiority. Independent budgets, selected-support validation and net utility under a satisfied SLA remain open.

AI.tldr: Audits conditional calibration contracts for a switched inference system in a discrete-event simulator and finds that the deployed wide branch has lower ordinal accuracy than the original teacher in all 40 cells, so the paper offers a scoped negative result rather than demonstrated routing superiority.
AI.motivation: Bursty serving changes queue states and the population selected for each model, so calibration properties need to be validated as a specification rather than assumed for an existing router.
AI.method: CA-MHD combines load-coupled distillation, closed-loop replay and a cost-informed Schmitt router in a discrete-event simulator with a hardware service table. Across 40 cells (ten training seeds and four content-load coupling levels), it compares the original teacher, frozen wide heads on an adapted trunk, and the narrow student.
AI.result: A common teacher-trajectory audit gives a median absolute student-teacher deficit of 0.06 percentage points but does not certify the student-selected deployment support. Student-only serving has a lower historical ordinal gap in 27/40 cells, routing exposes violation tails up to 17.5%, and student p99 latency remains above the 1.5 ms target. Retrospective temporal recalibration improves the ordinal gap in 39/40 cells, but causal delayed-label availability is unverified.
AI.conclusion: The results support a branch-aware audit and a scoped negative result; independent budgets, selected-support validation and net utility under a satisfied SLA remain open.

title: Test-Time Scaling for Open-Ended Reasoning at Small Model Scale
summary: A vote over a model's samples can only help when the samples disagree. For open-ended generation the binding question is therefore not how to combine samples but whether a model produces samples worth combining, a question test-time scaling has answered for math but not for free-form text. We study it at small scale with semantic cluster voting, a judge-free aggregator that groups a small instruct model's samples by meaning and returns the largest cluster's representative, with no reward model or self-judging. On a 250-prompt benchmark with three tiers of answer checkability, the same pattern holds across three model families (Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2B) and two generation seeds: voting raises accuracy on the math control, where samples vary but stay checkable (a gain of +10 to +29 points across the three models), yet adds at most +0.30 judge points on open-ended text. On a larger 200-problem MATH-500 run with the primary model, the math gain is +8.5 points (95% CI [+4.0, +13.0]). Almost every open-ended sample falls into one meaning cluster, so there is little to select over. The collapse is consistent with instruction-tuning rather than model size, and raising decoding temperature does not recover usable diversity, because it costs more quality than it adds (net -0.64 judge points, 95% CI [-0.93, -0.37]).

AI.tldr: Shows that semantic cluster voting, a judge-free test-time scaling method, raises accuracy by +10 to +29 points on checkable math tasks across three small models but adds at most +0.30 judge points on open-ended text.
AI.motivation: Voting-based test-time scaling has been established for math but not for free-form text, where the key question is whether a model produces diverse samples worth combining.
AI.method: Semantic cluster voting groups a small instruct model's samples by meaning and returns the representative of the largest cluster, with no reward model or self-judging. It is evaluated on a 250-prompt benchmark with three tiers of answer checkability, across Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-2-2B with two generation seeds.
AI.result: On the math control, voting gains are +10 to +29 points across the three models; on a 200-problem MATH-500 run with the primary model, the math gain is +8.5 points (95% CI [+4.0, +13.0]). Almost every open-ended sample falls into one meaning cluster, and raising decoding temperature costs more quality than it adds (net -0.64 judge points, 95% CI [-0.93, -0.37]).
AI.conclusion: Voting only helps when samples disagree; open-ended samples from these small instruct models collapse into one meaning cluster, a collapse the authors attribute to instruction tuning rather than model size.

title: Who Should Score the Cache? Mid-Depth Layers Are the Best Judges of KV-Cache Eviction
summary: Key-value (KV) cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention scores, and each layer scores its own cache. To our knowledge, no eviction method asks which layer should score. We find, across twenty-one models, that the depth of the scoring layer governs eviction quality. On the eighteen models with per-layer caches, spanning 0.5B to 109B, long-context retrieval accuracy collapses at shallow layers, peaks between 0.4 and 0.75 of depth, and degrades at the last layer. The curve arises because a layer judges tokens well only once it has used the question to find the answer, which takes several layers. Modeling eviction as a top-$k$ cut, we compute answer survival probability from prefill attention and reproduce the measured curves. This approach selects the scoring layer using calibration prompts with known answers, and the selected layer is the best layer measured on most models and never significantly below it. It improves on the own-layer default on sixteen of the eighteen models, with significant gains on seven, all at 14B or below, while on larger models the default is already close to the best mid-depth layer. Scoring every cache from the selected layer while keeping one set of tokens for all heads also beats per-head SnapKV by 18 to 43 points on five models up to 14B under tight budgets. This gain carries over to financial filings at 32K context, all at the same memory budget, with no extra forward pass. The same curve explains a penalty in shared-cache models, where several layers read one cache and the layer that writes it scores by default. On Gemma-4-E2B the writer is shallow and loses 28 points to a mid-depth reader at a 10% budget. We also find that in open-book question answering (LongBench) no mid-depth layer beats the own-layer default.

AI.tldr: Finds across 21 models that the depth of the layer used to score KV-cache tokens governs eviction quality, with mid-depth layers (about 0.4 to 0.75 of depth) judging best, and proposes selecting the scoring layer with calibration prompts that have known answers.
AI.motivation: KV-cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention scores and each layer scores its own cache, but no prior eviction method asks which layer should do the scoring.
AI.method: Eviction is modelled as a top-k cut, and answer survival probability is computed from prefill attention. The scoring layer is selected with calibration prompts that have known answers, and one set of tokens is kept for all heads.
AI.result: On the 18 models with per-layer caches (0.5B to 109B), long-context retrieval accuracy collapses at shallow layers, peaks between 0.4 and 0.75 of depth, and degrades at the last layer. The selected layer improves on the own-layer default on 16 of 18 models, significantly on seven, and beats per-head SnapKV by 18 to 43 points on five models up to 14B under tight budgets. In open-book LongBench no mid-depth layer beats the own-layer default.
AI.conclusion: The choice of scoring layer matters, and selecting it from calibration prompts works across models, with the largest gains on models of 14B or below; in shared-cache models, a shallow writing layer is penalized.

title: Metamorphic Testing for Evaluating Robustness of Sentiment Analysis Models
summary: Machine learning systems are challenging to test using traditional software testing methods because their behavior is learned from data rather than explicitly programmed. This challenge is particularly significant in natural language processing (NLP), where small input variations can lead to unexpected model behavior. Conventional evaluation metrics, such as accuracy and F1-score, often fail to capture such inconsistencies. Metamorphic testing addresses this limitation by evaluating expected relationships between original and transformed inputs. With the increasing prevalence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and language-based AI systems, the need for systematic robustness testing has become even more pronounced. Motivated by this growing need, this paper presents a lightweight, batch-based metamorphic testing approach for evaluating the robustness of such systems. In particular, we consider sentiment analysis as a representative NLP task and evaluate a pretrained classifier under four transformations: synonym replacement, typo injection, word-order variation, and negation. Using consistency score, flip accuracy, and confidence change, we identify strengths in handling semantic variations and vulnerabilities to textual noise and logical transformations. These findings highlight the value of metamorphic testing in identifying behavioral inconsistencies beyond conventional performance metrics and demonstrate its potential as a systematic framework for evaluating the robustness of language-based AI systems and guiding performance improvements before deployment.

AI.tldr: Applies a lightweight, batch-based metamorphic testing approach to a pretrained sentiment classifier under synonym replacement, typo injection, word-order variation and negation, and finds strengths on semantic variation but vulnerabilities to textual noise and logical transformations.
AI.motivation: Machine learning systems, and NLP models in particular, are hard to test with conventional methods because their behaviour is learned from data, and standard metrics such as accuracy and F1 often miss inconsistencies caused by small input variations.
AI.method: The approach checks expected relations between original and transformed inputs. It applies four transformations (synonym replacement, typo injection, word-order variation and negation) and measures consistency score, flip accuracy and confidence change.
AI.result: The pretrained classifier handles semantic variations well but is vulnerable to textual noise and logical transformations, behaviour that conventional performance metrics do not reveal.
AI.conclusion: Metamorphic testing can expose behavioural inconsistencies before deployment and offers a systematic robustness framework for language-based AI systems.

title: Hinted Scaling Laws
summary: Scaling laws predict the outcome of large, expensive training runs by extrapolating trends from smaller, cheaper runs. On downstream accuracy evaluations, these predictions fail when the weaker models produced by the cheaper runs score near zero accuracy, because these scores give no trend to extrapolate to larger scales. We introduce hinted scaling laws, which use privileged information to turn a benchmark into a continuum of easier versions so that even the small models score above zero. We find that accuracy rises smoothly and predictably with the hint level, enabling new types of scaling laws that operate below the noise threshold. On the Delphi pretraining ladder, a hinted scaling law fit on models trained with at most $10^{20}$ FLOPs forecasts the GSM8K accuracy of a $10^{23}$ FLOP model (25.9%) to within 3 percentage points; a standard scaling law under-forecasts it by 13 percentage points when fit on the same models and by 12 even with models up to $10^{22}$ FLOPs in the fit. Across both this pretraining ladder and a collection of post-trained model families, hinted scaling laws reduce the median forecasting error on GSM8K, AIME and HLE from 21 percentage points to 4.3. Hinting also reduces the number of test examples needed to tell whether one model is better than another by widening the accuracy gaps between models while approximately preserving their order: a single hinted rollout per problem ranks nearly indistinguishable models as accurately as five unhinted rollouts. Our results suggest that hinting is a general primitive for improving the accuracy and cost of downstream scaling laws and other prediction tasks in model development.

AI.tldr: Introduces hinted scaling laws, which use privileged information to turn a benchmark into easier versions so that small models score above zero, and shows that a hinted law forecasts a 10^23 FLOP model's GSM8K accuracy to within 3 points, where a standard law under-forecasts by 13 points.
AI.motivation: Scaling laws fail to extrapolate downstream accuracy when the cheap, small models score near zero, because those scores give no trend to extrapolate.
AI.method: Hints provide a continuum of easier versions of a benchmark, so accuracy rises smoothly with hint level and becomes measurable below the noise threshold. A scaling law is fit on hinted accuracies from smaller models.
AI.result: On the Delphi pretraining ladder, a hinted law fit on models up to 10^20 FLOPs forecasts the GSM8K accuracy of a 10^23 FLOP model (25.9%) to within 3 points; a standard law under-forecasts it by 13 points on the same models and by 12 even with models up to 10^22 FLOPs. Across pretraining and post-trained families, median forecasting error on GSM8K, AIME and HLE falls from 21 to 4.3 points.
AI.conclusion: Hinting is a general primitive for improving the accuracy and cost of downstream scaling laws and other prediction tasks in model development.

title: When the Text Is Silent: Memory Shortcuts and the Validity of LLM Annotation under Evidence Insufficiency
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate text for social science research, content moderation, and training data. Their broad knowledge of real-world entities raises a concern: when labeling a text, do they rely on its evidence or substitute what they already know? We call this behavior a memory shortcut and examine when it emerges, what amplifies it, and how to mitigate it. Using 995 widely recognized public figures and four matched control names per figure, we construct counterfactual texts that separate textual evidence from prior knowledge, and evaluate three commercial LLMs on 121,594 prompts each across five stages. We find a striking asymmetry. Although all models recognize nearly every figure, none follows memory over the text when the two conflict. Shortcuts instead emerge when evidence is absent: for one model, famous names raise the rate of remembered occupations, ages, and countries by 17.0, 14.9, and 6.8 percentage points relative to synthetic names. These effects occur only for recognized figures, and 98.6% of the resulting labels are factually correct about the namesake while none is supported by the text. Evaluation threats and answer-contingent rewards amplify shortcuts by 8.7 and 12.4 points. Famous names also raise leadership ratings of sparsely documented applicants by 0.22 and 0.28 points in two models. A namesake reminder and name masking each eliminate the shortcuts, with trade-offs in gender annotation. LLM annotations can thus be factually correct yet methodologically invalid. Trustworthy LLM annotation requires audits that test evidence absence, account for incentives in annotation instructions, and evaluate the attribute-specific trade-offs of mitigation.

AI.tldr: Finds that three commercial LLMs never follow memorized facts over conflicting text, but when text gives no evidence, famous names trigger memory shortcuts that yield factually correct yet unsupported labels, and a namesake reminder or name masking removes them.
AI.motivation: LLMs are used to annotate text for social science and content moderation, but it is unclear whether they rely on the text's evidence or substitute what they already know about real-world entities.
AI.method: Using 995 public figures with four matched control names per figure, counterfactual texts separate textual evidence from prior knowledge. Three commercial LLMs are evaluated on 121,594 prompts each across five stages, and amplifiers such as evaluation threats and answer-contingent rewards are tested.
AI.result: All models recognize nearly every figure, yet none follows memory over conflicting text. When evidence is absent, famous names raise remembered occupations, ages and countries by 17.0, 14.9 and 6.8 points for one model relative to synthetic names, and these effects occur only for recognized figures. 98.6% of resulting labels are factually correct about the namesake, but none is supported by the text. Evaluation threats and answer-contingent rewards amplify shortcuts by 8.7 and 12.4 points.
AI.conclusion: LLM annotations can be factually correct yet methodologically invalid, so audits must test evidence absence and incentives, and mitigation must be evaluated attribute by attribute.

title: Concise-9B: Removing the Slack from a Reasoning Model's Thinking
summary: Reasoning models answer better when they think longer, but a thinking trace keeps going well after its answer has formed. We measure this slack in Qwen3.5-9B and remove most of it with concise self-training: two rounds of on-policy rejection-sampling fine-tuning that keep the shortest correct samples, plus a small share of answer-synthesis targets, giving Concise-9B. On 8,983 held-out problems (competition and hard mathematics, SuperGPQA, a five-area confirmation set and MMLU-Pro), Concise-9B generates 0.66x the tokens of Qwen3.5-9B at a 32K thinking budget, with accuracy equivalent within +/-1 point (-0.20 [-0.77, +0.36] points). Forcing each trace on the hard and confirmation sets to answer every 2,048 thinking tokens, we find that 54-64% of Qwen3.5-9B's thinking tokens come after the point from which every forced answer equals the final one (41-48% for Concise-9B). Stopping there would keep every answer at 0.35-0.44x the base model's tokens, but finding that point takes hindsight: stopping when three consecutive forced answers agree costs the base model 2.4-9.2 points. Concise self-training removes slack without that cost: 86% [83, 90] of the thinking tokens it saves come after the answer has formed. It has a limit: with traces continued to 80K tokens, Concise-9B solves 25 fewer of 1,276 hard problems (-25 [-49, -1]), mostly in competition mathematics. The measurement also yields a cheap commit signal for adaptive sampling that matched two-sample escalation within +/-1 point at 0.67x its tokens in a pre-registered test. Results on Qwen3.5-4B, on which the recipe was developed, and a replication on Olmo-3-7B-Think suggest that the saving depends on how verbose the base model is.

AI.tldr: Presents Concise-9B, a Qwen3.5-9B model trained with concise self-training that generates 0.66x the tokens of the base model at a 32K thinking budget with accuracy within about one point, by removing thinking slack that comes after the answer has already formed.
AI.motivation: Reasoning models keep thinking well after their answer has formed, which wastes tokens; this slack can be measured, but finding where to stop requires hindsight.
AI.method: Two rounds of on-policy rejection-sampling fine-tuning keep the shortest correct samples, with a small share of answer-synthesis targets. Forced answers every 2,048 thinking tokens locate the point at which the answer has settled.
AI.result: On 8,983 held-out problems, Concise-9B generates 0.66x the tokens of Qwen3.5-9B at a 32K thinking budget, with accuracy equivalent within +/-1 point (-0.20 [-0.77, +0.36] points). For the base model, 54-64% of thinking tokens come after the answer has settled, and 86% [83, 90] of the thinking tokens Concise-9B saves come after that point. With traces continued to 80K tokens, it solves 25 fewer of 1,276 hard problems (-25 [-49, -1]).
AI.conclusion: Concise self-training removes slack without a hindsight stopping rule, but the saving depends on how verbose the base model is and it has a cost on the hardest problems.

title: Accessed, never disclosed: Silent access to protected health information by medical artificial intelligence agents
comment: 33 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, 3 Extended Data tables; includes Supplementary Information (12 tables, 6 figures)
summary: Medical artificial intelligence agents should retrieve patient identifiers only when a task requires them, the data-minimization principle behind the HIPAA minimum necessary standard for protected health information (PHI). An agent can retrieve identifiers without revealing them. Such silent access remains invisible to evaluations that inspect only the output. We embedded canaries in synthetic patient records and linked each tool invocation to canary exposure in the final answers across five language models, four boundary levels, and seven attack frames for identifier-free clinical tasks. Three models invoked the PHI tools unnecessarily, whereas Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 did not. Stronger boundaries reduced this access, and the residual access under the strictest policy was confined to frames in which the user overrode the policy or asserted approval. A pre-execution gate given the task-necessity criterion nearly eliminated this access. Output-only evaluation cannot verify minimum-necessary access; boundaries, gates, and access-log audits are required together.

AI.tldr: Shows that medical AI agents can access protected health information silently, retrieving identifiers that never appear in the output, and that a pre-execution gate given the task-necessity criterion nearly eliminates this access.
AI.motivation: The HIPAA minimum necessary standard requires agents to retrieve identifiers only when a task needs them, but output-only evaluations cannot see retrieval that is not revealed in the final answer.
AI.method: Canaries are embedded in synthetic patient records, and each tool invocation is linked to canary exposure in the final answers. The setup covers five language models, four boundary levels and seven attack frames for identifier-free clinical tasks.
AI.result: Three models invoke the PHI tools unnecessarily, whereas Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 do not. Stronger boundaries reduce this access, and the residual access under the strictest policy is confined to frames in which the user overrides the policy or asserts approval. A pre-execution gate given the task-necessity criterion nearly eliminates the access.
AI.conclusion: Output-only evaluation cannot verify minimum-necessary access, so boundaries, gates and access-log audits are required together.

title: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool-using language-model agents often execute actions that their domain policies forbid. We present LeanGuard, a runtime that checks every proposed tool call against a policy written in Lean4 before the call reaches the environment. Policies combine state predicates with scoped past-time temporal operators over the execution history, evaluation is fail-closed, and the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a LeanLTL semantics. A denied call can be corrected in two ways. With feedback, the agent receives the violated rule and a hint; with proof-guided repair, Lean metaprogramming searches for a nearby call that preserves the user's intent and proves that the policy admits it, without the model. On Tau-Bench with five Qwen models (0.8B-27B), unguarded agents execute at least 33 calls that the Lean policy forbids, while LeanGuard executes none; with feedback, task success does not change significantly. On DTap, LeanGuard reduces direct prompt-injection success from 57.9% to 5.9%, and in telecom, where benign tasks need no writes, benign success is unchanged. Feedback reduces repeated blocked calls and raises task success for four of five models over a bare denial. On replayed denials, repair proves an admissible edit for 88 of 252 denials caused by argument values, in a median of 2,ms.

AI.tldr: Presents LeanGuard, a runtime that checks each proposed tool call against a policy written in Lean 4 before it executes; it blocks every forbidden call on Tau-Bench and reduces direct prompt-injection success on DTap from 57.9% to 5.9%.
AI.motivation: Tool-using language-model agents often execute actions that their domain policies forbid.
AI.method: Policies combine state predicates with scoped past-time temporal operators over the execution history, and evaluation is fail-closed; the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a LeanLTL semantics. A denied call is handled either by feedback, which gives the agent the violated rule and a hint, or by proof-guided repair, where Lean metaprogramming searches for a nearby admissible call without involving the model.
AI.result: On Tau-Bench with five Qwen models (0.8B to 27B), unguarded agents execute at least 33 calls that the Lean policy forbids, while LeanGuard executes none; with feedback, task success does not change significantly. On DTap, direct prompt-injection success falls from 57.9% to 5.9%, and benign success in telecom is unchanged. Repair proves an admissible edit for 88 of 252 denials caused by argument values.
AI.conclusion: Formally checked policies can enforce domain rules on agent actions at runtime, and feedback reduces repeated blocked calls while keeping or improving task success.

title: When Does Adaptive Halting Win? Selection Rules Matter in Looped Language Models
comment: 21 pages, 1 figure. Code: this https URL
summary: Looped language models can stop iterating early, and recent work shows that post-hoc readouts of the loop trajectory often rival the learned exit gate of the looped model Ouro. Such comparisons reduce each method to one operating point chosen by a selection rule. We ask whether that rule decides the outcome. On a frozen Ouro-1.4B with four loops, we compared a trained stability probe ($\pi_1$-x) with Ouro's native gate, adapted to a per-question stopping decision, in pre-registered studies; the confirmatory study was designed after an exploratory finding on development data and evaluated once on a sealed test set of 8,517 questions. In the pre-registered confirmatory comparison, which selected operating points with a bootstrap-screened 1 pp accuracy-loss rule, the probe saved more of the four-loop budget than the native gate (+0.053 gross macro saving over three benchmarks, 95% CI [+0.049, +0.057]), mostly from CommonsenseQA, where the probe's test upper bound on accuracy loss exceeded 1 pp. Under a point-only rule, a pre-specified secondary analysis on the same test set reversed the preference (-0.022 [-0.026, -0.018]), with operating points that exceeded the budget. In pre-specified secondary comparisons, the probe showed no demonstrated advantage over an untrained KL divergence between successive loops (+0.00125 [-0.0041, +0.0065]); we emphasise this result post hoc and claim no equivalence. The probe also broke its budget on one of two out-of-distribution benchmarks (3.26 pp loss on Social IQa). Savings are estimated from stored full-depth traces, not measured inference time, and our screen carries no formal risk-control guarantee. We conclude that halting methods should be compared as signals together with selection procedures, with strong untrained baselines and out-of-distribution checks.

AI.tldr: Shows that the selection rule used to pick an operating point for adaptive halting in looped language models can change which halting signal looks better; a trained stability probe beats Ouro's native gate under the pre-registered accuracy-loss rule but shows no demonstrated advantage over an untrained KL baseline.
AI.motivation: Looped language models can stop early, and post-hoc readouts of the loop trajectory are often compared with the model's learned exit gate, but each comparison reduces a method to one operating point chosen by a selection rule.
AI.method: On a frozen Ouro-1.4B with four loops, a trained stability probe is compared with Ouro's native gate, adapted to a per-question stopping decision, in pre-registered studies. The confirmatory study was designed after an exploratory finding and evaluated once on a sealed test set of 8,517 questions.
AI.result: Under the pre-registered bootstrap-screened 1 pp accuracy-loss rule, the probe saves more of the four-loop budget than the native gate (+0.053 gross macro saving, 95% CI [+0.049, +0.057]), mostly on CommonsenseQA. Under a point-only rule the preference reverses (-0.022 [-0.026, -0.018]). Against an untrained KL divergence between successive loops, the probe shows no demonstrated advantage (+0.00125 [-0.0041, +0.0065]), and it exceeds its budget on one of two out-of-distribution benchmarks (3.26 pp loss on Social IQa).
AI.conclusion: Halting methods should be compared as signals together with their selection procedures, against strong untrained baselines and with out-of-distribution checks; the savings come from stored traces and carry no formal risk-control guarantee.

title: When Rewards Depend on the Group, GRPO Plays a Tournament
summary: Rewards for diversity, coverage and distribution matching make the reward of each sampled response depend on the rest of its group, and they are now routinely optimized with GRPO and RLOO. We prove that in this setting the group-relative baseline changes the objective. The expected update equals each response's own reward gradient plus $\alpha$ times its effect on its groupmates' rewards, with $\alpha=-1/(K-1)$ for groups of size $K$, so GRPO trains every response to beat its groupmates in a zero-sum tournament. It cannot see a pairwise diversity bonus when K=2, sees less than half of it at any K, and often does worse than using no baseline at all. Setting $\alpha=+1$ gives Team-GRPO, an unbiased estimator for any group-dependent reward that works with two samples per prompt and requires no extra model calls for pairwise rewards. The theory predicts training quantitatively. It locates the fixed points of a 9B policy to within 0.02 in $\ell_1$ and predicts how concentrated trained policies become with Pearson r=0.995. On GlobalOpinionQA, GRPO collapses onto the majority answer and ends further from human opinion than the untrained model, while Team-GRPO cuts the error from $0.20$ to $0.08$. On NoveltyBench, Team-GRPO avoids the diversity collapse of GRPO and significantly improves set utility.

AI.tldr: Proves that group-relative baselines such as GRPO change the objective when rewards depend on the group, turning training into a zero-sum tournament, and proposes Team-GRPO, an unbiased estimator that cuts GlobalOpinionQA error from 0.20 to 0.08.
AI.motivation: Rewards for diversity, coverage and distribution matching depend on the rest of each sampled group, yet they are routinely optimized with GRPO and RLOO, whose group-relative baseline changes the objective in this setting.
AI.method: The expected update equals each response's own reward gradient plus alpha times its effect on its groupmates' rewards, with alpha = -1/(K-1) for groups of size K. Setting alpha = +1 gives Team-GRPO, which works with two samples per prompt and needs no extra model calls for pairwise rewards.
AI.result: The theory locates the fixed points of a 9B policy to within 0.02 in l1 and predicts how concentrated trained policies become (Pearson r = 0.995). On GlobalOpinionQA, GRPO collapses onto the majority answer and ends further from human opinion than the untrained model, while Team-GRPO cuts the error from 0.20 to 0.08. On NoveltyBench, Team-GRPO avoids GRPO's diversity collapse and significantly improves set utility.
AI.conclusion: For group-dependent rewards the baseline changes what is optimized, and an unbiased estimator matched to the reward structure avoids the diversity collapse that GRPO shows.

title: InteractionBench: Measuring Timing, Task Accuracy, Whisper and Volume, and Grounding in Real-Time Voice Systems
summary: Most benchmarks for real-time voice systems focus on one aspect, such as turn-taking, instruction following, paralinguistic control, or conversational memory, each with its own data and set of systems. We present InteractionBench, a benchmark and evaluation harness that measures four dimensions on the same systems from the same recorded user audio: conversational timing, spoken-task accuracy, whisper and volume, and groundedness in conversations of more than twenty turns. The benchmark contains 221 items per system in thirteen scenarios. Before any system runs, we fix the expected floor-control actions for spoken tasks by rule and take the expected answers from scripted dialogues. We score whispering from the audio signal. We evaluate GPT-Live, GPT-Realtime, Gemini Live, Moshi, PersonaPlex, Freeze-Omni, and a turn-based cascade in 1,519 graded runs. Among the six full-duplex systems, timing and spoken-task accuracy are rank-correlated ($\rho = 0.83$), while the cascade has the highest spoken-task score (38/50) and the second-lowest timing score. No system corrects a user's grammar within the required window. Only Gemini Live whispers on most requests (8/10). Hosted systems pass 67-88% of groundedness probes, compared with 14-35% for open full-duplex models. Timing is measured where the client hears each system, so the timing of hosted systems includes network delay: for GPT-Live, whose server reports its own clock, removing a delay of about 1.5 s lowers its timing score from 86% to 56%. We also document where the protocol differs across systems, including the text instructions.

AI.tldr: Introduces InteractionBench, which measures timing, spoken-task accuracy, whisper and volume, and groundedness on the same real-time voice systems from the same recorded audio, and finds that network delay inflates hosted systems' timing scores.
AI.motivation: Existing real-time voice benchmarks each focus on one aspect, with their own data and system sets, which makes results across dimensions hard to compare.
AI.method: The benchmark has 221 items per system in thirteen scenarios. Floor-control actions for spoken tasks are fixed by rule and expected answers come from scripted dialogues before any system runs; whispering is scored from the audio signal. Seven systems are evaluated in 1,519 graded runs: six full-duplex systems and a turn-based cascade.
AI.result: Among the full-duplex systems, timing and spoken-task accuracy are rank-correlated (rho = 0.83), and the cascade has the highest spoken-task score (38/50). No system corrects a user's grammar within the required window, and only Gemini Live whispers on most requests (8/10). Hosted systems pass 67-88% of groundedness probes, against 14-35% for open full-duplex models. Removing a delay of about 1.5 s lowers GPT-Live's timing score from 86% to 56%.
AI.conclusion: Timing measured at the client includes network delay, so the protocol differences across systems must be documented, and the four dimensions should be reported together.

title: PixelBench: Can LLMs Understand and Generate Images Pixel by Pixel?
comment: Technical report, 38 pages, 7 figures. Project page: this https URL
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate visual assets through text-based formats such as SVG and CAD, but these symbolic representations describe images using high-level primitives rather than explicit raster values. We ask whether LLMs can instead generate pixel images directly through their existing vocabulary, without a learned image tokenizer or decoder. We introduce PixelBench, a benchmark for text-to-pixel (T2P) and image-to-pixel (I2P) generation across multiple resolutions, together with a complementary pixel-understanding evaluation. Models generate an RGB color palette followed by a grid of indices specifying the palette color of each output pixel. In T2P, the strongest models produce recognizable images directly from text. In I2P, the strongest models outperform palette-matched downsampling and specialized pixelization algorithms at low resolutions. Pixel-understanding performance correlates strongly with generation performance. A resolution-scaling study shows that pixel-generation performance often improves initially before declining at high resolutions. Finally, we introduce Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which augments visual instruction tuning with caption-palette-grid trajectories. We post-train Molmo2-4B from its pretraining checkpoint by mixing general instruction data with our curated PRT data, improving performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks, indicating that explicit pixel reconstruction can provide useful auxiliary supervision.

AI.tldr: Introduces PixelBench, which tests whether LLMs can generate and understand images directly as pixel grids of palette indices; the strongest models produce recognizable images from text, and Pixel Reconstruction Tuning improves Molmo2-4B across 16 visual benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLMs generate visual assets through symbolic formats such as SVG and CAD, which describe images with high-level primitives rather than raster values; the question is whether they can produce pixels directly, without a learned image tokenizer or decoder.
AI.method: Models output an RGB colour palette followed by a grid of palette indices, evaluated on text-to-pixel and image-to-pixel generation at several resolutions, with a complementary pixel-understanding evaluation. Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT) post-trains Molmo2-4B from its pretraining checkpoint by mixing general instruction data with caption-palette-grid trajectories.
AI.result: In image-to-pixel generation at low resolutions, the strongest models outperform palette-matched downsampling and specialized pixelization algorithms. Pixel-understanding performance correlates strongly with generation performance, and generation often improves at first and then declines at high resolution. PRT improves performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Explicit pixel reconstruction can provide useful auxiliary supervision for visual instruction tuning.

title: SMILE: A Structured Multi-Agent Clinical Reasoning for Liver Ultrasound Understanding
comment: Accepted at Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) 2027
summary: Automated liver ultrasound report generation improves the diagnosis of liver diseases by producing clinically structured descriptions of anatomical and disease-related findings. However, current generative vision-language models (VLMs) often rely on a single reasoning pathway that maps ultrasound appearance directly to textual descriptions. In addition to the inherent vision-language modality gap, this design is limited for liver ultrasound because disease interpretation is constrained by subtle visual evidence, heterogeneous disease patterns, and limited paired supervision. To address these limitations, we propose SMILE, a Structured Multi-agent clInicaL rEasoning framework that uses multiple complementary specialist agents to interpret ultrasound images and consolidates their outputs through a judge-guided consensus mechanism. Our approach employs three specialized agents: an image interpretation agent for morphological descriptions, a clinical-stage reasoning agent, and a visual question answering (VQA) agent for targeted queries. These agent responses are then aggregated and scrutinized by a judge VLM using a consensus filtering prompt to produce a unified, clinically coherent output. Across a public liver ultrasound dataset and an internal clinical dataset, SMILE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art VLMs, achieving up to 19.0\% improvement in ROUGE-1 and 18.8\% improvement in clinical F1-score, while reaching VQA F1-scores of 0.82 and 0.65 on public and internal datasets, respectively. These results demonstrate the potential of SMILE for data-scarce and limited-supervision clinical settings. Our models, datasets, and code are available \href{this https URL}{here}.

AI.tldr: Proposes SMILE, a multi-agent framework for liver ultrasound report generation in which image, clinical-stage and VQA specialist agents are consolidated by a judge VLM, with improvements of up to 19.0% in ROUGE-1 and 18.8% in clinical F1 over state-of-the-art VLMs.
AI.motivation: Generative vision-language models map ultrasound appearance directly to text through a single reasoning pathway, which is limited by subtle visual evidence, heterogeneous disease patterns and scarce paired supervision.
AI.method: Three specialist agents produce morphological descriptions, clinical-stage reasoning and answers to targeted VQA queries. A judge VLM aggregates and scrutinizes these outputs with a consensus filtering prompt to produce one clinically coherent report.
