summary: Decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev answer typed questions about a text (yes/no, multiple choice, or an ordinal score) with calibrated probabilities in a single forward pass and without generating text, which makes them an inexpensive candidate for LLM-as-a-judge workloads. We evaluate 14 System-1 decision models, selected with a pre-stated protocol, against four generative judges (Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-5.6 with and without reasoning, and Claude Opus 5.5 with thinking) on eleven established judge benchmarks. Five of the 14 are statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 without reasoning on all five pairwise and best-of-4 benchmarks, and the two strongest, DReX-Max and d1-ultra, are significantly more accurate than Haiku on JudgeBench, LLMBar and RewardBench 2. Conditioned on a reference answer generated once per prompt, eleven models reach 90.3-93.4% on JudgeBench, statistically indistinguishable from Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 with reasoning, and on PPE best-of-16 every reference-guided System-1 judge matches GPT-5.6 with reasoning at roughly one-sixteenth of its cost per prompt. Several System-1 judges are better calibrated than every generative judge and correlate more strongly with human helpfulness ratings. Robustness to instructions injected into the judged response is a property of the individual model rather than of the System-1 design: an appended note to the evaluator reverses 0-5% of the correct verdicts of five models but 17-49% for the other nine. Two general System-1 leaderboards that contain no judging tasks predict judging accuracy (Pearson r = 0.95-0.96), a well-calibrated System-1 first stage matches Opus on LLMBar while escalating 17% of items, and same-size controls show that the correctness deficit of a 4B decision model is a reasoning gap rather than a size gap.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates 14 System-1 decision models against four generative judges on eleven judge benchmarks, finding that several are statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 without reasoning and that reference-guided System-1 judges match GPT-5.6 with reasoning at about one-sixteenth of its cost per prompt.
AI.motivation: Decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev give calibrated probabilities in a single forward pass without generating text, making them candidates for LLM-as-a-judge workloads, but their judging quality is unknown.
AI.method: Fourteen System-1 decision models, selected with a pre-stated protocol, are compared with Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-5.6 with and without reasoning, and Claude Opus 5.5 with thinking on eleven established judge benchmarks. Conditioning on a reference answer generated once per prompt is evaluated, and robustness is tested with appended instructions injected into the judged response.
AI.result: Five of the 14 are statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 without reasoning on all five pairwise and best-of-4 benchmarks, and DReX-Max and d1-ultra are significantly more accurate than Haiku on JudgeBench, LLMBar and RewardBench 2. With a reference answer, eleven models reach 90.3% to 93.4% on JudgeBench, statistically indistinguishable from Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 with reasoning. Several System-1 judges are better calibrated than every generative judge. An appended evaluator note reverses 0% to 5% of correct verdicts for five models but 17% to 49% for the other nine.
AI.conclusion: System-1 judges can replace generative judges in some settings, but robustness to injected instructions is a property of the individual model rather than the design.

title: Low-Margin Branch Points in Deterministic LLM Deliberatio
summary: Deterministic multi-agent LLM deliberation can exactly re- play a fixed transcript, yet exact replay alone does not test local resistance to controlled internal interventions. Because each response becomes context for later agents, a changed greedy token can redirect a transcript-mediated execution. We present a white-box audit of this local failure mode in a five-agent committee under greedy decoding. We prospectively select low- and high-margin token positions, require exact no-op re- play, inject norm-relative residual displacements, and measure first transcript divergence within ten generated tokens. Low- margin positions are more branch-sensitive than high-margin controls, while matched margin-reducing gradient directions branch substantially more often than margin-increasing con- trols. We then continue selected realized branches through the committee to distinguish textual persistence from preference and final-decision changes. The contribution is a controlled audit for local branch susceptibility in this specified protocol, not an estimate of deployment frequency, decision correct- ness, or a phenomenon unique to multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: The paper audits local branch sensitivity in a deterministic five-agent LLM committee by injecting controlled residual displacements at chosen token positions and measuring first transcript divergence. Low-margin positions branch more readily than high-margin controls, and margin-reducing directions branch more often than margin-increasing ones.
AI.motivation: Exact replay of a deterministic multi-agent transcript does not test local resistance to internal interventions, and a changed greedy token can redirect the whole execution since each response becomes context for later agents.
AI.method: Low- and high-margin token positions are selected prospectively, exact no-op replay is required, and norm-relative residual displacements are injected. First transcript divergence is measured within ten generated tokens, and selected branches are continued through the committee to distinguish textual persistence from preference and final-decision changes.
AI.result: Low-margin positions are more branch-sensitive than high-margin controls, and matched margin-reducing gradient directions branch substantially more often than margin-increasing controls.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a controlled audit of local branch susceptibility under this protocol, and does not estimate deployment frequency, decision correctness or a phenomenon unique to multi-agent systems.

title: Governing Equations of Human Sleep Macro-Structure:Symbolic Discovery from 1,106 Nights
summary: Human sleep is organized into a small number of cycles per night: deep sleep dominates early cycles, REM lengthens toward morning, and light sleep clusters at cycle boundaries. These regularities have long been described qualitatively but never distilled into closed-form laws from large-scale data. A total of 1,106 nights (Sleep-EDF 153 + SHHS 953) are segmented into REM-anchored cycles, and four cycle-indexed statistics follow simple closed-form equations: cycle length declines nearly linearly (R^2=0.996), REM duration follows an inverted U (R^2=0.873), deep-sleep (N3) run length decays exponentially (R^2=0.987) with a time constant of 2.94 cycles, consistent with the homeostatic Process S of the two-process model, and light-sleep (N1) run length follows a U shape (R^2=0.956), confirming a "long-short-long" pattern across the night. The laws are reproduced by per-night differentiable fitting (142/142 and 773/773 nights converge), by unconstrained symbolic regression (PySR), and by a 500-night generative synthesizer built from them. Their robustness is established against the two main methodological threats: bootstrap CIs computed by resampling whole nights (1,000 replications) exclude zero for every shape term, and a five-level scan of the REM-merge segmentation threshold preserves every qualitative form. These appear to be the first closed-form laws governing the macro-structure of sleep, distilled and tested across an age-mixed sample (healthy young adults and community-based older adults).

AI.tldr: Symbolic regression and differentiable fitting on 1,106 nights of sleep data yield closed-form laws for the macro-structure of sleep cycles, including a near-linear decline in cycle length and an exponential decay of N3 run length. The laws are reported to be robust to bootstrap resampling and segmentation threshold changes.
AI.motivation: Sleep macro-structure is described qualitatively but has never been distilled into closed-form laws from large-scale data.
AI.method: 1,106 nights (Sleep-EDF 153 and SHHS 953) are segmented into REM-anchored cycles, and four cycle-indexed statistics are fit with closed-form equations. The laws are checked by per-night differentiable fitting, unconstrained symbolic regression (PySR) and a 500-night generative synthesizer built from them. Robustness is tested with whole-night bootstrap CIs (1,000 replications) and a five-level scan of the REM-merge threshold.
AI.result: Cycle length declines nearly linearly (R^2 = 0.996), REM duration follows an inverted U (R^2 = 0.873), N3 run length decays exponentially (R^2 = 0.987) with a time constant of 2.94 cycles, and N1 run length follows a U shape (R^2 = 0.956). Per-night fits converge for 142/142 and 773/773 nights, and bootstrap CIs exclude zero for every shape term.
AI.conclusion: The N3 decay is consistent with the homeostatic Process S of the two-process model, and the laws appear to be the first closed-form description of sleep macro-structure across an age-mixed sample.

title: WAR-CRAFT: Refining Web API Recommendations through Requirement Auditing
summary: Web API recommenders return a set of APIs for a mashup request but do not check it against provider documentation, the main public evidence of an API's capabilities. The set can therefore contain unsupported or redundant APIs and miss requested capabilities. Filling every apparent gap does not fix this, because a gap may already be served, may not need its own API, or may have no documented provider. We study post-recommendation refinement, which revises a frozen recommender's output using only the request, the catalog, and provider documentation. We propose WAR-CRAFT, which treats refinement as three decisions. An LLM removes unsupported or subsumed APIs by judging candidates jointly, then audits the remaining set against a requirement checklist derived from the request. For each uncovered requirement, a fine-tuned catalog-constrained Resolver proposes a catalog API or abstains, and an independent documentation check admits only supported proposals. On ProgrammableWeb with 7 heterogeneous upstream recommenders, WAR-CRAFT raises mean SetF1 from 0.558 to 0.644, above the strongest of 5 refinement baselines (62.5%), and roughly halves functional redundancy (0.127 to 0.065) without changing mean functional coverage. Gains range from +2.2 points on generative recommenders to +18.2 on fixed-cutoff rankers. At matched set sizes, WAR-CRAFT still outperforms truncating the upstream output, so the gain is not explained by set-size calibration alone. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: WAR-CRAFT refines the output of a frozen Web API recommender by removing unsupported or redundant APIs and filling uncovered requirements only with documented catalog APIs. On ProgrammableWeb it raises mean SetF1 from 0.558 to 0.644, above the strongest of five refinement baselines.
AI.motivation: Web API recommenders do not check their sets against provider documentation, so the output can contain unsupported or redundant APIs and miss requested capabilities. Filling every apparent gap is not a fix, since a gap may already be served or need no API.
AI.method: An LLM removes unsupported or subsumed APIs by judging candidates jointly and then audits the set against a requirement checklist derived from the request. For each uncovered requirement, a fine-tuned catalog-constrained Resolver proposes a catalog API or abstains, and an independent documentation check admits only supported proposals.
AI.result: Across seven heterogeneous upstream recommenders on ProgrammableWeb, WAR-CRAFT raises mean SetF1 from 0.558 to 0.644, above the strongest of five refinement baselines (62.5%), and roughly halves functional redundancy (0.127 to 0.065) without changing mean functional coverage. Gains range from +2.2 points on generative recommenders to +18.2 on fixed-cutoff rankers, and it still outperforms truncating the upstream output at matched set sizes.
AI.conclusion: Auditing recommendations against provider documentation improves API sets beyond what set-size calibration alone explains.

title: Evolving Scientific Intelligence: From Fragmented Evidence to Distributed Experimental Loops
summary: Scientific discovery advances when evidence from different investigations is brought into contact. Yet paper-centric communication leaves experimental results fragmented, delayed, or unreported, creating a "scientific memory wall" between growing computational capabilities and the evidence accessible to AI systems. We envision a different dynamic: in a network of intelligent laboratories, a failed or overlooked experiment in one domain could trigger a hypothesis in another, whose testing generates evidence that stimulates further investigations. Such chains of information collision and empirical validation could transform isolated discovery loops into a cumulative scientific process. We propose Evolving Scientific Intelligence (ESI), an architectural blueprint for enabling these evidence-driven chain reactions. ESI preserves experimental records in shared, computable scientific memory, where evidence from different domains can be recombined into testable hypotheses. It jointly selects candidates and evaluation methods according to scientific value, reliability, and cost, then coordinates physical tests across distributed experimental nodes. Their feedback revises hypotheses and evaluators, while slower meta-control reassesses research objectives and decision criteria to guard against self-reinforcing errors and misguided optimization. We call for an Information Manhattan Project to build the infrastructure for scientific intelligence that evolves through experimentally grounded chains of discovery.

AI.tldr: Evolving Scientific Intelligence (ESI) is an architectural blueprint for networks of intelligent laboratories in which evidence from failed or overlooked experiments in one domain triggers hypotheses in another. It proposes shared computable scientific memory and coordinated physical testing across distributed experimental nodes.
AI.motivation: Paper-centric communication leaves experimental results fragmented, delayed or unreported, creating a scientific memory wall between computational capability and the evidence AI systems can access.
AI.method: ESI preserves experimental records in shared, computable scientific memory where evidence from different domains can be recombined into testable hypotheses. It jointly selects candidates and evaluation methods by scientific value, reliability and cost, coordinates tests across distributed nodes, and uses slower meta-control to reassess objectives and guard against self-reinforcing errors.
AI.result: The abstract is a vision and architecture proposal and reports no experimental results.
AI.conclusion: The authors call for an Information Manhattan Project to build the infrastructure for scientific intelligence that evolves through experimentally grounded chains of discovery.

title: State-Aware Activation Recomputation with Replay Contracts and Selective Preservation
summary: Activation recomputation saves accelerator memory by replaying forward segments during the backward pass, but replay is only correct if it sees the state the original forward pass saw. Mutable buffers, aliased bytes and random-generator state can change in between, so re-executing unchanged code can differentiate a different computation. We make this state explicit. A versioned replay contract specifies what replay must restore, and a joint planner chooses, per segment, between activation retention, whole-buffer snapshots and selective-region preservation, charging each option its measured memory and recovery cost. Independent derivative and byte-level checks validate the contract, and a Torch/JAX cohort retains all 5,900 execution records, including matches, rejections and divergences. On frozen sparse-write H100 workloads, each measured over fifty fresh processes, joint planning reduces paired step time by 18.16% against a correctly costed eager/whole planner at a 44 GiB budget (approximate 97.5% ratio interval $[.8172,.8195]$). At 32 GiB, where the eager/whole planner has no feasible static policy, joint planning is 4.98% faster than fixed regions at 29.94 rather than 26.20 GiB. A complete CIFAR-100 dense-queue application runs seven methods for 100 encoder and 25 probe epochs at six training seeds, with byte-identical test scores within each seed. There, joint planning uses 22.41% more allocated memory than whole snapshots, with a process-time geometric-mean ratio of 1.0080 (seed range $[.9845,1.0191]$). Together, the results map where selective preservation pays off: sparse writes with large activations benefit, while in the dense-queue workload whole snapshots use less allocated memory.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes state-aware activation recomputation, which makes replay contracts explicit so that recomputed segments see the same mutable state as the original forward pass. Joint planning cuts paired step time by 18.16% against a costed eager/whole planner at a 44 GiB budget on sparse-write H100 workloads.
AI.motivation: Activation recomputation is correct only if replay sees the state the original forward pass saw, but mutable buffers, aliased bytes and random-generator state can change in between, so re-executing unchanged code can differentiate a different computation.
AI.method: A versioned replay contract specifies what replay must restore. A joint planner chooses per segment among activation retention, whole-buffer snapshots and selective-region preservation, charging each its measured memory and recovery cost. Independent derivative and byte-level checks validate the contract, and a cohort of 5,900 execution records is retained.
AI.result: On frozen sparse-write H100 workloads, joint planning reduces paired step time by 18.16% against a correctly costed eager/whole planner at 44 GiB (ratio interval [.8172, .8195]). At 32 GiB, where the eager/whole planner has no feasible static policy, joint planning is 4.98% faster than fixed regions at 29.94 GiB rather than 26.20 GiB. On CIFAR-100 dense-queue training, joint planning uses 22.41% more allocated memory than whole snapshots.
AI.conclusion: Selective preservation pays off for sparse writes with large activations, while whole snapshots use less allocated memory in the dense-queue workload.

title: X-World 1.6: Building Controllable Virtual Cities with World Models
summary: Deploying generative world models for end-to-end closed-loop evaluation and policy learning requires precise scenario control, consistent observations, and sustained generation quality during extended interactions. This report presents \emph{X-World~1.6}, advancing X-World~1.0 toward a more reliable and versatile driving simulator. The upgraded base model offers finer-grained control over traffic semantics, including traffic lights and road markings, together with improved spatial consistency across cameras. Virtual City capabilities broaden scenario construction through a family of models conditioned on diverse 2D and 3D references, including support for generating multi-camera future videos from a single image. An enhanced post-training framework enables efficient causal, few-step generation with stronger temporal coherence, better quality retention over longer rollouts, and improved alignment with human preferences. We also introduce a dedicated evaluation suite to support systematic assessment and guide model iteration. Together, these upgrades expand the scenarios X-World can simulate and improve the efficiency and reliability of its generated observations, supporting broader use in autonomous-driving development.

AI.tldr: X-World 1.6 is an upgraded generative world model for controllable virtual driving scenes, adding finer traffic-semantic control, multi-camera consistency and few-step causal generation. The report also introduces a dedicated evaluation suite for guiding model iteration.
AI.motivation: Closed-loop evaluation and policy learning with generative world models need precise scenario control, consistent observations and sustained quality over long rollouts.
AI.method: The base model gives finer control over traffic semantics such as traffic lights and road markings. Virtual City models are conditioned on diverse 2D and 3D references, including generating multi-camera future videos from one image. Post-training enables efficient causal, few-step generation with better temporal coherence and alignment with human preferences.
AI.result: The abstract reports improved spatial consistency across cameras, stronger temporal coherence and better quality retention over longer rollouts, and it introduces an evaluation suite, but it gives no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The upgrades expand the scenarios X-World can simulate and improve the reliability of generated observations for autonomous-driving development.

title: Editing the Goal: Per-Token SAE Steering and Its Depth Limits in $π_{0.5}$
comment: Accepted to the Science of Physical AI Safety (SPAIS) Workshop at CoRL 2026. 6 pages, 2 figures
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recovered interpretable, causally relevant features in robot foundation models (RFMs) such as $\pi_{0.5}$ (arXiv:2603.19183, arXiv:2603.19233). SAE features on individual instruction tokens are less interpretable than timestep-pooled ones (arXiv:2603.19183), and whether they can redirect a robot's goal remains untested. We show that replacing the SAE features of a single goal word with those of an alternative goal word, leaving the instruction text unchanged, steers $\pi_{0.5}$-LIBERO into completing the alternative task. At layer 0, BatchTopK feature swaps redirect behavior in up to 20/20 rollouts in a scene where random-feature swaps redirect none, with success varying across six scenes in two LIBERO suites and across layers. The effect depends on SAE architecture: word-selected Matryoshka edits largely do not outperform random ones. SAEs are also not required. Adding a fixed difference-in-means vector at twice its natural magnitude redirects 8-10/10 rollouts. Layer-wise activation patching shows that goal-word edits remain effective up to layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity, and up to layer 13 in both cases when patching also covers camera tokens. These results are proof of existence in an RFM in simulation and an initial map of how deep goal-redirecting edits remain effective. Visit this https URL for video rollouts.

AI.tldr: Replacing the sparse autoencoder (SAE) features of a single goal word in the instruction redirects the robot policy pi0.5 in LIBERO to an alternative task, and the paper maps how deep in the network such goal-redirecting edits stay effective.
AI.motivation: SAE features on individual instruction tokens are less interpretable than timestep-pooled ones, and it was untested whether such features can redirect a robot foundation model's goal.
AI.method: Swap the SAE features of one goal word with those of an alternative goal word while leaving the instruction text unchanged, using BatchTopK and Matryoshka SAEs at layer 0, and also test a fixed difference-in-means vector scaled to twice its natural magnitude, plus layer-wise activation patching that also covers camera tokens.
AI.result: BatchTopK feature swaps redirect behavior in up to 20/20 rollouts in one scene, where random-feature swaps redirect none, with success varying across six scenes in two LIBERO suites; word-selected Matryoshka edits largely do not outperform random ones; the difference-in-means vector redirects 8-10/10 rollouts; goal-word edits remain effective up to layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity, and up to layer 13 in both cases when camera tokens are also patched.
AI.conclusion: The results are a proof of existence that goal-redirecting edits work in a robot foundation model in simulation, and they give an initial map of how deep such edits remain effective; SAEs are not required for the effect.

title: Conversational Interaction for LLM-Based Clinical Text-to-SQL: A User Study with Healthcare Professionals
summary: Conversational text-to-SQL interfaces could give healthcare professionals natural-language access to electronic health record (EHR) data, but evidence for their real-world usability remains limited: prior evaluations have relied largely on curated benchmarks with fully specified questions or on simulated users. We report a user study in which 14 physicians who regularly work with EHR data used both a single-turn and a conversational multi-turn text-to-SQL interface over the MIMIC-IV database in a within-subjects design; dialogue analyses additionally drew on interaction logs from 21 healthcare professionals across the main study and two pilot studies. The conversational interface was consistently favored: mean System Usability Scale scores rose from 68.2, near the industry average, to 85.9 (p<0.001), with significant advantages across technology-acceptance constructs including performance expectancy, effort expectancy, self-efficacy, and behavioral intention. In post-study forced-choice comparisons, 93% of participants reported greater overall satisfaction with the conversational interface, 86% preferred it for real-world adoption, and 71% trusted its results more; no participant preferred or trusted the single-turn interface more. Turn-level analysis of 425 logged user turns showed that freely composed queries triggered clarification requests in 24.8% of cases versus 1.8% for predefined, fully specified questions, and 64.3% of clarification episodes stemmed from EHR- or clinical-domain knowledge. Conversational interaction is a practical prerequisite, rather than a convenience, for natural-language EHR access. The frequent need for clarification in realistic clinical queries further underscores the importance of conversational interfaces, while benchmark-style evaluation can substantially underrepresent the ambiguity of real clinical use.

AI.tldr: A user study with 14 physicians finds that a conversational multi-turn text-to-SQL interface over MIMIC-IV is consistently preferred to a single-turn interface and gets higher usability scores.
AI.motivation: Evidence for real-world usability of clinical text-to-SQL is limited, since prior evaluations relied on curated benchmarks with fully specified questions or on simulated users.
AI.method: Within-subjects comparison of a single-turn and a conversational multi-turn text-to-SQL interface over the MIMIC-IV database, with dialogue analysis drawing on interaction logs from 21 healthcare professionals across the main study and two pilot studies, using System Usability Scale and technology-acceptance constructs.
AI.result: Mean System Usability Scale scores rose from 68.2 to 85.9 (p<0.001), with significant gains in performance expectancy, effort expectancy, self-efficacy and behavioral intention; 93% reported greater satisfaction, 86% preferred the conversational interface for adoption and 71% trusted its results more; of 425 logged user turns, freely composed queries triggered clarification requests in 24.8% of cases versus 1.8% for predefined fully specified questions, and 64.3% of clarification episodes stemmed from EHR or clinical-domain knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Conversational interaction is a practical prerequisite for natural-language EHR access, and benchmark-style evaluation can substantially underrepresent the ambiguity of real clinical queries.

title: Trail: Accurate Local Smart Home Control Using Decision Models
summary: Natural-language driven smart home control remains challenging: cloud-hosted Large Language Models (LLMs) raise privacy concerns, while local Small Language Models (SLMs) can generate invalid actions or misinterpret requests. We introduce Trail (Typed Registry-Anchored Inference for Language commands in Smart Homes), a fully local framework that replaces open-ended command generation with hierarchical typed decisions. Trail exploits the natural structure of a home's action space, selecting a room, device, and operation from candidates derived from the runtime device registry. This ensures valid actions while enabling confidence-based abstention when requests cannot be reliably resolved. We also design a structured memory module that uses typed decisions to support user preferences, device references, and multi-turn interactions. To evaluate Trail, we extend HomeBench and generate three datasets: Trek-Base, which tests natural-language variation; Trek-Robust, which evaluates robustness to changes in the home and its description; and Trek-Memory, which assesses conversational memory across multi-turn interactions. Trail achieves 85.3% accuracy on Trek-Robust versus 69.8% for a finetuned Qwen3.5-4B baseline, while remaining competitive on Trek-Base requests. With memory, Trail resolves 75.6% of the requests that depend on earlier turns, compared with 42.5% for the finetuned baseline given conversation history.

AI.tldr: Trail is a fully local smart home control framework that replaces open-ended command generation with hierarchical typed decisions over room, device and operation candidates drawn from the device registry, with confidence-based abstention.
AI.motivation: Cloud LLMs raise privacy concerns, while local small language models can generate invalid actions or misinterpret requests.
AI.method: Trail selects a room, device and operation from candidates derived from the runtime device registry, abstains when confidence is low, and uses a structured memory module that stores typed decisions for user preferences, device references and multi-turn context; the authors extend HomeBench to build Trek-Base, Trek-Robust and Trek-Memory datasets.
AI.result: Trail reaches 85.3% accuracy on Trek-Robust versus 69.8% for a finetuned Qwen3.5-4B baseline, remains competitive on Trek-Base, and with memory resolves 75.6% of requests that depend on earlier turns versus 42.5% for the finetuned baseline given conversation history.
AI.conclusion: Constraining the decision space to typed candidates from the registry allows a local model to produce valid actions and handle multi-turn requests more accurately than a finetuned small model.

title: LM6-CastBench: A Geometry-Aware Simulation Dataset for Transient Thermal Prediction in LM6 Sand Casting
summary: Transient thermal fields during solidification connect casting process conditions and cooling behaviour to the formation of defect-prone regions in aluminum cast ings. Repeatedly solving this thermal problem across geometries and process conditions is computationally expensive, motivating data-driven surrogate models. However, existing machine-learning studies on casting thermal behaviour rely on study-specific simulation databases that do not support reproducible geometry-level benchmarking. We introduce LM6-CastBench, an open simulation dataset for geometry-aware learning of transient thermal fields in LM6 aluminum sand casting, combining three geometry families, ten variants per family, five pouring tempera tures, and three mould temperatures (450 geometry-process cases in total). Each case retains CAD geometry, unstructured mesh connectivity, spatial descriptors, process metadata, and time-resolved nodal temperatures. We benchmark a point wise MLP against a spatially structured U-Net under geometry-level data splits; the U-Net reduces temperature-field errors by a large margin, with the biggest gains on geometries with localized features and abrupt section changes. LM6-CastBench gives researchers a reproducible dataset and benchmark for geometry-aware surro gate modelling of casting thermal behaviour.

AI.tldr: LM6-CastBench is an open simulation dataset of transient thermal fields in LM6 aluminum sand casting, covering 450 geometry-process cases, with benchmarks of a pointwise MLP and a spatially structured U-Net.
AI.motivation: Existing machine-learning studies of casting thermal behaviour use study-specific simulation databases, which do not support reproducible geometry-level benchmarking of surrogate models.
AI.method: The dataset combines three geometry families with ten variants each, five pouring temperatures and three mould temperatures, and each case keeps CAD geometry, unstructured mesh connectivity, spatial descriptors, process metadata and time-resolved nodal temperatures; models are evaluated under geometry-level data splits.
AI.result: The U-Net reduces temperature-field errors by a large margin relative to the pointwise MLP, with the largest gains on geometries with localized features and abrupt section changes.
AI.conclusion: The dataset and benchmark give researchers a reproducible basis for geometry-aware surrogate modelling of casting thermal behaviour.

title: XLA from the Trenches: Correctness on TPU Workloads at Scale
summary: Accelerating modern foundational models has pushed domain-specific compilers toward increasingly complex, multi-tiered optimization pipelines. However, this heavy optimization focus introduces delicate tradeoffs between peak execution performance and correctness. Subtle codegen defects can trigger numerical degradation and memory or buffer corruption, invalidating multi-million-dollar training runs and degrading live serving quality without raising obvious compiler errors. In this paper, we present a battle-tested methodology for verifying and triaging Google's XLA:TPU compiler at hyperscale. We leverage fuzzing techniques, combining synthetic program generation with real production traces, while orchestrating AI agent swarms to autonomously generate stress tests, reproduce failures, and draft fixes. To pinpoint root causes in full workloads, we pair this with a hierarchical differential pipeline that bisects large graphs down to individual failing operations inside fused kernels. Deployed in production, our framework has already driven the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs (with 103 additional findings under review), from which we distill pragmatic lessons learned.

AI.tldr: The paper describes a production methodology for finding correctness bugs in Google's XLA:TPU compiler, combining fuzzing, AI agent swarms and a hierarchical differential pipeline, which has led to the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs.
AI.motivation: Aggressive optimization in domain-specific compilers can introduce subtle codegen defects that cause numerical degradation or buffer corruption without raising compiler errors, which can invalidate large training runs and degrade serving quality.
AI.method: The approach combines fuzzing based on synthetic program generation and real production traces, orchestrates AI agent swarms to generate stress tests, reproduce failures and draft fixes, and uses a hierarchical differential pipeline that bisects large graphs down to individual failing operations inside fused kernels.
AI.result: The deployed framework has driven the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs, with 103 additional findings under review.
AI.conclusion: The authors distill pragmatic lessons from operating this verification and triage methodology at hyperscale.

title: Autonomous Analysis of Thermoelectric Materials Big Data by Multi-Agentic AI and Construction of a Knowledge Base and Specialized AI
comment: 74 pages (28 pages main text with 5 figures; 46 pages Supplementary Information with 7 Supplementary Notes, 10 Supplementary Tables and 3 Supplementary Figures). Analysis records, Supplementary Data 1-5 and code are available from the corresponding authors upon request
summary: Extracting knowledge from large databases of experimental materials data requires repeated analyses and reusable records of their choices and results. We developed Multi-Agentic AI (MAA), a multi-agent system in which AI agents with distinct roles analyze experimental thermoelectric data under predefined instructions and quality checks, saving analysis records traceable to their sources. In four experiments varying theme and cycle counts, we measured what accumulated in these records. In the largest experiment (100 analyses across 10 themes and 10 cycles), concept co-occurrences were concentrated within themes, vocabulary was shared across themes and some relation descriptions were first detected in later cycles. A specialized AI that searches this experiment's knowledge bases and reads their analysis records answered materials questions with cited sources. Retrospective checks, including tracing an answer generated with a preliminary corpus back to the source data, exposed errors: traceability makes errors findable but not absent.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent system (MAA) analyses experimental thermoelectric materials data with traceable analysis records, and a specialized AI that searches the resulting knowledge bases answers materials questions with cited sources.
AI.motivation: Extracting knowledge from large experimental materials databases requires repeated analyses and reusable, traceable records of the choices and results behind them.
AI.method: AI agents with distinct roles analyse experimental thermoelectric data under predefined instructions and quality checks, saving analysis records traceable to their sources; four experiments vary theme and cycle counts, and a specialized AI reads the knowledge bases and their records to answer questions.
AI.result: In the largest experiment (100 analyses across 10 themes and 10 cycles), concept co-occurrences concentrated within themes, vocabulary was shared across themes, and some relation descriptions were first detected in later cycles; retrospective checks, including tracing an answer back to its source data, exposed errors.
AI.conclusion: Traceability makes errors findable but does not make them absent.

title: TopoQuant: Topological Framework to Characterize Behavioral Shifts in Quantized Large Language Models
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the com putational cost of large language models (LLMs), but it can introduce internal structural and behavioral changes that are not captured by traditional metrics such as accuracy and per plexity. We present TopoQuant, a topological framework that uses topological data analysis (TDA) to quantify structural drift in self-attention weights and relate it to behavioral changes in quantized LLMs. Across four LLM families and multiple quantization levels, we show that topological drift remains stable at moderate compression levels but increases sharply below 4 bit precision, closely tracking declines in attention agreement. Our results reveal a strong relationship between topological drift and attention agreement, indicating that structural changes in model parameters closely reflect behavioral degradation under quantization. We further demonstrate that topological features can accurately predict attention consistency using lightweight machine learning models, achieving R2 scores of up to 0.85. Predicting attention agreement enables efficient assessment of be havioral consistency in quantized LLMs, allowing quantization induced degradation to be detected without running expensive downstream tasks. The results indicate that topological drift pro vides an efficient early-warning signal for quantization-induced degradation and can help identify safe compression limits without extensive downstream evaluation.

AI.tldr: TopoQuant uses topological data analysis to measure structural drift in self-attention weights of quantized LLMs and shows that this drift tracks behavioural degradation, rising sharply below 4-bit precision.
AI.motivation: Post-training quantization reduces LLM cost but can change internal structure and behaviour in ways that accuracy and perplexity do not capture.
AI.method: Topological drift in self-attention weights is quantified with topological data analysis across four LLM families and multiple quantization levels, and lightweight machine learning models predict attention agreement from topological features.
AI.result: Topological drift stays stable at moderate compression but increases sharply below 4-bit precision, closely tracking declines in attention agreement; topological features predict attention consistency with R2 scores of up to 0.85.
AI.conclusion: Topological drift can serve as an efficient early-warning signal for quantization-induced degradation and help identify safe compression limits without extensive downstream evaluation.

title: Evidence-grounded large language models guide perovskite solar cell design and optimization
comment: 67 pages: 18-page main manuscript with 4 figures, plus 49-page Supplementary Information with 24 figures and 3 tables
summary: Using large language models to interpret experimental evidence, design discriminating experiments and formulate well-supported mechanistic explanations remains a central challenge in materials research. Here we establish PSM-Bench, an 800-question benchmark developed by perovskite researchers to evaluate scientific reasoning in perovskite photovoltaics. We also introduce OpenPerov, an expert-informed language-model framework that learns from expert-calibrated evidence records reconstructed from 4,532 articles; these records link experimental strategies, controls and observations to mechanistic interpretations. Structured-evidence adaptation outperformed conventional question-answer training, and OpenPerov Flash ranked first among 13 closed-book systems. OpenPerov Pro raised Scientific Mastery further, from 87.6 to 89.1, by revising selected passages with retrieved evidence. On questions derived from subsequent studies, both models also outscored expert-authored answers. In an experimental test of self-assembled monolayer design, OpenPerov selected a K analogue that outperformed the Na analogue preferred by experts. Devices incorporating the selected contact reached a power conversion efficiency of 27.05% and retained 96.74% of their steady-state reference efficiency after 1,000 h of dark thermal ageing at 85 $^\circ$C. These results show that reconstructed scientific reasoning provides an effective basis for building domain models that interpret experiments and inform materials design.

AI.tldr: PSM-Bench is an 800-question perovskite photovoltaics benchmark, and OpenPerov is an evidence-grounded language model framework trained on evidence records from 4,532 articles that ranks first among closed-book systems and proposes a selected contact yielding a 27.05% device efficiency.
AI.motivation: Using LLMs to interpret experimental evidence, design discriminating experiments and build mechanistic explanations remains a central challenge in materials research.
AI.method: The authors build PSM-Bench with perovskite researchers and train OpenPerov on expert-calibrated evidence records that link experimental strategies, controls and observations to mechanistic interpretations, comparing structured-evidence adaptation with conventional question-answer training; OpenPerov Pro further revises selected passages with retrieved evidence.
AI.result: OpenPerov Flash ranks first among 13 closed-book systems, and OpenPerov Pro raises Scientific Mastery from 87.6 to 89.1; both models outscore expert-authored answers on questions derived from subsequent studies; in a self-assembled monolayer test, OpenPerov selected a K analogue over the Na analogue preferred by experts, and devices with it reach 27.05% power conversion efficiency and retain 96.74% of steady-state efficiency after 1,000 h of dark thermal ageing at 85 °C.
AI.conclusion: Reconstructed scientific reasoning provides an effective basis for domain models that interpret experiments and inform materials design.

title: FastAgent: A Physics-Aware FastFluent-to-Fluent Workflow for Rapid CFD Screening and Industrial Steam Dewaxing Design
comment: 47 pages, 6 main-text figures. Supplementary Information included
summary: Industrial computational fluid dynamics (CFD) becomes costly when complex geometries, long transients and coupled physics must be evaluated across large design spaces. We introduce FastAgent, a physics-aware campaign controller built around FastFluent, a lightweight numerical engine for rapid physical screening. FastFluent supplies stage-specific fields and diagnostics; FastAgent allocates physical models, numerical resolution and simulation horizons by the active quantities of interest (QoIs), while returned Fluent discrepancies update subsequent decisions. Across six public CFD benchmark campaigns, the framework reduces normalised worst-QoI error by 5.68-99.14% and accelerates decision-relevant computation by factors of 1.53-15.36 relative to a matched Generic Agent control. Applied to high-pressure steam dewaxing in investment casting, FastAgent identifies nonuniform condensation heating as the dominant startup mechanism and separates rapid risk-window localisation from high-fidelity melt-completion confirmation. The rapid route requires 81.39% fewer cell-time updates than a fine-grid, small-time-step reference. Structural analysis localises fracture at the observed blade edge. Screening 131,072 outlet layouts and selectively evaluating candidates with Fluent and Abaqus identifies Sparse-6, which reduces simulated crack opening by 96.0% and connected crack extent by 66.7% relative to the Original design. These results demonstrate how rapid numerical evidence and adaptive fidelity control connect large CFD search spaces to mechanism-guided industrial design.

AI.tldr: FastAgent is a physics-aware campaign controller built on the lightweight FastFluent numerical engine that allocates physical models, resolution and horizons by quantities of interest, and is applied to steam dewaxing design in investment casting.
AI.motivation: Industrial CFD is costly when complex geometries, long transients and coupled physics must be evaluated across large design spaces.
AI.method: FastFluent provides stage-specific fields and diagnostics for rapid screening; FastAgent allocates physical models, numerical resolution and simulation horizons by the active quantities of interest, and uses Fluent discrepancies to update later decisions; it is compared with a matched Generic Agent control and, in the case study, screens 131,072 outlet layouts before selectively evaluating candidates with Fluent and Abaqus.
AI.result: Across six public CFD benchmark campaigns, the framework reduces normalised worst-QoI error by 5.68-99.14% and accelerates decision-relevant computation by factors of 1.53-15.36; the rapid route needs 81.39% fewer cell-time updates than a fine-grid, small-time-step reference; the selected Sparse-6 layout reduces simulated crack opening by 96.0% and connected crack extent by 66.7% relative to the Original design.
AI.conclusion: Rapid numerical evidence and adaptive fidelity control can connect large CFD search spaces to mechanism-guided industrial design.

title: Designing Behavioral Profiles for Language Model Simulation of Out-of-Distribution Human Behavior
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but which descriptions of people improve prediction when experimental designs change remains unclear. We develop a framework that draws candidate behavioral features from the literature and constructs profiles from earlier human experiments. A profile-generation LLM assigns feature values from observed actions, messages, and surveys; a separate LLM simulates behavior using these profiles. By comparing simulated and observed outcomes in the learning data, we select profile contents through forward feature selection, adding features while they improve prediction. We then evaluate the selected contents without modification against outcomes from new participants under new designs. Across 616 public-goods games, 144 multi-party bargaining games, and 1,480 generalized 11-20 money-request designs, leading one-feature profiles predict human outcome distributions better than no profile or general-purpose personas. Profiles with more features provide no clear additional benefit, and features' relative predictive value largely persists across learning and validation. Using profiles from one game family to simulate another produces uneven gains and can make predictions less accurate than simulations without profiles. The framework makes the choice of behavioral information a testable part of simulation design, helping researchers assess which descriptions remain useful as experimental conditions change.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework for selecting behavioural profile contents, chosen by forward feature selection on earlier human experiments, that improve LLM simulations of human behaviour under new experimental designs.
AI.motivation: It is unclear which descriptions of people improve LLM simulation of human behaviour when experimental designs change.
AI.method: Candidate behavioural features are drawn from the literature and profiles are generated by an LLM from observed actions, messages and surveys; a separate LLM simulates behaviour with these profiles, and features are added by forward selection while they improve prediction on learning data, then evaluated unchanged on new participants and designs.
AI.result: Across 616 public-goods games, 144 multi-party bargaining games and 1,480 generalized 11-20 money-request designs, leading one-feature profiles predict human outcome distributions better than no profile or general-purpose personas; profiles with more features give no clear extra benefit; profiles from one game family give uneven gains and can be less accurate than no profile when applied to another.
AI.conclusion: The choice of behavioural information becomes a testable part of simulation design, helping researchers judge which descriptions remain useful as conditions change.

title: Can Jev Improve Demonstration Retrieval for In-Context Learning?
summary: Demonstration selection plays a crucial role in the effectiveness of in-context learning (ICL) for large language models (LLMs). Extensive research has explored various retrieval strategies to identify informative demonstrations and improve downstream performance. Recently, the emergence of Jev, a decision-oriented language model capable of producing probabilistic judgments, offers a new perspective on evaluating demonstration utility. This motivates us to investigate a fundamental question: Can Jev improve demonstration retrieval for in-context learning? In this paper, we demonstrate that Jev can effectively enhance demonstration retrieval by directly assessing the utility of candidate demonstrations for a given query. However, applying Jev to large-scale retrieval introduces substantial computational overhead, as each candidate requires an additional decision-making inference. To address this limitation, we propose a simple yet effective knowledge distillation approach that transfers Jev's utility estimation capability to a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP). By learning to approximate Jev's probabilistic judgments, the distilled model enables efficient demonstration ranking while maintaining competitive retrieval performance. Our study highlights the potential of decision-oriented language models for demonstration selection and provides an efficient framework for integrating their decision-making capabilities into ICL.

AI.tldr: The paper asks whether Jev, a decision-oriented language model that produces probabilistic judgments, can improve demonstration retrieval for in-context learning, and distills its utility estimates into a lightweight MLP to make this scalable.
AI.motivation: Demonstration selection strongly affects in-context learning, but applying Jev directly to large-scale retrieval requires an extra decision inference for every candidate, which is computationally expensive.
AI.method: Jev is used to directly assess the utility of candidate demonstrations for a query, and a knowledge distillation approach trains a multilayer perceptron to approximate Jev's probabilistic judgments for efficient ranking.
AI.result: The abstract states that Jev can effectively enhance demonstration retrieval and that the distilled MLP enables efficient ranking while maintaining competitive retrieval performance; no numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Decision-oriented language models show potential for demonstration selection, and their decision-making can be integrated into in-context learning efficiently via distillation.

title: Inherited or Learned? Backdoor Selectivity in Distilled Language Models
summary: Distillation is a routine step in building small language models, and a backdoored teacher can pass its backdoor to the student. We study what a student inherits when the backdoor is a rare string that triggers a fixed refusal. Keeping the trigger fixed, we vary only where it appears, at a random word boundary or appended to the instruction, and compare teachers and students on the exact trigger, six control strings and clean inputs. Across Qwen2.5, Llama 3.2 and Gemma 3, with 5% of transfer prompts triggered, randomly inserted triggers become less selective after distillation in all nine teacher-student pipelines, while appended triggers gain selectivity in Qwen and Llama and change little in Gemma. Students trained on the same prompts without a teacher show that much of this is not inherited. Llama and Gemma students learn an appended backdoor from the 150 poisoned examples alone, and only Qwen's 0.5B student needs the teacher. The data also sets where the trigger works. Gemma teachers respond to it anywhere, but their students only when it is appended. Audits should compare teacher and student on the same inputs, probe several trigger positions and include a student trained without the teacher.

AI.tldr: Studying a rare-string backdoor that triggers a fixed refusal, the paper finds that distillation makes randomly placed triggers less selective in all nine teacher-student pipelines, while appended triggers become more selective in Qwen and Llama, and that much of the behaviour is learned by students without a teacher.
AI.motivation: A backdoored teacher can pass its backdoor to a student during distillation, but it is unclear what the student actually inherits and how trigger position affects this.
AI.method: The trigger is kept fixed while its position varies, either at a random word boundary or appended to the instruction; teachers and students from Qwen2.5, Llama 3.2 and Gemma 3 are compared on the exact trigger, six control strings and clean inputs, with 5% of transfer prompts triggered; students are also trained on the same prompts without a teacher.
AI.result: Randomly inserted triggers become less selective after distillation in all nine pipelines, while appended triggers gain selectivity in Qwen and Llama and change little in Gemma; Llama and Gemma students learn an appended backdoor from 150 poisoned examples alone, and only Qwen's 0.5B student needs the teacher; Gemma teachers respond to the trigger anywhere, but their students only when it is appended.
AI.conclusion: Backdoor audits should compare teacher and student on the same inputs, probe several trigger positions and include a student trained without the teacher.

title: Reading Between the Chapters: A Graph-Free RAG Rebuilt With AI and Human Feedback
summary: Many questions about a book can only be answered by connecting passages chapters apart, such as a cough heard three times across a horse's life. We introduce CrossChapterQA, 1,853 such questions over 14 public-domain books. Each question lists the two to six chapters it needs (spanning half the book at the median) and the relation linking them, cites evidence from each, and has two independent reference answers graded blind. We use it to build LadderRAG, which indexes a book as passages, summaries and book-level cards for about $0.41 and answers a question for under a cent. Its first version failed mostly at retrieval. We redesigned it four times, steered by an LLM judge's verdicts and our analyses of failed answers: a design-level counterpart of RLAIF and RLHF in which feedback changes the architecture, not model weights. We also report the two redesigns that made answers worse. On the 191 questions its first version got wrong, the final version retrieves over twice as many required chapters on held-out books (recall 0.36 to 0.79), and ten annotators rate its answers 6.5/10 on average (764 ratings).

AI.tldr: CrossChapterQA is a benchmark of 1,853 questions over 14 public-domain books that require linking distant chapters, and LadderRAG, a graph-free RAG system redesigned four times using LLM-judge feedback, improves recall of required chapters on held-out books.
AI.motivation: Many book questions require connecting passages chapters apart, which existing retrieval approaches handle poorly.
AI.method: Each question lists the two to six chapters needed and the relation linking them, with evidence and two blind-graded reference answers; LadderRAG indexes a book as passages, summaries and book-level cards, and its architecture was revised four times guided by an LLM judge's verdicts and analyses of failed answers.
AI.result: On the 191 questions the first version got wrong, the final version raises chapter recall from 0.36 to 0.79 on held-out books, and ten annotators rate its answers 6.5/10 on average (764 ratings); indexing costs about $0.41 per book and answering costs under a cent per question; two redesigns made answers worse.
AI.conclusion: Feedback can change the retrieval architecture rather than model weights, a design-level analogue of RLAIF and RLHF.

title: Designing Informative Actions: Action Construction for Long-Horizon Research Agents
summary: Large language model agents support automated scientific research by connecting literature analysis and planning with experimentation. Evaluating which action an agent selects does not establish which experiment its instruction specifies, because omitted interventions or replication counts leave consequential choices to the executor. We introduce a reading-set framework for evaluating action construction under a common cost rule. Across 30 synthetic states, complete-design requests increase affordable efficiency by 465.98% and 327.91% relative to the action-name baseline in the two model families, respectively. An author-constructed research-action evaluation dataset provides 60 scenarios for complementary judgment evaluation. On this dataset, the scenario-level information-per-cost measure has a mean within-scenario correlation of 0.733 with judgments from 18 human participants. The framework makes design specification and execution ambiguity measurable, providing a reproducible basis for assessing how research agents translate scientific intent into informative, budget-feasible experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a reading-set framework for evaluating how research agents construct experimental actions under a common cost rule, showing that complete-design requests improve affordable efficiency substantially over an action-name baseline.
AI.motivation: Evaluating which action an agent selects does not reveal which experiment its instruction specifies, because omitted interventions or replication counts leave consequential choices to the executor.
AI.method: The reading-set framework evaluates action construction under a common cost rule across 30 synthetic states, and an author-constructed dataset of 60 research-action scenarios is used for judgment evaluation against 18 human participants.
AI.result: Complete-design requests increase affordable efficiency by 465.98% and 327.91% relative to the action-name baseline in the two model families; on the 60 scenarios, the scenario-level information-per-cost measure has a mean within-scenario correlation of 0.733 with human judgments.
AI.conclusion: The framework makes design specification and execution ambiguity measurable and provides a reproducible basis for judging whether research agents turn scientific intent into informative, budget-feasible experiments.

title: Decision-Centric Research: A Calibrated Decision Model and Benchmark for Scientific Agents
summary: Scientific agents make consequential choices about evidence, next actions and research strategy, but choices embedded in generated text are difficult to evaluate independently. Decision-Centric Research (DCR) is introduced to make individual choices the common unit of supervision, prediction and evaluation through typed predictions over an explicit Research State. DCR defines 24 decision types, ten of which are instantiated in the Research Decision Benchmark (RD-Bench) of 2,000 rule-generated cases. The Decision-Centric Research Model (DCRM) shares a candidate-token readout across types to produce answers and option probabilities in one forward pass. Under a held-out research-domain split, a 0.6B DCRM (state-aware) achieves 89.4% Top-1 accuracy, compared with 27.8% for DCRM (question-only) trained with the same recipe and 36.4% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. All 30 type-seed comparisons against DCRM (question-only) are significant after Holm correction. After held-out calibration, the resulting prediction sets contain a mean of 1.515 candidates at 97.1% empirical label coverage, reducing mean set size by 57.4% relative to DCRM (question-only) at similar coverage. These results establish a compact state-aware decision layer with accurate typed prediction and an inspectable uncertainty interface.

AI.tldr: Decision-Centric Research (DCR) makes individual choices the unit of supervision and evaluation through typed predictions over an explicit Research State, and a 0.6B state-aware model (DCRM) reaches 89.4% Top-1 accuracy on the RD-Bench benchmark.
AI.motivation: Choices embedded in the text generated by scientific agents are difficult to evaluate independently.
AI.method: DCR defines 24 decision types, ten of which are instantiated in RD-Bench with 2,000 rule-generated cases; DCRM shares a candidate-token readout across types to produce answers and option probabilities in one forward pass, and prediction sets are calibrated on held-out data.
AI.result: Under a held-out research-domain split, the 0.6B DCRM (state-aware) reaches 89.4% Top-1 accuracy, versus 27.8% for the question-only DCRM trained with the same recipe and 36.4% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash; all 30 type-seed comparisons against the question-only model are significant after Holm correction; after calibration, prediction sets average 1.515 candidates at 97.1% empirical coverage, reducing mean set size by 57.4% relative to the question-only model.
AI.conclusion: A compact state-aware decision layer can provide accurate typed prediction together with an inspectable uncertainty interface.

title: Who Schedules Agent Memory? A Sidecar Approach to Long-Horizon Tasks
summary: As large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks, memory has become an important component for supporting sustained decision-making and action. Existing methods primarily focus on memory storage, updating, and retrieval, but often overlook how memory scheduling affects task execution: the main agent must identify memory needs, initiate retrieval, and wait for results while advancing the task, increasing both scheduling burden and execution time. To address this problem, we propose MemSidecar, which decouples memory scheduling from task execution through two independently selectable modes. Hooks directly delivers bound memory to the main agent when execution events match predefined conditions. Foresight uses an independent agent to predict potential queries, retrieve results in parallel, and store them in a cache, delivering matching and valid results when actual requests arrive. Hooks and Foresight achieve scores of 41.23% and 44.34% on MCP-Persona, respectively, while effectively reducing execution costs and latency and improving the efficiency of long-horizon agent execution.

AI.tldr: MemSidecar separates memory scheduling from task execution for LLM agents through two selectable modes, Hooks and Foresight, which reach 41.23% and 44.34% on MCP-Persona respectively.
AI.motivation: Existing memory methods focus on storage, updating and retrieval but ignore the scheduling burden and added execution time when the main agent must decide when to retrieve memory and wait for results.
AI.method: In Hooks mode, bound memory is delivered to the main agent when predefined execution events match conditions; in Foresight mode, an independent agent predicts potential queries, retrieves results in parallel and stores them in a cache for delivery when real requests arrive.
AI.result: Hooks and Foresight achieve scores of 41.23% and 44.34% on MCP-Persona, respectively, while reducing execution cost and latency.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling memory scheduling from execution can reduce cost and latency and improve the efficiency of long-horizon agent tasks.

title: One Offset, Two Directions: Baseline Adjustment via Subgroup Offsets
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) estimates advantages against the within-prompt mean reward, a baseline shared across the group. In practice, rollouts within a prompt are not always homogeneous, differing in their solution strategies and reasoning trajectories, along which they may group into subgroups. We further find that these heterogeneous subgroups may exhibit distinct reward distributions. The global baseline, however, collapses them onto a single credit axis, where the credit reflects neither a rollout's standing within its subgroup nor the subgroup's standing relative to the rest. We therefore study how to adjust the baseline when the rollouts of a prompt fall into heterogeneous subgroups. We define the \emph{subgroup offset} as the deviation of a subgroup mean from the global mean, and shift the baseline along it by a single signed coefficient $\lambda$. The sign of $\lambda$ yields two opposing directions: \emph{Alignment} ($\lambda{>}0$) adds the offset to the baseline, drawing credit toward a rollout's relative position within its subgroup; \emph{Contrast} ($\lambda{<}0$) subtracts it, drawing a rollout's credit toward the relative quality of the subgroup it belongs to. The adjustment acts on the baseline alone, leaving the reward signal and the optimization objective unchanged. In this work, we induce subgroups from strategies, grouping rollouts that share a strategy into the same subgroup. We evaluate both directions on Qwen3-8B-Base and Olmo3-7B-Base across four competition-level math benchmarks, against a $\lambda{=}0$ anchor that shares the same strategy-conditioned sampling and differs only in the baseline. Against this anchor each direction yields modest but consistent gains in multi-sample coverage, with Contrast the stronger of the two.

AI.tldr: The paper adjusts the GRPO baseline by a signed subgroup offset, where a positive coefficient gives Alignment and a negative one gives Contrast, and both directions yield modest but consistent gains in multi-sample coverage, with Contrast stronger.
AI.motivation: The global within-prompt mean baseline in GRPO merges rollouts from heterogeneous solution-strategy subgroups that have distinct reward distributions, so credit reflects neither a rollout's standing within its subgroup nor the subgroup's standing overall.
AI.method: The subgroup offset is the deviation of a subgroup mean from the global mean, and the baseline is shifted by this offset with a single signed coefficient lambda; subgroups are induced by solution strategy, and only the baseline changes, leaving the reward and objective untouched.
AI.result: Against a lambda=0 anchor with the same strategy-conditioned sampling, each direction gives modest but consistent gains in multi-sample coverage on four competition-level math benchmarks with Qwen3-8B-Base and Olmo3-7B-Base, with Contrast the stronger of the two.
AI.conclusion: Adjusting the baseline along subgroup offsets is a simple lever for credit assignment in GRPO, with the sign of the coefficient selecting between two credit-allocation directions.

title: A Tool in the Forward Pass: Frozen Tape Modules as Layers of a Small Language Model
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, 9 tables. Code, configurations, results and frozen modules: this https URL
summary: Calling a tool through generated text adds decoding steps, even when the computation itself is short. We study an alternative: a small neural module that runs inside a language model's forward pass. A learned writer turns hidden states into a symbolic tape, a short sequence of discrete symbols that encodes the computation. The module, trained separately and then frozen, reduces the tape to a result, and a learned reader returns that result to the model. We evaluate arithmetic and object tracking in gemma-3-1b-it. With a writer trained on labelled tapes, the layer answers all 750 items of BIG-Bench Hard's tracking shuffled objects correctly. At seven people it needs about 1/10 of the GPU kernel time of a text-tool baseline that uses the same host model and exact code, with accuracy 1.00 against 0.99. The writer can also be learned from answers alone, guided by a hand-written copying prior, but less reliably: 5 of 6 runs succeed in the 1B host and 2 of 4 in the 4B host. Two independently trained layers keep their task accuracy when attached to one model, and a learned gate keeps them silent on the tested general-text and look-alike prompts. The results support a narrow use case: a bounded computation that returns one symbol can avoid the decoding cost of a textual tool call. Extracting the right input reliably, and deciding when to act, remain the main open problems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a frozen tape module that runs inside a small language model's forward pass, turning hidden states into a short symbolic tape that a learned reader converts back, which answers tracking tasks in gemma-3-1b-it with about one tenth of the GPU kernel time of a text-tool baseline.
AI.motivation: Calling a tool through generated text adds decoding steps even when the computation is short.
AI.method: A learned writer maps hidden states to a symbolic tape, a frozen module reduces the tape to a result, and a learned reader returns the result to the model; the paper evaluates arithmetic and object tracking in gemma-3-1b-it and also tests writers learned from answers alone with a hand-written copying prior, together with a learned gate that keeps the layers silent on general-text and look-alike prompts.
AI.result: With a writer trained on labelled tapes, the layer answers all 750 BIG-Bench Hard tracking shuffled objects items correctly; at seven people it needs about 1/10 of the GPU kernel time of the text-tool baseline, with accuracy 1.00 against 0.99; writers learned from answers alone succeed in 5 of 6 runs on the 1B host and 2 of 4 on the 4B host; two independently trained layers keep their accuracy on one model.
AI.conclusion: The approach suits only narrow cases where a bounded computation returns one symbol, and reliable input extraction and deciding when to act remain the main open problems.

title: BridgeDock: Taming Generative Co-Folding Prior for Molecular Docking with Diffusion Bridge
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 29 pages, 4 figures, including appendices
summary: Molecular docking aims to predict the three-dimensional structure of a protein-ligand complex; in the conventional structure-based setting, it is conditioned on an input protein structure and ligand, often starting from an apo receptor in flexible docking or a holo receptor in rigid docking. Recent co-folding models exemplified by AlphaFold 3 achieve strong accuracy in protein-ligand complex prediction, but they typically generate complexes from sequence-derived inputs and therefore do not directly use apo structures as structural priors in docking, leading to a larger conformational search space and weaker robustness in difficult or few-step settings. We present BridgeDock, a framework that adapts pretrained co-folding backbones to flexible docking by modeling the apo-to-holo transition as a diffusion bridge, allowing generation from the initial protein-ligand state rather than from Gaussian noise. To make this bridge formulation compatible with pretrained denoisers, we introduce an alignment mechanism that maps bridge states to the original denoising schedule of the pretrained model. Experiments on standard flexible docking benchmarks show that BridgeDock consistently outperforms strong co-folding baselines. Moreover, BridgeDock is computationally efficient at inference time and remains effective even with very few denoising steps.

AI.tldr: BridgeDock adapts pretrained co-folding models such as AlphaFold 3 to flexible docking by modelling the apo-to-holo transition as a diffusion bridge, which outperforms strong co-folding baselines on standard flexible docking benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Co-folding models generate complexes from sequence-derived inputs and do not use apo structures as priors, which leads to a larger conformational search space and weaker robustness in difficult or few-step settings.
AI.method: The method models generation as a diffusion bridge starting from the initial protein-ligand state rather than Gaussian noise, and adds an alignment mechanism that maps bridge states to the original denoising schedule of the pretrained model.
AI.result: BridgeDock consistently outperforms strong co-folding baselines on standard flexible docking benchmarks and remains effective with very few denoising steps; it is also computationally efficient at inference.
AI.conclusion: Adapting pretrained co-folding backbones through a bridge formulation makes them effective for flexible docking with efficient inference.

title: A Discrete-Time Variational Objective for Degenerate Diffusion and Equivalence to Flow Matching
summary: Diffusion models and more recently Flow models have widespread application. In this work we consider degenerate Diffusion models in which the per-step generator is deterministic. We construct a modified variational framework and show a formal equivalence between Flow models and Degenerate Diffusion models. For our discrete-time variational objective we show that the optimal degenerate generator recovers the data distribution in the limit of an infinite number of generator steps. Our work therefore provides a unified perspective, showing that discrete-time implementations of flow matching and the discrete-time Degenerate Diffusion model can be considered within the same simple variational framework, removing the need for the continuous-time machinery normally used to justify flow matching models.

AI.tldr: The paper considers degenerate diffusion models with deterministic per-step generators, constructs a discrete-time variational objective, and shows a formal equivalence between flow models and degenerate diffusion models.
AI.motivation: Flow matching is usually justified with continuous-time machinery, and a unified discrete-time view of diffusion and flow models is missing.
AI.method: A modified variational framework is built for degenerate diffusion with a deterministic per-step generator, and a formal equivalence to flow models is established.
AI.result: The optimal degenerate generator recovers the data distribution in the limit of infinitely many generator steps, and discrete-time flow matching and degenerate diffusion fall within the same variational framework.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a unified perspective that removes the need for continuous-time machinery to justify flow matching models.

title: AI Data Analysis: A New Approach - Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis
comment: Code and data: this https URL
summary: AI data analysis today is three fragmented worlds: LLMs understand semantics but cannot compute; BI aggregates precisely but is stateless; ML processes large-scale data on a stateful kernel but lacks semantics. This paper proposes a combination mechanism, named Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis, that fills a still-open gap - the multi-engine joint context: the data context is embedded into LLM conversational analysis, where the LLM serves only as the semantic, reasoning, and orchestration layer (not computation) and connects four engines through the 1M context window - Python and R ML kernels, SQL over relational databases, Cypher over graph databases - yielding two multiplications, "semantics and precise computation" and "relational and graph", under enterprise-grade governance. The novelty is a four-dimensional coordinate system: horizontal (engine kinds), vertical (state flow - the watershed), spatial (business generalization), temporal (iterative convergence); a deterministic grounding method (one-shot injection of this http URL + this http URL, M+S) carries the spatial and temporal dimensions. Empirically, all four dimensions are substantiated: horizontally, four engines are quantified - SQL, Cypher (96.5% on CypherBench movie), ML in Python and R (TabReD weather); vertically, state flows across engines and grounding is reused across kernels; spatially, SQL generalizes across three business databases - AdventureWorks 91.3%, financial 95.3%, formula_1 94.6% (average), about 20-23 points above single-shot SOTA 74.45%; temporally, accuracy converges monotonically as notes accumulate. The core invariant - the separation of semantics from computation plus a cross-data-domain persistent context - does not expire as LLMs and agents evolve or engine forms change.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis, in which an LLM acts only as the semantic and orchestration layer over Python and R ML kernels, SQL and Cypher engines, with reported gains on text-to-SQL and graph query benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLMs understand semantics but cannot compute, BI tools aggregate precisely but are stateless, and ML kernels process data with state but lack semantics, leaving a gap in multi-engine joint context.
AI.method: Data context is embedded into LLM conversational analysis with a 1M-token context window, connecting Python and R ML kernels, SQL over relational databases and Cypher over graph databases; a four-dimensional coordinate system (engine kinds, state flow, business generalization, iterative convergence) and a deterministic one-shot grounding injection are used.
AI.result: The abstract reports Cypher at 96.5% on CypherBench movie, SQL accuracy of 91.3% on AdventureWorks, 95.3% on a financial database and 94.6% on formula_1, about 20-23 points above a single-shot state-of-the-art of 74.45%, and monotonic accuracy convergence as notes accumulate; ML results are reported on TabReD weather.
AI.conclusion: Separating semantics from computation together with a persistent cross-domain context is presented as an invariant that does not expire as LLMs and engines evolve.

title: VCoT-SQL: Enhancing Text-to-SQL Generation through Dual Chain-of-Thought Validation Training
summary: Open-source LLMs provide a flexible alternative to closed-source models for Text-to-SQL but still struggle with complex queries. Finetuning with chain-of-thought (CoT) data improves reasoning, yet standard datasets lack CoT annotations, requiring synthetic generation. Existing synthesis methods only verify the final answer, allowing flawed reasoning steps to corrupt the training data.
