We propose VCoT-SQL, a framework that improves Text-to-SQL generation through intermediate-step validated CoT supervision and a dedicated SQL validator, which enables small open-source models to outperform frontier closed-source models. VCoT-SQL trains two complementary models on curated reasoning traces: an SQL generator using clause-level CoT templates where reasoning steps are verified via execution and schema alignment checks, and an SQL validator using diagnostic CoT templates to detect syntactic, semantic, and type level errors. We further design a hierarchical schema filtering pipeline that integrates and refines complementary retrieval strategies to distill relevant database elements. VCoT-SQL achieves 66.82% execution accuracy on challenging dataset BIRD dev and 86.8% on Spider test, improving the base 7B model by 7% on BIRD. Notably, our CoT synthesis relies on 7B models yet outperforms methods that use 72B-scale or even proprietary closed source teachers for data generation, demonstrating that rigorous step-level validation can be more effective than scaling up teacher model size. Our dataset and code are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: VCoT-SQL trains a 7B text-to-SQL generator and a SQL validator on chain-of-thought traces whose intermediate steps are verified, reaching 66.82% execution accuracy on BIRD dev and 86.8% on Spider test.
AI.motivation: Standard text-to-SQL datasets lack chain-of-thought annotations, and existing synthesis methods verify only the final answer, so flawed reasoning steps can corrupt the training data.
AI.method: The generator uses clause-level CoT templates whose steps are verified by execution and schema alignment checks; the validator uses diagnostic CoT templates to detect syntactic, semantic and type-level errors; a hierarchical schema filtering pipeline combines complementary retrieval strategies.
AI.result: VCoT-SQL reaches 66.82% execution accuracy on BIRD dev and 86.8% on Spider test, improving the base 7B model by 7% on BIRD; its 7B-based CoT synthesis outperforms methods using 72B-scale or proprietary teachers for data generation.
AI.conclusion: Step-level validation can be more effective than scaling up the teacher model, letting small open-source models outperform frontier closed-source models on text-to-SQL.

title: AdKnob: Ad Intensity Control and Labeling for LLM-Native Advertising
summary: Large language model (LLM)-native advertising has emerged as a viable monetization channel as LLM service providers seek sustainable revenue streams. However, integrating native ads into LLM responses introduces two largely understudied challenges: (1) controlling ad intensity -- how prominently advertising content appears -- and (2) ad labeling -- identifying which segments of the generated text constitute advertising. We propose AdKnob, a framework jointly addressing both challenges. For ad intensity control, we introduce new ad control tokens without pretrained semantic associations and align the model via direct preference optimization to generate ads at each desired level. For ad labeling, we propose an attention rollout-based attribution mechanism that identifies ad segments by tracing their attribution to input ad-related tokens, requiring no additional inference cost. We further construct MI-KnobSet, the first multi-level ad intensity preference dataset for LLM-native ads. Experiments across six LLMs and human evaluations show that AdKnob achieves uniformly spaced ad intensities where baselines collapse to a narrow range, achieves the highest ad labeling accuracy while being over 500x faster than the strongest baseline, and is preferred over baselines by human evaluators up to 89.6% of the time.

AI.tldr: AdKnob controls ad intensity in LLM responses with new control tokens aligned by direct preference optimization, and labels ad segments with an attention-rollout attribution that adds no inference cost.
AI.motivation: LLM-native advertising raises two understudied challenges: controlling how prominently ads appear and identifying which generated segments are advertising.
AI.method: New ad control tokens without pretrained semantic associations are aligned with direct preference optimization to generate ads at each desired level; ad segments are identified by attention rollout that traces attribution to input ad-related tokens; the authors also build MI-KnobSet, a multi-level ad intensity preference dataset.
AI.result: Across six LLMs and human evaluations, AdKnob reaches uniformly spaced ad intensities where baselines collapse to a narrow range, achieves the highest ad labeling accuracy while running over 500x faster than the strongest baseline, and is preferred by human evaluators up to 89.6% of the time.
AI.conclusion: Joint control and labeling of ad intensity is feasible for LLM-native advertising, with better calibration of intensity levels and faster labeling than the baselines.

title: Can Agentic AI Undermine Its Own Assurance Loop? Closed-Loop Dependency Assurance for Cognitive Network Digital Twins
summary: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Network Digital Twins (NDTs) are increasingly combined to form Cognitive Digital Twins (CDTs) that translate operational intents into network changes and support closed-loop management. However, a network change may achieve its intended objective while disrupting the monitoring or recovery mechanisms needed for subsequent decisions. For example, a service may be rerouted while its latency-monitoring traffic continues along the original path, producing measurements that no longer reflect the service's performance. We propose Closed-Loop Dependency Assurance (CLDA), an assurance mechanism that augments agentic AI-enabled NDTs with dependency-aware validation. In our framework, an agentic AI planner generates and refines network plans, while the NDT evaluates the projected network outcomes of these plans. CLDA extends this analysis using a Loop Dependency Graph (LDG) that connects service requirements to monitoring mechanisms, forwarding paths, failure domains, and recovery prerequisites. CLDA projects candidate actions onto these dependencies, checks intermediate states of multistep plans, and supports deterministic make-before-break repairs using temporary monitoring mechanisms. Unlike the Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner, CLDA uses explicit, deterministic rules for assurance decisions and repair. We evaluate CLDA through controlled reconfigurations, a 240-trial LLM-based planning campaign, and live network execution. A separate synthetic study examines deterministic assurance scalability across network models representing up to 1,024 routers.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Closed-Loop Dependency Assurance (CLDA), which adds dependency-aware, deterministic validation to agentic AI planning on network digital twins so that a network change does not break the monitoring or recovery mechanisms needed for later decisions.
AI.motivation: A network change can meet its objective while disrupting monitoring or recovery, for example rerouting a service while its latency-monitoring traffic stays on the original path, which yields misleading measurements.
AI.method: A Loop Dependency Graph links service requirements to monitoring mechanisms, forwarding paths, failure domains and recovery prerequisites; CLDA projects candidate actions onto these dependencies, checks intermediate states of multistep plans and performs make-before-break repairs with temporary monitoring, using explicit deterministic rules rather than an LLM.
AI.result: CLDA is evaluated through controlled reconfigurations, a 240-trial LLM-based planning campaign and live network execution, and a separate synthetic study examines assurance scalability across network models with up to 1,024 routers; the abstract gives no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic dependency-aware assurance can check and repair agentic AI network plans, and the authors report that it scales to networks of up to 1,024 routers in synthetic tests.

title: Benchmarking Machine-Learning Classifiers for Neoantigen Immunogenicity Prediction and the Limits of SHAP Interpretability
summary: Personalized cancer vaccines require prioritizing, among hundreds of candidate mutant peptides, the few that will induce a T-cell response. This study asks what general-purpose machine learning achieves on that task, and whether the features such models identify as important can be trusted. We make three contributions. The first is a benchmark of sixty models: twelve supervised classifier families, each in five configurations, evaluated on the Immunogenic Tumor Specific Neoantigen database (ITSNdb; 199 experimentally validated neoantigens, 129 immunogenic and 70 non-immunogenic). All sixty are compared under one stratified k-fold cross-validation protocol, in which the data used to choose a configuration are never the data used to score it. The second is an interpretability study that combines SHAP with feature ablation. The third is a shuffled-label control that tests whether a SHAP value has been earned. Two results follow, and both run against current practice. First, the classical linear models lead the ranking. The gradient-boosted ensembles and neural networks that dominate recent work bring no advantage. Second, SHAP can fail on high-cardinality categorical features. Ablation establishes the presenting HLA allele as the dominant input and the source gene as dispensable. SHAP reports the opposite, assigning 68.7% to 81.7% of its total value to the source gene in every model that gives each gene its own weight. Shuffling the gene labels at random among the peptides resolves the contradiction: the meaningless column earns the same SHAP value as the real one. That value measures only that ITSNdb contains 173 genes for 199 peptides. We therefore recommend that SHAP values for high-cardinality categorical annotations in cohorts of this size always be reported against such a shuffled-label control, and we describe one in full.

AI.tldr: A benchmark of sixty classifier configurations on 199 neoantigens from ITSNdb finds that linear models lead, and shows that SHAP values can be misleading for high-cardinality gene features, which a shuffled-label control exposes.
AI.motivation: Personalized cancer vaccines need to prioritize the few mutant peptides that induce a T-cell response, and it is unclear what general-purpose machine learning achieves on this task or whether the features it highlights can be trusted.
AI.method: Twelve supervised classifier families, each in five configurations, are compared under one stratified k-fold cross-validation protocol on ITSNdb (129 immunogenic and 70 non-immunogenic peptides), with SHAP combined with feature ablation and a shuffled-label control for SHAP values.
AI.result: The classical linear models lead the ranking, with gradient-boosted ensembles and neural networks bringing no advantage; ablation identifies the presenting HLA allele as the dominant input and the source gene as dispensable, whereas SHAP assigns 68.7% to 81.7% of its total value to the source gene; shuffling gene labels gives the meaningless column the same SHAP value as the real one.
AI.conclusion: SHAP values for high-cardinality categorical annotations in cohorts of this size should always be reported against a shuffled-label control.

title: Pulse: Long-Horizon Tasks Need Streaming Personalization
summary: Large language model agents increasingly undertake complex, long-horizon tasks that benefit from sustained personalized support through long-term memory. Existing memory-augmented methods retrieve and use memory primarily from the initial request, with limited awareness of ongoing execution and emerging personalization needs. Agents may therefore overlook user preferences and project constraints during multistep tasks. We propose Pulse, a streaming personalization method for long-horizon tasks. An independent, lightweight memory agent continuously monitors execution, identifies emerging personalization needs and potential preference conflicts, and uses user and project memories to provide targeted interventions at appropriate stages. Reinforcement learning optimizes when and how the memory agent intervenes, improving the timeliness and accuracy of personalized support. Pulse scores 71.9% on $\pi$-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, achieving the highest overall scores among the compared methods on both datasets while improving task execution efficiency.

AI.tldr: Pulse is a streaming personalization method in which a lightweight memory agent, trained with reinforcement learning, monitors long-horizon execution and intervenes with user and project memories, scoring 71.9% on pi-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona.
AI.motivation: Existing memory-augmented methods retrieve memory mainly from the initial request and miss emerging personalization needs and preference conflicts during multistep tasks.
AI.method: An independent lightweight memory agent continuously monitors execution, identifies emerging personalization needs and potential preference conflicts, and uses reinforcement learning to optimize when and how it intervenes.
AI.result: Pulse scores 71.9% on pi-Bench and 46.4% on MCP-Persona, achieving the highest overall scores among the compared methods on both datasets while improving task execution efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Streaming, timed interventions during execution are presented as an effective way to deliver personalization in long-horizon agent tasks.

title: GURU: A Hierarchical Neuro-Symbolic Multi-Agent System for Verification-Aware Automation of Mission-Critical Digital Engineering and Operations
summary: An AI can find a safe action faster than any human, but it must never decide what counts as safe. We present GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical digital engineering and operations, built on one partition of authority: learned models propose, rank, and accelerate; a symbolic rules engine checks every consequential action against hard limits before it executes; and validated physics confirms and decides. GURU runs a workflow as a closed control loop, with Navigation, Action, and Planning agents sharing one Common Internal Language and one training factory. Nuclear, aviation, and national-security guidance now requires this pattern; a harnessed language model keeps the model at the center, GURU puts a validated reference there. In computational fluid dynamics, the workflow raised the converged-simulation rate on unseen aircraft geometries from under 1 percent to 74 percent over 100 single-attempt cases, ran 54 live cases to Mach 6 on three facilities, and an ablation put the symbolic layer at 13 points of boundary-layer capture. Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters raised ParaView control success from 55 to 75 percent. In space domain awareness, where a language model cannot be trusted to decide, a frozen self-supervised world model under validated propagation scored highest of five methods at conjunction risk, including fully fine-tuned language models, with several-times-lower seed variance: the trustworthy design gives up nothing in accuracy, and the recipe transferred to reactor anomaly detection. A radar-to-avoidance debris pipeline was demonstrated in stages on a 2026 reentry; the hierarchy coordinates simulated teams of 200 aircraft. Training scaled near-linearly past 1,000 Aurora nodes and ran at 8,000. The approach extends to a control-grade microreactor digital twin with validated physics, not a learned model, as the safety basis.

AI.tldr: GURU is a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system in which learned models propose and accelerate, a symbolic rules engine checks each consequential action against hard limits, and validated physics makes the final decision, with reported gains in CFD convergence and space domain awareness.
AI.motivation: Mission-critical digital engineering and operations need AI that can speed up search without deciding what counts as safe, and existing LLM-centred designs keep the model at the centre of decisions.
AI.method: Navigation, Action and Planning agents share one Common Internal Language and one training factory and run a workflow as a closed control loop; the symbolic layer checks every consequential action before execution, and validated physics confirms outcomes.
AI.result: In CFD, the converged-simulation rate on unseen aircraft geometries rose from under 1% to 74% over 100 single-attempt cases, and an ablation put the symbolic layer at 13 points of boundary-layer capture; ParaView control success rose from 55% to 75% with knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters; in space domain awareness, a frozen self-supervised world model scored highest of five methods at conjunction risk.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that a trustworthy design with validated physics as the decision basis gives up nothing in accuracy and extends to a control-grade microreactor digital twin.

title: Leap-VLA: High-Rate Robot Control from a Low-Rate VLM Backbone
comment: 21 pages, 14 figures. Corresponding author: Lin Yang
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models re-encode the full observation through a multi-billion-parameter vision-language model (VLM) at every control step, even though scene semantics evolve at roughly 1 Hz while reactive control requires 20-50 Hz. We present a VLA that decouples the two: a VLM runs as a low-frequency semantic anchor whose cached context is reused across control steps, while a flow-matching action expert operates at high frequency, consuming the cached semantics with a fresh, low-latency visual stream from a compact encoder pretrained on robot video with masked reconstruction, optical flow, and depth. The measured age $\tau$ of the cache conditions the expert through adaptive layer normalization. Reusing the cache makes the policy a function of its age, and training covers that function explicitly: cache ages sampled from real episode history, plus an age-ramped pixel corruption that erases the stale snapshot the way deployed staleness corrupts content. On the asynchronous deployment stack, the recipe closes most of the staleness gap: on LIBERO-Spatial, 61.4% to 95.5% at a 2 s semantic refresh (95.9% at 1 s, within 1.6 points of the frequency-matched anchor); averaged over the four LIBERO suites, the deployed policy holds 95.2% at a 1 s refresh and 94.5% at 2 s against a 96.3% matched anchor. A forward-only chunk-boundary correction (soft-nudge), an autograd-free reformulation of real-time-chunking guidance, carries per-control-step re-planning without loss (97.1%) at zero added latency. The same lens exposes a second defect: under an instruction-scene mismatch the policy keeps manipulating the scene, and a chain-of-thought verdict gate trained on zero-cost negative episodes freezes execution exactly on mismatched instructions without hurting feasible success.

AI.tldr: Leap-VLA decouples a low-frequency VLM, whose cached context is reused, from a high-frequency flow-matching action expert, and trains the policy over cache age so that stale semantics do not degrade control.
AI.motivation: VLA models re-encode the full observation through a multi-billion-parameter VLM at every control step, although scene semantics change at about 1 Hz while reactive control needs 20-50 Hz.
AI.method: A flow-matching action expert consumes the cached VLM semantics with a fresh visual stream from a compact encoder pretrained on robot video, with the cache age conditioning the expert through adaptive layer normalization; training samples cache ages from episode history and applies an age-ramped pixel corruption; a forward-only soft-nudge correction handles chunk boundaries.
AI.result: On LIBERO-Spatial, success rises from 61.4% to 95.5% at a 2 s semantic refresh (95.9% at 1 s); averaged over the four LIBERO suites, the deployed policy holds 95.2% at a 1 s refresh and 94.5% at 2 s against a 96.3% frequency-matched anchor; soft-nudge keeps 97.1% at zero added latency; a chain-of-thought verdict gate trained on negative episodes freezes execution on mismatched instructions.
AI.conclusion: Most of the staleness gap can be closed by the training recipe, and the same cache-age view exposes an instruction-scene mismatch failure that a verdict gate can catch without hurting feasible success.

title: IJev: Order-Invariant Decisions via Iterated Cyclic Reordering
summary: System One decision models answer a choice question in one forward pass, but their answer depends on the order in which options are listed, and their probabilities carry a prior over answer labels. An invariant ordering operator is any fixed function that returns the same ordered option list for every input order of a fixed option set. Starting from any such order and averaging a listwise readout over its K cyclic shifts removes the input order, but the decision still depends on the chosen cyclic class: those $K$ shifts are only one of the (K-1)! classes, and different invariant operators can select different classes. We propose IJev, which repeatedly reorders the options by the cyclic-averaged, label-prior-corrected distribution and runs another cyclic average. Every iterate is exactly input-order-invariant. When the iteration does not converge, we average the round distributions rather than return the last round. On five benchmarks and five models, IJev has flip rate zero in every cell. The default uniform average over T=20 rounds substantially improves calibration over a single cyclic average, and its accuracy is comparable. A descriptive choice of horizon and averaging rule is best or tied-best for accuracy in all 25 settings.

AI.tldr: IJev makes System One decision models order-invariant by repeatedly reordering options by their cyclic-averaged, label-prior-corrected distribution and cyclically averaging again, with flip rate zero in every cell across five benchmarks and five models.
AI.motivation: Single-pass decision models depend on option order and carry a prior over answer labels, and averaging over cyclic shifts removes input order only up to the chosen cyclic class, which different invariant operators can select differently.
AI.method: Starting from any invariant ordering, IJev repeatedly reorders the options by the cyclic-averaged, label-prior-corrected distribution and runs another cyclic average, averaging the round distributions when the iteration does not converge; the default uses T=20 rounds with a uniform average.
AI.result: IJev has flip rate zero in every cell over five benchmarks and five models; the default uniform average over T=20 rounds substantially improves calibration over a single cyclic average with comparable accuracy; the descriptive choice of horizon and averaging rule is best or tied-best for accuracy in all 25 settings.
AI.conclusion: Iterated reordering yields exactly order-invariant decisions with better calibration than a single cyclic average, at comparable accuracy.

title: Constraint Dependency Graph Retrieval for Compliance Detection on Long SKILL Documents
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents carry out business operations under enterprise documents we refer to as SKILL documents, which take the form of standard operating procedures (SOPs) that state the conditions to verify and the actions to take before an operation proceeds. Long, densely cross-referenced SKILL documents exceed the context budget of small deployed auditors. Similarity-based retrieval then brings in irrelevant rules while omitting mandatory prerequisites, and the two-stage audit policy provides no trainable signal for the retrieval stage. We present SkillCDG, a compliance detection framework that reformulates each SKILL document as a constraint dependency graph, shifting rule retrieval from similarity-based matching to closure-based selection under the deployment's context budget. Each atomic rule is anchored to its source text span as a graph node, and mandatory prerequisite relations form the sole edge type. Policy-generated retrieval keywords activate seed rules, whose dependency closure yields a compact and conditionally complete rule context within that budget. The same graph also supports a joint optimization scheme. The retrieval stage is trained with group-relative policy optimization using a verifiable reward that combines output-format validity with downstream verdict correctness, with closure non-emptiness serving as a validity gate, while selective on-policy distillation concentrates teacher supervision on high-entropy reasoning tokens, with verdict and termination tokens always included, to improve verdict accuracy. Experiments on three enterprise datasets and two public benchmarks show that SkillCDG improves accuracy and F1 over the full-document and retrieval-based baselines.

AI.tldr: SkillCDG reformulates long SKILL documents, which are enterprise standard operating procedures, as constraint dependency graphs and retrieves rules by dependency closure, improving compliance detection accuracy and F1 over full-document and retrieval baselines.
AI.motivation: Long, densely cross-referenced SKILL documents exceed the context budget of small deployed auditors, and similarity-based retrieval brings irrelevant rules while omitting mandatory prerequisites.
AI.method: Each atomic rule is a graph node anchored to its source text span, mandatory prerequisite relations are the only edge type, policy-generated keywords activate seed rules, and their dependency closure forms the context; the retrieval stage is trained with group-relative policy optimization on a verifiable reward, and selective on-policy distillation focuses on high-entropy reasoning tokens.
AI.result: SkillCDG improves accuracy and F1 over full-document and retrieval-based baselines on three enterprise datasets and two public benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Closure-based selection over a constraint dependency graph gives compact, conditionally complete rule contexts that improve compliance verdicts under a fixed context budget.

title: Temperature, Not Knowledge: What Recursive Self-Training and Its Remedies Do to a Language Model's Confidence
summary: Recursive self-training can collapse language models, and many proposed remedies target overconfidence, yet their effects on confidence are rarely measured. We study a five-round self-training loop on Qwen3-1.7B, using three seeds per compared method, and distinguish confidence temperature (drift from a calibrated starting point) from discrimination (ranking correct answers above incorrect ones). Accuracy and overall discrimination remain nearly unchanged, but confidence sharpens and the most confident answers become less reliable. Matching predictive entropy to the calibrated starting model each round recalibrates nearly as well as label-based temperature fitting, at both 1.7B and 8B. Sharpening is not inherent to self-training: exact samples from a model's distribution have zero expected gradient. Instead, most drift comes from fitting each generated answer twice, with top-p truncation contributing the rest; removing both keeps entropy on generated outputs flat. Remedies affect the two properties differently: truncated cross-entropy, an entropy bonus, and single-pass training preserve temperature without improving discrimination, while focal loss and multi-sample targets improve discrimination but cause underconfidence. Reference-data mixing also overshoots. Pairing a ranking-improving loss with label-free recalibration achieves both.

AI.tldr: Five rounds of recursive self-training on Qwen3-1.7B mainly sharpen confidence temperature rather than discrimination, and the paper traces most of this drift to fitting each generated answer twice, with top-p truncation contributing the rest.
AI.motivation: Remedies for recursive self-training collapse are said to target overconfidence, but their effects on confidence are rarely measured, and temperature must be separated from discrimination.
AI.method: A five-round self-training loop on Qwen3-1.7B with three seeds per method compares confidence temperature against a calibrated starting point with discrimination between correct and incorrect answers; predictive entropy matching and label-based temperature fitting are compared at 1.7B and 8B, and remedies such as truncated cross-entropy, entropy bonus, single-pass training, focal loss and multi-sample targets are evaluated.
AI.result: Accuracy and overall discrimination stay nearly unchanged while confidence sharpens and the most confident answers become less reliable; entropy matching recalibrates nearly as well as label-based temperature fitting at both scales; removing double fitting and top-p truncation keeps entropy on generated outputs flat; focal loss and multi-sample targets improve discrimination but cause underconfidence.
AI.conclusion: Temperature and discrimination respond differently to remedies, and pairing a ranking-improving loss with label-free recalibration achieves both.

title: Appointed-Time Fault-Tolerant Fast Terminal Sliding Control for UAVs with a Tracking Error-Based Disturbance Observer
summary: This paper addresses the critical challenge of high-performance fault-tolerant tracking control for quadrotor UAVs under complex conditions including external disturbances, parameter uncertainties, and actuator faults. A synergistic control framework is proposed by decoupling the system into position and attitude loops, each governed by the following three innovations. First, an Appointed-Time Prescribed Performance Function (AT-PPF) is developed to strictly constrain the tracking error within a predefined funnel boundary, ensuring convergence within a fixed time regardless of initial conditions. Second, a Tracking Error-Based Fixed-Time Composite Disturbance Observer (TFxTCDO) is developed to enable fast and accurate estimation of lumped disturbances without requiring full-state information or precise system modeling. This observer directly couples disturbance estimation with the control objective, thereby enhancing robustness and convergence. Third, a Fast Second-Order Terminal Sliding Mode Controller (NFSO-TSMC) is designed to achieve faster convergence and effective chattering mitigation. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed control strategy significantly outperforms conventional methods in terms of tracking accuracy, fault recovery speed, and robustness against uncertainties.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a quadrotor UAV controller combining an appointed-time prescribed performance function, a fixed-time composite disturbance observer driven by tracking error, and a fast second-order terminal sliding mode controller for fault-tolerant tracking.
AI.motivation: Quadrotor tracking must remain accurate under external disturbances, parameter uncertainty and actuator faults, and conventional methods are limited in tracking accuracy, fault recovery speed and robustness.
AI.method: The system is decoupled into position and attitude loops, each using an appointed-time prescribed performance function to keep tracking error inside a funnel, a tracking-error-based fixed-time composite disturbance observer that estimates lumped disturbances without full-state information or precise modelling, and a fast second-order terminal sliding mode controller for convergence and chattering mitigation.
AI.result: Simulation results are reported to significantly outperform conventional methods in tracking accuracy, fault recovery speed and robustness against uncertainties; the abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: The combined framework is presented as a practical fault-tolerant tracking controller for quadrotor UAVs under complex conditions.

title: Robust Reward Machine Learning and Execution in Noisy Environments
comment: 44 pages, 21 figures, 5 tables. Published in the Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research. Code: this https URL
summary: Background: Reward machines (RMs) represent non-Markovian reward functions as finite-state machines over high-level propositional events. Traditionally, these events are generated by a deterministic labelling function that maps environment states to proposition sets. However, real-world labelling functions are inherently noisy. Objectives: Design and implement a method that learns RMs in the presence of noisy labelling functions and exploits them for policy learning in both discrete and continuous environments. Methods: We propose Prob-IRM, a method that learns RMs from noisy proposition histories using inductive logic programming (ILP) and exploits them for policy learning. Noisy proposition histories are represented as training examples for ILP, which learns an RM that maximises coverage of low-uncertainty histories. RM learning is interleaved with policy optimisation. Prob-IRM uses a belief over RM states to determine when to relearn the RM and to provide additional guiding rewards. Results: Prob-IRM is evaluated on environments with discrete and continuous state spaces under varying levels of labelling noise. Prob-IRM performs comparably to baselines using handcrafted RMs and outperforms approaches that use recurrent neural networks to encode history, despite operating with noisy labels. Conclusions: Prob-IRM represents a step towards deploying reward machines in noisy, real-world environments.

AI.tldr: Prob-IRM learns reward machines from noisy proposition histories with inductive logic programming and interleaves relearning with policy optimization, performing comparably to handcrafted reward machines and outperforming recurrent baselines under varying labelling noise.
AI.motivation: Reward machines assume a deterministic labelling function, but real-world labelling functions are noisy, which hinders learning and exploiting reward machines in practice.
AI.method: Noisy proposition histories are used as ILP training examples to learn a reward machine that maximises coverage of low-uncertainty histories; a belief over reward-machine states decides when to relearn and supplies additional guiding rewards, with relearning interleaved with policy optimization.
AI.result: Prob-IRM performs comparably to baselines using handcrafted reward machines and outperforms approaches that use recurrent neural networks to encode history, in environments with discrete and continuous state spaces under varying levels of labelling noise.
AI.conclusion: Prob-IRM is a step toward deploying reward machines in noisy, real-world environments.

title: HiGenTrans: Hierarchical LLM Knowledge Transfer for Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation promises to simplify conventional multi-stage recommender systems by generating item Semantic IDs (SIDs) autoregressively. However, two obstacles limit its effective- ness in industrial settings: interaction-only supervision underuses the semantic knowledge encoded in pretrained language models, while beam-search likelihood ranks token sequences rather than directly estimating item relevance. To address these limitations, we propose HiGenTrans, a three-level framework that introduces LLM knowledge at the input, representation, and decision levels. First, Global Semantic Priming (GSP) adds an LLM-derived user representation to the beginning-of-sequence embedding, provid- ing a semantic prior before SID generation. Second, Hierarchi- cal Representation Transfer (HRT) aligns intermediate LLM representations with depth-matched GenRec layers through mean- centered projections and gated residual connections. Finally, Multi- Signal Decision Calibration (MDC) uses a lightweight mixture- of-experts calibrator to combine semantic relevance, generation confidence, and candidate-set context when reranking beam-search outputs. All semantic features are computed only from the observ- able interaction prefix, preventing target leakage, and can be cached offline. Experiments on three public benchmarks show that HiGen- Trans improves Recall@10 by up to 12.9% and NDCG@10 by up to 33.7% over the strongest baselines. These results demonstrate the value of transferring LLM knowledge at complementary stages of the generative recommendation pipeline.

AI.tldr: HiGenTrans transfers LLM knowledge into generative recommendation at three levels, input, representation and decision, and improves Recall@10 by up to 12.9% and NDCG@10 by up to 33.7% over the strongest baselines on three public benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Generative recommendation over Semantic IDs underuses semantic knowledge in pretrained language models when supervision is interaction-only, and beam-search likelihood ranks token sequences rather than estimating item relevance.
AI.method: Global Semantic Priming adds an LLM-derived user representation to the beginning-of-sequence embedding; Hierarchical Representation Transfer aligns intermediate LLM representations with depth-matched generative recommendation layers through mean-centred projections and gated residual connections; Multi-Signal Decision Calibration uses a lightweight mixture-of-experts calibrator to rerank beam-search outputs using semantic relevance, generation confidence and candidate-set context; semantic features use only the observable interaction prefix and can be cached offline.
AI.result: HiGenTrans improves Recall@10 by up to 12.9% and NDCG@10 by up to 33.7% over the strongest baselines on three public benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Transferring LLM knowledge at complementary stages of the generative recommendation pipeline is valuable.

title: Compile as Hypothesis: A Headroom Typology for Prompt Optimization on Real Reasoning Models
summary: Automated prompt compilers search for or rewrite prompts under the implicit assumption that optimization consistently improves downstream task performance. We evaluate this assumption on frontier reasoning models through rigorous paired, same-day measurements. Across four optimizer families (genome search, profile-guided mutation, GEPA, and ESPO) and eight tasks, structured search yields no statistically significant accuracy gains on strong reasoners. However, a discrete structural genome provides essential architectural stability, preventing catastrophic bimodal seed-collapse (where unconstrained search collapses toward the judge floor in 3/5 runs). Through 190-problem evaluations on knowledge-intensive benchmarks, we establish a three-dimensional headroom typology: prompt optimization cannot compensate for intrinsic knowledge deficits or physical token truncation, but successfully resolves protocol and formatting errors. On gpt-6, while free-text reflective search (GEPA) yields a +.14 gain on a task where structured search remains flat, qualitative ablation reveals that ~.035 stems from judge-rubric reconstruction while ~.105 reflects genuine instruction refinement. Our pre-registered AutoAPC-Select deployment gate matches the oracle policy in 5/7 groups and rescues seed-collapse arms with zero regret. Finally, we expose silent backend-mixing in commercial APIs during outage windows and provide automated per-call audit verification tools to ensure empirical evaluation fidelity.

AI.tldr: Across four prompt optimizer families and eight tasks, structured prompt search yields no statistically significant accuracy gains on strong reasoning models, and the paper introduces a headroom typology and a pre-registered deployment gate for when optimization can help.
AI.motivation: Automated prompt compilers assume that optimization consistently improves downstream performance, and this assumption has not been tested rigorously on frontier reasoning models.
AI.method: Paired, same-day measurements compare genome search, profile-guided mutation, GEPA and ESPO over eight tasks, with 190-problem evaluations on knowledge-intensive benchmarks; a three-dimensional headroom typology is established, and a pre-registered AutoAPC-Select gate selects the policy; the authors also audit backend mixing in commercial APIs during outage windows.
AI.result: Structured search yields no significant accuracy gains on strong reasoners, but a discrete structural genome prevents bimodal seed collapse seen in unconstrained search in 3 of 5 runs; prompt optimization cannot compensate for intrinsic knowledge deficits or token truncation but resolves protocol and formatting errors; on gpt-6, GEPA gains +.14, of which about .035 comes from judge-rubric reconstruction and about .105 from instruction refinement; the AutoAPC-Select gate matches the oracle policy in 5 of 7 groups.
AI.conclusion: Prompt optimization should be treated as a hypothesis to test rather than a default, and the typology indicates which error types it can fix; the authors also expose silent backend mixing in commercial APIs.

title: EMG-Hybrid: A Dual-Engine Elite Memory--Guided Adaptive Optimization Framework for High-Dimensional Feature Selection
summary: Feature selection in ultra-high-dimensional, noisy datasets remains a critical challenge due to exponential search space growth, where conventional binary metaheuristics often suffer from premature convergence. To address this, EMG-Hybrid is introduced as a novel three-level hierarchical optimization architecture designed around decoupled operational planes, feedback-driven scheduling, and isolated state refinement. At Level 1, a Dual-Engine Controller monitors population Shannon entropy and empirical fitness velocity, functioning as an architectural master-switch that dynamically routes execution between global exploration and local intensification. This control loop conditions the Level 2 active optimization plane, where an Adaptive Black Hole Gravity (ABHG) execution layer performs aggressive feature manifold pruning via a distance-decoupled penalty kernel driven by fitness similarities and Hamming metrics. To structurally isolate macro-exploration from micro-exploitation, Level 3 encapsulates an autonomous Elite Memory Archive that preserves high-fidelity sub-schemas and hosts a discrete bitwise Differential Evolution (DE) micro-refinement sandbox for resolving complex parameter epistasis. Theoretically, uniform combinatorial bounds derived via Vapnik--Chervonenkis (VC) dimension criteria demonstrate that this multi-level restriction mitigates high-dimensional overfitting. Empirical results across manifolds scaling up to $d > 100{,}000$ features, complemented by high-performance computing (HPC) profiling under lock-free atomic Compare-and-Swap (CAS) primitives, indicate strong performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines. The framework exhibits near-linear parallel speedups, sub-quadratic runtime scaling, and substantial dimensionality reduction, offering a scalable and structurally innovative paradigm for large-scale data mining.

AI.tldr: EMG-Hybrid is a three-level hierarchical metaheuristic for high-dimensional feature selection that switches between exploration and intensification using population entropy and fitness velocity, reporting gains on datasets with over 100,000 features.
AI.motivation: Binary metaheuristics for feature selection in ultra-high-dimensional noisy data often converge prematurely as the search space grows exponentially.
AI.method: A Dual-Engine Controller monitors population Shannon entropy and empirical fitness velocity to route between global exploration and local intensification; an Adaptive Black Hole Gravity layer prunes features with a distance-decoupled penalty; an Elite Memory Archive stores high-fidelity sub-schemas and runs a discrete bitwise Differential Evolution micro-refinement; the authors derive VC-dimension-based combinatorial bounds and profile lock-free atomic Compare-and-Swap parallelism.
AI.result: Empirical results on datasets scaling to more than 100,000 features show strong gains over state-of-the-art baselines, with near-linear parallel speedups, sub-quadratic runtime scaling and substantial dimensionality reduction; the abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The framework is presented as a scalable paradigm for large-scale feature selection, with theoretical and HPC support claimed.

title: CivicBench: A Benchmark and Memory Framework for Web-Based Civic Data Analytics
summary: Municipalities publish service requests, geographic boundaries, weather observations, demographic estimates, and operational guidance through independently maintained Web portals. Civic analysis must combine these sources while preserving their schemas, source links, spatial and temporal scopes, and interpretive limits. Tool-using language agents can perform this integration, but existing task benchmarks rarely test whether a computed claim remains supported by the records used. We present CivicBench, a 400-task benchmark over four cities and two years that materializes civic Web data into frozen bundles for reproducible evaluation. Executable contracts score computation, source linkage, coverage, scope, qualified answers, and refusal when the requested conclusion is not supported. We also introduce Task-State Memory (TSM), which compiles tool observations into typed assertions, reconciles records only within compatible scopes, and retrieves a bounded state organized around unresolved constraints. Across nine completed model pairs, eight yield positive mean-score differences with 95\% semantic-contract-cluster bootstrap intervals excluding zero; the ninth interval crosses zero. The benchmark and memory framework make the records behind a claim inspectable at the point of decision.

AI.tldr: CivicBench is a 400-task benchmark over four cities and two years for tool-using agents on web-based civic data analytics, with executable contracts that check computation, source linkage and refusal, and Task-State Memory (TSM) improves agent performance.
AI.motivation: Civic analysis must combine municipal Web portals while preserving schemas, source links, spatial and temporal scopes and interpretive limits, and existing task benchmarks rarely test whether a computed claim remains supported by its records.
AI.method: Civic Web data are materialized into frozen bundles for reproducible evaluation, and executable contracts score computation, source linkage, coverage, scope, qualified answers and refusal; Task-State Memory compiles tool observations into typed assertions, reconciles records only within compatible scopes and retrieves a bounded state organized around unresolved constraints.
AI.result: Across nine completed model pairs, eight yield positive mean-score differences whose 95% semantic-contract-cluster bootstrap intervals exclude zero, and the ninth interval crosses zero.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark and memory framework make the records behind a claim inspectable at the point of decision.

title: Capacity Planning for Resource-Constrained Clinical LLM Serving
comment: Accepted to the 9th Special Session on Healthcare Data at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (IEEE BigData 2026)
summary: Deploying large language models (LLMs) under a fixed accelerator budget requires jointly deciding how computational capacity is allocated across model sizes and how incoming requests are routed across that capacity. Although prior work has extensively studied LLM routing and serving efficiency, the relative importance of fleet composition and routing under resource constraints remains less understood. We investigate this question using a controlled four-GPU serving environment with heterogeneous clinical NLP workloads spanning short factual verification, biomedical semantic matching, and long-context clinical summarization. We systematically vary fleet composition, routing policy, and offered load while holding the workload trace and hardware budget fixed. Across 24 configurations, descriptive main-effect shares attribute more variation to fleet composition than to the evaluated routing policies in time to first token, latency, and long-context coverage. All-small fleets provide the best responsiveness and throughput but substantially lower long-context coverage, whereas larger-model capacity improves coverage at the cost of serving efficiency. Heterogeneous fleets provide intermediate operating points but can introduce strong-model bottlenecks when large-model capacity is scarce. In a focused evaluation of this bottleneck, capacity-aware routing reduces mean latency and increases throughput while incurring a small reduction in long-context coverage. Within this measured regime, the results support prioritizing capacity allocation, with routing managing demand within the provisioned capacity.

AI.tldr: In a controlled four-GPU serving study of clinical NLP workloads, fleet composition matters more than routing policy for latency, time to first token and long-context coverage, and capacity-aware routing mainly manages demand within the provisioned capacity.
AI.motivation: Deploying LLMs under a fixed accelerator budget requires deciding both how capacity is split across model sizes and how requests are routed, and the relative importance of these choices is less understood.
AI.method: Fleet composition, routing policy and offered load are varied across 24 configurations on a four-GPU environment with heterogeneous clinical NLP workloads (short factual verification, biomedical semantic matching and long-context clinical summarization), with the workload trace and hardware budget held fixed; main-effect shares are reported descriptively.
AI.result: Descriptive main-effect shares attribute more variation to fleet composition than to the evaluated routing policies in time to first token, latency and long-context coverage; all-small fleets give the best responsiveness and throughput but much lower long-context coverage; heterogeneous fleets can create strong-model bottlenecks when large-model capacity is scarce; capacity-aware routing reduces mean latency and increases throughput at a small cost in long-context coverage.
AI.conclusion: Within the measured regime, capacity allocation should be prioritized, with routing managing demand inside the provisioned capacity.

title: OntoDoc: Automatically Generating Ontology Resource Descriptions
summary: Knowledge graphs and ontologies form the backbone of structured, machine-readable knowledge representation, yet ontology terms often lack natural language descriptions, limiting their accessibility and reuse. Existing ontology verbalization approaches tend to rely on rule-based or template-driven techniques that operate on strict, formal schema axioms, resulting in rigid verbalizations that fail to convey richer contextual semantics. We present OntoDoc, a multi-agent framework for automatically generating natural language descriptions for any Internationalized Resource Identifier (IRI) within a SPARQL endpoint or RDF file. OntoDoc operates through a four-stage pipeline: (1) a Database Context agent that adaptively explores the knowledge graph via SPARQL to collect semantically informative triples about the target IRI; (2) a Web Context agent that retrieves and re-ranks encyclopedic background knowledge from Wikipedia and the open web; (3) an Assumption Generation agent that synthesizes both contexts into a structured, evidence-grounded list of intermediate assumptions; and (4) a Description Generation agent that produces the final natural language description from the grounded assumptions. We evaluate OntoDoc on three knowledge graphs spanning biomedical, agricultural, and cross-domain settings, using both automatic scoring via Large Language Models (LLMs) and human evaluation with 11 annotators. OntoDoc consistently matches or exceeds a naive LLM baseline and a template-based ontology verbalizer in accuracy. Furthermore, it vastly outperforms both baselines in the completeness of the generated descriptions, delivering an average 12% improvement in completeness over the naive baseline across all domains, and improving completeness scores by as much as 2.8 points on a 5-point scale relative to the ontology verbalizer.

AI.tldr: OntoDoc is a multi-agent framework that generates natural-language descriptions for ontology IRIs by combining SPARQL-based knowledge graph exploration, web context retrieval, assumption generation and description generation.
AI.motivation: Ontology terms often lack natural-language descriptions, and existing rule-based or template-driven verbalizers produce rigid descriptions that miss richer contextual semantics.
AI.method: A four-stage pipeline runs a Database Context agent that explores the knowledge graph via SPARQL, a Web Context agent that retrieves and re-ranks Wikipedia and open-web background, an Assumption Generation agent that builds grounded intermediate assumptions, and a Description Generation agent that writes the final description; evaluation uses LLM scoring and 11 human annotators on three knowledge graphs.
AI.result: OntoDoc matches or exceeds a naive LLM baseline and a template-based ontology verbalizer in accuracy and substantially outperforms both in completeness, with an average 12% completeness improvement over the naive baseline across domains and up to 2.8 points on a 5-point scale over the verbalizer.
AI.conclusion: Grounding description generation in retrieved graph and web context improves completeness without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Urban functional knowledge transfer through global representations amid uneven data
summary: Urban functional observations are unevenly distributed worldwide, limiting analysis of how places are organised and used. AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) provides a globally consistent physical representation. Whether this representation can support transfer of functional knowledge to locations with sparse or absent functional observations, and what governs transfer, remain unclear. We introduce POI-aligned Urban Embedding (PURE), which learns physical-functional relationships between POI-derived semantics and AEF. Across five urban analysis tasks covering 142 countries and territories, PURE increases mean $R^2$ from 0.792 to 0.830, with gains across widely different levels of POI availability. When target-city POIs are excluded, country-level alignment retains 87.9% of its performance gain. Cross-country experiments show that transfer is selective rather than universal, with larger gains between physically similar and geographically closer contexts, particularly among pairs within the same continent. Our findings reveal spatially structured urban functional knowledge transfer, offering a route to reduce reliance on dense local observations.

AI.tldr: PURE learns physical-functional relationships between POI-derived urban semantics and AlphaEarth Foundations embeddings, raising mean R2 from 0.792 to 0.830 across five urban tasks in 142 countries and territories and enabling transfer to sparsely observed places.
AI.motivation: Urban functional observations are unevenly distributed worldwide, and it is unclear whether a globally consistent physical representation can transfer functional knowledge to locations with sparse or absent observations.
AI.method: POI-aligned Urban Embedding learns the relationship between POI-derived semantics and AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) embeddings, and transfer is tested at country level, including experiments where target-city POIs are excluded.
AI.result: Mean R2 rises from 0.792 to 0.830 across five urban analysis tasks covering 142 countries and territories, with gains across different levels of POI availability; country-level alignment retains 87.9% of its performance gain when target-city POIs are excluded; transfer is selective, with larger gains between physically similar and geographically closer contexts, especially within the same continent.
AI.conclusion: Urban functional knowledge transfer is spatially structured, which offers a route to reduce reliance on dense local observations.

title: Large language models underrepresent malice and overreport virtue
comment: 41 pages, 5 figures, 5 Extended Data figures, 2 Extended Data tables; Supplementary Information included
summary: People increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to interpret others' behaviour, often assuming that LLMs infer motives as humans do. Aligned LLMs attribute more benevolent and less malevolent motives to a whistleblower than humans do, but ratings alone cannot reveal whether these differences arise in internal representations or at report. Here we compare linear-probe readouts of LLMs' internal states with their own ratings at the same prompt position for four motives, in two preregistered studies. For the two malevolent motives, self-interest and intent to harm, internal and expressed readouts did not differ: the lower ratings reflect weaker signal along the probed directions, not suppression at output. For the two benevolent motives, duty and concern for others, expressed ratings exceeded the internal readouts, indicating amplification at report. In free text the model rarely volunteered a motive against the colleague, far less often than humans did, yet produced one readily once the scenario supplied a reason. Shifting the internal representation along a malevolent-motive direction brought both malevolent ratings to the human level, whereas the rating of duty yielded only past a threshold at which the other motives had overshot. LLMs' more charitable motive profile thus has two distinct sources: reduced malevolent signal in the probed representation and amplified benevolent attribution at report.

AI.tldr: The paper compares linear-probe readouts of LLM internal states with the models' own ratings of four motives in a whistleblower scenario. It finds that LLMs under-represent malevolent motives internally and amplify benevolent motives at report.
AI.motivation: People increasingly use LLMs to interpret others' behaviour and assume they infer motives as humans do, but ratings alone cannot show whether differences from humans arise in internal representations or at the point of report.
AI.method: Two preregistered studies compare linear-probe readouts at the same prompt position with expressed ratings for self-interest, intent to harm, duty and concern for others. The authors also test free-text generation and steer the internal representation along a malevolent-motive direction.
AI.result: For self-interest and intent to harm, internal and expressed readouts did not differ, so lower ratings reflect weaker signal. For duty and concern for others, expressed ratings exceeded internal readouts, indicating amplification at report. The model rarely volunteered a motive against the colleague in free text, less often than humans, but produced one when given a reason. Steering along the malevolent direction brought malevolent ratings to the human level, while the duty rating changed only past a threshold where other motives overshot.
AI.conclusion: The charitable motive profile of LLMs has two distinct sources: reduced malevolent signal in the probed representation and amplified benevolent attribution at report. Ratings alone cannot distinguish these, so representation-level evidence is needed when LLMs are used to interpret behaviour.

title: A Self-Exploring and Self-Evolving Paradigm for Adaptive Edge AI Development
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit powerful code generation abilities, fostering agentic systems to automate edge AI application development. However, existing agents typically operate via fixed agentic workflows and predefined design spaces, struggling to handle rapidly evolving demands of real-world scenarios (e.g., heterogeneous data modalities, diverse task pipelines). Unlike prior systems that treat LLMs mainly as code generators following rigid workflows, we fully exploit their reasoning capabilities to allow agents to determine their own workflows on the fly. To this end, we propose SE2, a self-exploring and self-evolving paradigm for adaptive edge AI development. Inspired by human learning processes, we distill development into four atomic operations (retrieve, reason, code, test), and empower agents to explore workflows by dynamically and adaptively selecting an appropriate next operation based on the current context. Extensive evaluations show that, with adaptive workflows, the synthesized programs achieve up to 26% higher accuracy and consume 28% lower resources than state-of-the-art baselines, while maintaining superior adaptability to unforeseen edge AI scenarios. This highlights the potential of reasoning-driven adaptive agentic workflow in edge AI development.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SE2, an agent paradigm in which LLM agents choose their own development workflow on the fly for adaptive edge AI application development. It reports up to 26% higher accuracy and 28% lower resource use than state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents for edge AI development follow fixed agentic workflows and predefined design spaces, which struggle with the rapidly evolving demands of real scenarios such as heterogeneous data modalities and diverse task pipelines.
AI.method: Development is decomposed into four atomic operations: retrieve, reason, code and test. At each step the agent dynamically and adaptively selects the next operation based on the current context, treating the LLM as a reasoner rather than only a code generator.
AI.result: With adaptive workflows, the synthesized programs achieve up to 26% higher accuracy and consume 28% lower resources than state-of-the-art baselines. The system also remains adaptable to unforeseen edge AI scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning-driven adaptive agentic workflows show potential for edge AI development, where fixed pipelines are a poor match for changing requirements.

title: FOCUS: Closed-Loop Attention Feedback for Efficient Vision-Language Understanding
summary: Processing every video frame through Vision-Language Models (VLMs) adds significant inference cost and limits their ability to comprehend real-time video. Existing approaches either sub-sample frames uniformly, ignoring content and missing important events, or prune visual tokens inside the VLM to cut per-call cost while still invoking the model on every sampled frame. We introduce FOCUS, a training-free three-layer framework that reduces the number of invocations and steers each one towards what matters. Temporal gating measures inter-frame dissimilarity in the patch-embedding space of a smaller VLM from the same family, triggering burst captures only when the scene changes in a semantically meaningful way. Patch-level dissimilarity is then accumulated across the burst and fused with a top-down attention prior into a spatial focus map that encodes where motion and semantic relevance coincide. That map calibrates the VLM's value cache during generation, progressively amplifying vision tokens in task-relevant regions and attenuating off-target ones, without removing any token from the context. The loop closes after each response: text-to-vision cross-attention is extracted from the decoder and fed back as the prior for the next burst, letting the system converge on semantically important regions over successive observations. We evaluate FOCUS on the 500-video EgoSchema subset in streaming mode, with a single Qwen3-VL-8B backbone shared by every method. It reaches 74.8% accuracy using 25.4 VLM calls per clip, against 74.6% with 55 calls for uniform sampling and 74.2% with 55 calls for BOLT. On egocentric video captioning across four domains, it matches the best baseline's quality while issuing 57% fewer VLM invocations than uniform sampling.

AI.tldr: FOCUS is a training-free framework that reduces the number of VLM invocations on streaming video and steers each call toward relevant regions. On EgoSchema it reaches 74.8% accuracy with 25.4 VLM calls per clip, compared with 74.6% for uniform sampling using 55 calls.
AI.motivation: Running a VLM on every video frame is expensive and limits real-time video understanding. Uniform sampling ignores content and can miss key events, while in-model token pruning still calls the VLM on every sampled frame.
AI.method: A temporal gate uses inter-frame dissimilarity in the patch-embedding space of a smaller VLM from the same family to trigger burst captures. Patch-level dissimilarity is accumulated across the burst and fused with a top-down attention prior into a spatial focus map, which calibrates the VLM value cache by amplifying relevant vision tokens without removing any token. Cross-attention from the decoder is fed back as the prior for the next burst.
AI.result: On the 500-video EgoSchema subset in streaming mode with a shared Qwen3-VL-8B backbone, FOCUS reaches 74.8% accuracy using 25.4 VLM calls per clip, against 74.6% with 55 calls for uniform sampling and 74.2% with 55 calls for BOLT. On egocentric captioning across four domains it matches the best baseline's quality with 57% fewer VLM invocations than uniform sampling.
AI.conclusion: Gating invocations and steering attention on the value cache can cut VLM cost on streaming video without training, while keeping accuracy at or above the baselines.

title: I-PTC: Interactive Programmatic Tool Calling for Stateful Tool-Augmented Agents
summary: Large language models are increasingly capable of writing and executing code, suggesting a natural paradigm for tool-augmented agents: expressing tool use as programs rather than isolated calls. Programmatic tool calling (PTC) captures this idea through loops, batching, abstraction, and structured computation, but existing PTC approaches are largely stateless, limiting their ability to reuse intermediate results and adapt over time. This is problematic for real-world tasks, where tool environments and problem-solving processes are inherently stateful. We therefore present I-PTC, an interactive framework that executes stateful PTC: models issue code snippets that call tools, maintain reusable state, and evolve the tool interface through API corrections. To evaluate the effectiveness of I-PTC and the general PTC setting, we introduce PTC-Bench, a benchmark of long-tail, production-style user requests whose difficulty comes from large initial environments, many dependent API interactions, extended planning, and recovery across follow-ups and transient failures. Experiments on PTC-Bench show that I-PTC improves performance on complex multi-step tasks with large tool sets while substantially reducing token consumption over conventional tool-calling baselines and the original PTC baseline, highlighting stateful programmatic tool calling as a promising direction for scalable tool-augmented agents.

AI.tldr: I-PTC is an interactive framework for stateful programmatic tool calling, in which models issue code that calls tools, keeps reusable state and corrects APIs. The paper also introduces PTC-Bench, a benchmark of long-tail, production-style requests.
AI.motivation: Existing programmatic tool calling approaches are largely stateless, which limits reuse of intermediate results and adaptation over time. This is a problem for real tasks whose tool environments and problem-solving processes are stateful.
AI.method: Models write code snippets that call tools, maintain reusable state, and evolve the tool interface through API corrections. PTC-Bench targets large initial environments, many dependent API interactions, extended planning, and recovery across follow-ups and transient failures.
AI.result: On PTC-Bench, I-PTC improves performance on complex multi-step tasks with large tool sets. It also substantially reduces token consumption compared with conventional tool-calling baselines and the original PTC baseline.
AI.conclusion: Stateful programmatic tool calling is presented as a promising direction for scalable tool-augmented agents.

title: CONFIRM: Governing Scientific Reporting for Trustworthy Agentic Neuroimaging
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can autonomously run neuroimaging analyses from research questions to reported findings. Existing agentic systems use tools to check that code runs and reported values match its output, but rely on LLM judgment to decide which results warrant scientific reporting. We show that LLM judges endorse site-confounded findings even when the confound is presented as evidence. We present \textbf{CONFIRM}, a framework that separates running an analysis from deciding which findings to report. CONFIRM encodes each hypothesis as a machine-readable, pre-specified analysis plan that fixes the claim and its pass criteria before computing results. It then filters results through five deterministic gates (search history and multiplicity, confounds, power, analytic stability, and replication) under three configurable reporting standards, from least to most demanding: \textit{Screen}, \textit{Replicate}, and \textit{Full}. Failed claims receive diagnoses that guide follow-up analyses. To evaluate reporting decisions at the claim level, we introduce \textbf{NeuroClaimBench}, comprising 489 executable neuroimaging claims with frozen data, including literature-supported findings and 150 controls designed to violate individual methodological requirements. On NeuroClaimBench, CONFIRM falsely supports at most 3\% of controls, compared with 23--38\% for the baselines, while recovering up to 61\% of literature-supported claims. When auditing an existing agent, CONFIRM reduces false support on controls from 23\% to 0\% while retaining the agent's literature-supported claims. Its diagnostic feedback also produces more supported revisions than Self-Refine with fewer LLM calls. Together, CONFIRM and NeuroClaimBench show that basing reporting decisions on pre-specified analysis plans and deterministic gates is essential for trustworthy autonomous scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: CONFIRM separates running an analysis from deciding which findings to report, using pre-specified analysis plans and five deterministic gates. On NeuroClaimBench it falsely supports at most 3% of controls, compared with 23-38% for baselines.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can run neuroimaging analyses end to end, but existing systems rely on LLM judgment to decide which results warrant reporting. The authors show that LLM judges endorse site-confounded findings even when the confound is presented as evidence.
AI.method: Each hypothesis is encoded as a machine-readable, pre-specified analysis plan that fixes the claim and its pass criteria before results are computed. Results pass through five deterministic gates (search history and multiplicity, confounds, power, analytic stability, replication) under three configurable reporting standards, Screen, Replicate and Full. Failed claims receive diagnoses that guide follow-up analyses.
AI.result: On NeuroClaimBench, which has 489 executable claims with frozen data including 150 controls, CONFIRM falsely supports at most 3% of controls against 23-38% for baselines, while recovering up to 61% of literature-supported claims. When auditing an existing agent, it reduces false support on controls from 23% to 0% while retaining the agent's literature-supported claims. Its feedback yields more supported revisions than Self-Refine with fewer LLM calls.
AI.conclusion: Basing reporting decisions on pre-specified plans and deterministic gates is presented as essential for trustworthy autonomous scientific discovery.

title: From Tool State to Scientific Action: Auditing Decision Provenance in Biomedical Research Agents
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 AgenticLS Workshop; adds one experiment
summary: A scientific agent can give the same verdict while reading and citing different evidence. BioAgent-DF tests this separation using paired reference and candidate values saved at the same scientific computation site. It restores or transplants those values at their original coordinates, then runs the agent on healthy hardware. Across eight SciFact batches, Qwen3.5-4B shows repeatable citation changes in three capture-claim combinations, and Gemma 3 4B IT shows repeatable read and citation changes in four. These seven combinations cover two claims. Full restoration recovers the reference evidence sets while verdicts remain unchanged. Verdict changes observed under the baseline prompt did not recur under the explicit-example prompt. Complementary tool and optimizer experiments distinguish recovery of numerical state, recovery of ranked lists, and restoration of an agent's visible history. These results show that an audit should track both the evidence an agent uses and its final answer. In hERG cardiac-safety assay allocation, silent numerical faults changed testing decisions while the fixed-budget shortlist kept the same number of compounds labeled as blockers. After the agent had used faulty values, restoring its earlier execution state and supplying certified scores recovered all 39 changed decisions, whereas replacing the prediction file recovered none; no incorrect action was committed. A streaming implementation of the arithmetic checks reduced the total time for forward execution and verification by 42.4% relative to the original FP64 implementation, with identical flags and recovery outputs.

AI.tldr: BioAgent-DF audits whether a biomedical research agent uses the same evidence to reach a verdict, by restoring or transplanting saved numerical values at their original computation sites. It finds citation and read changes in some model and claim combinations, and it recovers faulty execution state in a hERG assay allocation task.
AI.motivation: A scientific agent can reach the same verdict while reading and citing different evidence, so final answers alone do not audit its reasoning. The authors want to track the evidence an agent uses as well as its answer.
AI.method: Paired reference and candidate values are saved at the same scientific computation site, then restored or transplanted at their original coordinates and the agent is rerun on healthy hardware. Complementary tool and optimizer experiments separate recovery of numerical state, ranked lists and visible history. A streaming implementation of the arithmetic checks is also tested.
AI.result: Across eight SciFact batches, Qwen3.5-4B shows repeatable citation changes in three capture-claim combinations and Gemma 3 4B IT shows repeatable read and citation changes in four, covering two claims. Full restoration recovers the reference evidence sets while verdicts stay unchanged. In hERG assay allocation, restoring earlier execution state with certified scores recovers all 39 changed decisions, while replacing the prediction file recovers none. The streaming arithmetic checks reduce total forward and verification time by 42.4% relative to the original FP64 implementation, with identical flags and recovery outputs.
AI.conclusion: An audit should track both the evidence an agent uses and its final answer, since silent numerical faults can change decisions even when the shortlist count stays the same.

title: \textsc{ChatDify}: Automating End-to-End Dify Workflow Synthesis from Natural Language via Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: The proliferation of Large Language Models has catalyzed powerful application development platforms like Dify, which enable users to build sophisticated LLM-powered workflows through modular node orchestration. However, manually configuring these workflows requires deep platform expertise and remains time-consuming and error-prone, creating a significant barrier for non-expert users. To address this challenge, we propose \textsc{ChatDify}, a novel multi-agent framework that automates end-to-end Dify workflow synthesis from natural language descriptions. \textsc{ChatDify} employs an Actor-Critic architecture comprising three specialized agents: the \textit{Planner Agent} that decomposes user requests into structured execution plans, the \textit{Executor Agent} that performs context-aware parameter synthesis and schema-augmented DSL compilation, and the \textit{Reviewer Agent} that ensures reliability through hybrid verification with closed-loop refinement. We evaluate \textsc{ChatDify} on a curated benchmark of 100 production-inspired tasks across three state-of-the-art LLM backends, achieving 0.96, 0.91, and 0.75 success rates with Qwen-3.7, GLM-5.1, and DeepSeek-v4, respectively. These results demonstrate its robustness and practical applicability for lowering the technical barrier to creating sophisticated LLM applications.

AI.tldr: ChatDify is a multi-agent framework that synthesizes end-to-end Dify LLM workflows from natural-language descriptions using Planner, Executor and Reviewer agents. It achieves success rates of 0.96, 0.91 and 0.75 with three LLM backends on a 100-task benchmark.
AI.motivation: Building Dify workflows by hand needs deep platform expertise and is slow and error-prone, which blocks non-expert users.
AI.method: An Actor-Critic architecture is used. The Planner Agent decomposes requests into structured execution plans, the Executor Agent performs context-aware parameter synthesis and schema-augmented DSL compilation, and the Reviewer Agent checks reliability through hybrid verification with closed-loop refinement.
AI.result: On a curated benchmark of 100 production-inspired tasks, ChatDify achieves success rates of 0.96, 0.91 and 0.75 with Qwen-3.7, GLM-5.1 and DeepSeek-v4 respectively.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest the framework is robust and practical for lowering the technical barrier to building LLM applications, though the success rate depends on the backend model.

title: Seeing What Matters, Verifying What Pays: Load-Adaptive Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language model (VLM) inference without altering the output distribution, yet two factors limit its gains. Existing drafters either lack the image evidence required for visually grounded tokens or pay to condition on every visual token, although a short draft block typically depends on only a few image regions. Moreover, the value of verifying additional candidates varies with GPU load, so no fixed verification structure is efficient across serving conditions. We present Uni-LaSpec, a block-parallel speculative decoding framework that addresses both factors. To improve draft quality, Uni-LaSpec reuses the verifier's own attention: the query retained from the preceding verification ranks the cached, int8-quantized visual keys, and a cross-layer vote selects a few visual tokens that the drafter fuses through gated cross-attention. Acceptance-aware training further weights each draft position by its contribution to the accepted prefix. To allocate verification, a marginal-cost criterion selects the structure per request and per round: draft trees exploit idle verifier capacity under light load, whereas a dynamic head truncates linear drafts under heavy load. Across six VLMs from three model families and 17 text and multimodal benchmarks, selecting eight visual tokens retains at least 98.6% of the acceptance obtained from the full image at sub-millisecond selection cost. With greedy decoding at concurrency one, Uni-LaSpec achieves up to 5.11x text and 3.24x multimodal throughput over autoregressive decoding. Across six load levels and three GPU types, it outperforms autoregressive decoding in every setting and matches or exceeds the best fixed verification strategy in 123 of 144 settings; under bursty arrivals, it reduces mean end-to-end latency by 47.6% relative to linear verification.

AI.tldr: Uni-LaSpec is a block-parallel speculative decoding framework for VLMs that selects a few visual tokens for the drafter and adapts verification structure to GPU load. It retains at least 98.6% of acceptance with eight visual tokens and reaches up to 5.11x text and 3.24x multimodal throughput at concurrency one.
