AI.motivation: Existing drafters either lack the image evidence needed for visually grounded tokens or pay to condition on every visual token. Fixed verification structures are also inefficient because the value of extra verification varies with GPU load.
AI.method: The drafter reuses the verifier's own attention: the retained query ranks cached int8-quantized visual keys, and a cross-layer vote picks a few visual tokens fused through gated cross-attention. Acceptance-aware training weights each draft position by its contribution to the accepted prefix. A marginal-cost criterion chooses draft trees under light load and a dynamic head that truncates linear drafts under heavy load.
AI.result: Across six VLMs from three model families and 17 text and multimodal benchmarks, eight visual tokens retain at least 98.6% of the acceptance obtained from the full image at sub-millisecond selection cost. At concurrency one with greedy decoding, the speedups are up to 5.11x for text and 3.24x for multimodal throughput. Across six load levels and three GPU types it outperforms autoregressive decoding in every setting and matches or exceeds the best fixed strategy in 123 of 144 settings. Under bursty arrivals it cuts mean end-to-end latency by 47.6% relative to linear verification.
AI.conclusion: Reusing verifier attention for visual token selection and choosing verification structure by load gives large throughput gains for VLM speculative decoding across serving conditions.

title: Chain-of-Thought Oversight Requires Separate Evidence for Faithfulness and Monitorability
comment: The paper is accepted by Neurips 2026 Position Track
summary: A common assumption in chain-of-thought (CoT) oversight is that a visible reasoning trace makes model behavior easier to monitor. We argue that this assumption can conflate distinct properties along a chain linking a model's internal computation, reasoning artifacts, outputs, and monitor judgments. We identify four properties along this chain: reasoning visibility (whether a trace is accessible), mechanistic faithfulness (whether a trace reflects internal computation), mechanistic localizability (whether a compact causal mechanism can be isolated), and behavioral monitorability (whether a monitor can detect the target behavior). Two complementary case studies across three open-weight reasoning models show why these distinctions matter. In the security vulnerability reasoning study, probes and activation ablations provide evidence of internal representation and causal influence, but a monitor with access to the reference answer does not outperform the majority-class baseline in a held-out test. In authority-hint factual reasoning study, a monitor correctly distinguishes changed from unchanged answers, but seven mechanistic analyses do not isolate a compact causal mechanism. These results show that evidence for one claim does not establish the others. We therefore propose an evidential-chain reporting standard. Each claim carries a licensing statement that specifies its target property, access tier, and artifact, and labels each required link as supported, unsupported, or assumed. These assessments determine whether the conclusion is licensed, conditionally licensed, or not licensed.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that a visible reasoning trace does not by itself make model behaviour monitorable, and separates four properties: visibility, mechanistic faithfulness, mechanistic localizability and behavioural monitorability. It proposes an evidential-chain reporting standard with per-claim licensing statements.
AI.motivation: A common assumption in chain-of-thought oversight is that a visible trace makes behaviour easier to monitor, but this assumption conflates distinct properties along the chain from internal computation to monitor judgments.
AI.method: The authors define four properties along the chain and present two case studies on three open-weight reasoning models. One study covers security vulnerability reasoning with probes, activation ablations and a monitor. The other covers authority-hint factual reasoning with a monitor and seven mechanistic analyses. The reporting standard requires each claim to state its target property, access tier and artifact, and to label each required link as supported, unsupported or assumed.
AI.result: In the security study, probes and ablations show internal representation and causal influence, but a monitor with the reference answer does not beat the majority-class baseline on a held-out test. In the authority-hint study, a monitor distinguishes changed from unchanged answers, but seven mechanistic analyses do not isolate a compact causal mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Evidence for one claim does not establish the others, so each claim should be reported as licensed, conditionally licensed or not licensed according to its evidential chain.

title: Local or Escalate? Post-Training Expert Routing for Real-Time Duplex Speech Models
summary: A full-duplex model should answer easy questions immediately, but hard questions often need stronger reasoning, which may require waiting. The challenge is to choose between these paths at the moment the model begins to speak. Recent systems learn related mode decisions through special-token generation inside the dialogue model, coupling routing to turn-taking and temporally annotated full-duplex training. We study a post-training alternative. We freeze MiniCPM-o 4.5, using only its speech input and output, and fit a logistic failure readout on hidden states already available at its native listen-to-speak transition. The resulting gate requires no additional model generation and exposes thresholds that can be retuned without changing the duplex policy. A probe fitted on text-input states also reads the states of spoken questions, including unseen human recordings. On the internal benchmark, selective handoff improves answer accuracy by 27.1 points. Compared with always using the expert, it reduces mean server time to first answer audio by 31.5 percent. It also outperforms matched random routing across external speech question-answering pools, as well as a zero-shot GPT-5.4 mini router that rates the transcribed question. The training recipe also transfers to a second duplex model family. These results show that an existing duplex model can be equipped to answer easy turns immediately and wait for stronger reasoning or fresher knowledge on the turns that need it, without further duplex training.

AI.tldr: The paper post-trains a routing gate for a frozen full-duplex speech model, MiniCPM-o 4.5, so it answers easy questions immediately and hands hard ones to a stronger expert. Selective handoff improves answer accuracy by 27.1 points and cuts mean server time to first answer audio by 31.5% compared with always using the expert.
AI.motivation: Full-duplex models must decide at the start of speaking whether to answer directly or wait for stronger reasoning. Recent systems learn this through special-token generation, which couples routing to turn-taking and to temporally annotated duplex training.
AI.method: The model is frozen and only its speech input and output are used. A logistic failure readout is fitted on hidden states available at the native listen-to-speak transition. The gate needs no extra generation, and its thresholds can be retuned without changing the duplex policy. A probe fitted on text-input states is also applied to spoken questions.
AI.result: On the internal benchmark, selective handoff improves answer accuracy by 27.1 points and reduces mean server time to first answer audio by 31.5% compared with always using the expert. It outperforms matched random routing across external speech QA pools and a zero-shot GPT-5.4 mini router that rates the transcribed question. The recipe also transfers to a second duplex model family.
AI.conclusion: An existing duplex model can be equipped to answer easy turns immediately and wait for stronger reasoning or fresher knowledge when needed, without further duplex training.

title: Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0: Causal World Models for Real-World Driving and Embodied Intelligence
comment: 40 pages, 20 figures. Project page: this https URL
summary: We present Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0, a unified streaming causal world model for Physical AI. It models and generates causal physical evolution in the real world, and unifies heterogeneous conditioning inputs for view-consistent generation. The architecture integrates View-Temporal Attention (VTA) to capture cross-view spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics, together with Multi-view Rotary Position Encoding (RoPE) to encode positional relationships across views and time. WorldRec 2.0 reconstructs static and dynamic 3D Gaussians from multi-view, multi-temporal observations in a single forward pass and uses their renderings as explicit scene context to preserve geometry and appearance during long-horizon generation. Conditioning inputs are fused through VAE latent concatenation in a shared representation space. We incorporate Gated Linear Attention (GLA) into the temporal layers of VTA for efficient streaming inference, reducing computation and KV-cache memory during multi-view rollouts. A physical-interaction data pipeline covers diverse interactions and long-tailed events. From Pre-train onward, these data are combined with large-scale videos and heterogeneous visual modalities to learn visual, geometric, and dynamic priors. During Mid-train, training across diverse view configurations further improves the model's ability to capture how actions and object states shape subsequent scene evolution. After distillation-based Post-train, we apply the model to closed-loop simulation, closed-loop training, and World Action Model (WAM) applications. These applications generate physically consistent future states and support world-state prediction, policy learning, and action generation for Physical AI.

AI.tldr: Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0 is a unified streaming causal world model for driving and embodied physical AI. It generates view-consistent multi-view futures and supports closed-loop simulation, closed-loop training and world action model applications.
AI.motivation: The abstract frames the work as a need for causal, view-consistent generation of physical evolution that unifies heterogeneous conditioning inputs, with efficient streaming inference over long multi-view rollouts.
AI.method: The architecture uses View-Temporal Attention for cross-view spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics, and Multi-view Rotary Position Encoding for positions across views and time. WorldRec 2.0 reconstructs static and dynamic 3D Gaussians in a single forward pass to supply explicit scene context. Conditioning inputs are fused by VAE latent concatenation, and Gated Linear Attention is added to the temporal layers. Training runs in pre-train, mid-train and distillation-based post-train stages on physical-interaction and large-scale video data.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results. It states that the model generates physically consistent future states and supports world-state prediction, policy learning and action generation.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents the model as a foundation for physical AI in driving and embodied settings, but the abstract gives no benchmark figures to support the claims.

title: SPAR: Experience-Driven Strategy Evolution in Multi-Session B2B Sales
summary: B2B outbound sales involves high transaction values and relationship-based trust, so closing a deal typically requires multiple rounds of outreach building on prior context. Existing LLM-based sales agents operate within single sessions and cannot carry forward context or refine strategies from experience. Methods that do learn from experience store lessons as unstructured text and treat all outcomes as equally informative, with no mechanism to distinguish a flawed strategy from an external factor. We propose SPAR, a self-evolving framework that models selling strategies as testable hypotheses and refines them without parameter updates. A double-loop architecture lets an inner loop adapt to individual merchants through episodic memory while an outer loop evolves a shared strategy playbook through causal attribution and hypothesis-driven evolution. In a live A/B test on the 1688 platform with over 200,000 merchants, SPAR achieves +15.8% conversion lift and +35.8% high-intent merchant growth. Human evaluation by domain experts rates SPAR at 4.62 out of 5 on overall sales quality, the highest among all methods.

AI.tldr: SPAR is a self-evolving framework that treats B2B sales strategies as testable hypotheses and refines them without parameter updates. In a live A/B test on the 1688 platform with over 200,000 merchants it achieves +15.8% conversion lift and +35.8% high-intent merchant growth.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM sales agents work within single sessions and cannot carry context forward. Experience-based methods store lessons as unstructured text and treat all outcomes as equally informative, so they cannot separate a flawed strategy from external factors.
AI.method: A double-loop architecture is used. The inner loop adapts to individual merchants through episodic memory, and the outer loop evolves a shared strategy playbook through causal attribution and hypothesis-driven evolution.
AI.result: In a live A/B test on 1688 with over 200,000 merchants, SPAR achieves +15.8% conversion lift and +35.8% high-intent merchant growth. Domain-expert human evaluation rates it 4.62 out of 5 on overall sales quality, the highest among compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Modelling strategies as hypotheses and attributing outcomes causally improves multi-session sales agents without retraining, according to both live and expert-rated evidence.

title: MemHarmBench: Evaluating Cross-Session Prompt Injection in Memory-Persistent AI Agents
summary: AI agents often rely on persistent memory to retain user preferences and operational rules across sessions. However, this capability introduces a new safety risk: malicious instructions from messages, documents, or Web content can be retained in memory and influence future tasks even after the original attack content is removed. Existing attack success metrics, however, fail to capture who is affected and how attacks translate into downstream harm during otherwise normal task execution. We introduce MemHarmBench, a victim-centric benchmark for evaluating cross-session prompt injection in memory-persistent AI agents. MemHarmBench considers three categories of potential victims: users, workspace/project owners, and external stakeholders. Our evaluation first exposes an agent to malicious instructions and tests whether they are retained in memory. We then remove the attack content and initiate a new session with a legitimate task while preserving the agent's memory. We jointly evaluate whether the agent follows the attacker's intent, completes the legitimate task, and exhibits observable execution anomalies. Across multiple agent systems, we find that cross-session attacks can remain behaviorally stealthy: agents often complete tasks normally and exhibit no detectable anomalies while still making critical decisions aligned with the attacker's intent. By connecting malicious memory retention to downstream decisions and affected parties, MemHarmBench provides a systematic framework for exposing safety risks that conventional attack- and task-success metrics may overlook. We publicly release MemHarmBench at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MemHarmBench is a victim-centric benchmark for cross-session prompt injection in memory-persistent AI agents. It finds that attacks can stay behaviourally stealthy, with agents completing tasks normally while still making decisions aligned with the attacker.
AI.motivation: Persistent memory lets malicious instructions survive into future sessions after the attack content is removed. Existing attack success metrics do not capture who is affected or how attacks turn into downstream harm.
AI.method: Agents are first exposed to malicious instructions and tested for whether they are retained in memory. The attack content is then removed and a new session with a legitimate task is started with memory preserved. Three victim categories are considered: users, workspace or project owners, and external stakeholders. Attacker intent, legitimate task completion and execution anomalies are scored jointly.
AI.result: Across multiple agent systems, cross-session attacks often remain behaviourally stealthy. Agents often complete tasks normally with no detectable anomalies while still making critical decisions aligned with the attacker's intent.
AI.conclusion: Conventional attack and task-success metrics may miss these risks, and linking memory retention to downstream decisions and affected parties exposes them. The benchmark is publicly released.

title: Just-in-Time Skill Retrieval via Long-Horizon State Tracking
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external skill libraries to support complex task execution. However, determining which skills are needed remains challenging in long-horizon tasks. Existing methods typically select a fixed skill set before execution, implicitly assuming that a task's procedural requirements can be determined from its initial description. This assumption is restrictive for long-horizon interaction, where new requirements emerge from intermediate observations, execution outcomes, and newly revealed constraints. This motivates just-in-time skill retrieval, which dynamically selects skills as execution unfolds. Just-in-time skill retrieval is promising but challenging: the utility of a skill depends not only on the current context, but also on the evolving task state shaped by prior steps. To this end, we propose JitSkill, a state-grounded framework that addresses this challenge through continuous task-state tracking. By connecting emerging requirements with accumulated task progress, JitSkill provides procedural support throughout execution without treating each retrieval decision independently. Experiments across three agent benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness in improving long-horizon task completion. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: JitSkill performs just-in-time skill retrieval for LLM agents by tracking the evolving task state, so skills are selected as execution unfolds rather than fixed before it starts. It improves long-horizon task completion across three agent benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing methods choose a fixed skill set before execution, which assumes procedural needs can be read from the initial task description. In long-horizon tasks new requirements emerge from observations, outcomes and newly revealed constraints.
AI.method: JitSkill is a state-grounded framework. It performs continuous task-state tracking and connects emerging requirements with accumulated task progress, so retrieval decisions are not made independently at each step.
AI.result: Experiments across three agent benchmarks show improved long-horizon task completion. The abstract gives no numerical figures.
AI.conclusion: Skill utility depends on the evolving task state, so state-grounded, just-in-time retrieval is a useful way to supply procedural support during long-horizon execution.

title: Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair for Safe Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models can generate task-oriented robot actions, but they do not guarantee safe execution in obstacle-rich manipulation scenes. Although CBF-QP safety filters can locally project unsafe actions into a safe set, such correction may push the robot away from the learned task trajectory and leave the VLA policy without a reliable recovery direction. We propose Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair, a post-hoc repair module that uses the short-horizon action chunk predicted by the VLA to detect blocked nominal trajectories and generate entry-exit-rejoin guidance around obstacles. The selected route is added to the CBF-QP objective as a soft guidance term, while the CBF safety constraint remains hard. On SafeLIBERO, our method improves collision avoidance, task success, and SafeSuccess compared with AEGIS. Our project page is available at GitHub.

AI.tldr: Route-Guided CBF-QP Repair is a post-hoc module that adds route guidance to a control barrier function safety filter for vision-language-action models. The safety constraint stays hard while the route is a soft term, and the method improves collision avoidance, task success and SafeSuccess over AEGIS on SafeLIBERO.
AI.motivation: VLA models do not guarantee safe execution in obstacle-rich scenes. CBF-QP safety filters can project unsafe actions into a safe set, but this can push the robot away from the learned trajectory and leave the policy without a reliable recovery direction.
AI.method: The module uses the short-horizon action chunk predicted by the VLA to detect blocked nominal trajectories. It generates entry-exit-rejoin guidance around obstacles and adds the selected route to the CBF-QP objective as a soft guidance term, while the CBF safety constraint remains hard.
AI.result: On SafeLIBERO, the method improves collision avoidance, task success and SafeSuccess compared with AEGIS. The abstract gives no numerical figures.
AI.conclusion: Route guidance can keep the safety filter from detaching the robot from the task trajectory, which supports a recovery direction for the VLA policy.

title: Delivered, Not Used: Evaluating Agent Memory at Its Point of Use
summary: Task success, retrieval quality, and cost do not show whether an LLM agent used a delivered memory or what followed from that use. We introduce MemUse, which evaluates memory at its point of use in recorded trajectories: each memory delivery is compared with what the agent could already see and followed through the agent's later actions and their consequences. An agentic judge rates each delivered entry's relevance, accuracy, novelty, influence, and observed effect; programmatic checks enforce complete reading of cited evidence, and fixed rules aggregate the ratings into verdicts linked to memory histories and delivery cost. On 8,000 SWE-bench Verified episodes from three memory systems, resolve rates stay within 0.4 percentage points of a no-memory baseline, yet MemUse shows that most delivered entries were irrelevant, most relevant entries went unused, and in two systems most deliveries restated content the agent could still see. It also surfaces effects that outcomes hide: 23.2\% of episodes with beneficial memory use still failed, and 5 of 16 with harmful use still succeeded.

AI.tldr: MemUse evaluates agent memory at its point of use by checking whether each delivered memory was relevant, accurate, novel, influential and beneficial. On 8,000 SWE-bench Verified episodes from three memory systems, resolve rates stay within 0.4 percentage points of a no-memory baseline.
AI.motivation: Task success, retrieval quality and cost do not show whether an LLM agent used a delivered memory or what followed from that use.
AI.method: Each memory delivery is compared with what the agent could already see and followed through its later actions and their consequences. An agentic judge rates relevance, accuracy, novelty, influence and observed effect. Programmatic checks enforce full reading of cited evidence, and fixed rules aggregate the ratings into verdicts linked to memory histories and delivery cost.
AI.result: Resolve rates stay within 0.4 percentage points of a no-memory baseline. Most delivered entries were irrelevant, most relevant entries went unused, and in two systems most deliveries restated content the agent could still see. Outcomes hide effects: 23.2% of episodes with beneficial memory use still failed, and 5 of 16 with harmful use still succeeded.
AI.conclusion: Outcome metrics alone are insufficient for evaluating agent memory, since point-of-use analysis reveals effects that resolve rates conceal.

title: CoGSeq-LTV: Scalable Missing-Aware Graph-Sequence Modeling for Multi-Business Transaction Analytics
summary: Large-scale super-apps generate heterogeneous transaction logs in which users interact with multiple businesses, item identifiers are only partially available, and future value targets are sparse, heavy-tailed, and cumulative over time. We study multi-business, multi-horizon value prediction as a data-intensive analytics problem over such logs, rather than as a single-table task. (i) a batch-induced user-item graph that provides collaborative signals without materializing a global graph and remains applicable when item identifiers are missing through reserved unknown-item handling, (ii) business-aware sequence encoders that preserve recency, inter-event gaps, payment context, and goods-table availability, and (iii) cross-view contrastive alignment that transfers user-level intent across businesses while retaining business-specific temporal patterns. To handle zero-inflated and long-tailed cumulative targets, CoGSeq-LTV adopts a zero-inflated mixture log-normal head with MAE-aligned point supervision and validation-calibrated zero-aware inference. Experiments on the BiBiSheng transaction-log dataset show that CoGSeq-LTV improves over representative LTV baselines across businesses and horizons, including under a later out-of-time evaluation window.

AI.tldr: CoGSeq-LTV is a graph-sequence model for multi-horizon customer value prediction on heterogeneous super-app transaction logs across several businesses. It improves over representative LTV baselines across businesses and horizons, including under a later out-of-time evaluation window.
AI.motivation: Super-app logs are heterogeneous, item identifiers are partly missing, and cumulative future value targets are sparse, heavy-tailed and zero-inflated, so single-table approaches are poorly matched to the problem.
AI.method: The model combines a batch-induced user-item graph that handles missing item identifiers through reserved unknown-item handling, business-aware sequence encoders that preserve recency, inter-event gaps, payment context and goods-table availability, and cross-view contrastive alignment across businesses. A zero-inflated mixture log-normal head with MAE-aligned point supervision and validation-calibrated zero-aware inference handles the targets.
AI.result: On the BiBiSheng transaction-log dataset, CoGSeq-LTV improves over representative LTV baselines across businesses and horizons, including under a later out-of-time evaluation window. The abstract gives no specific numerical figures.
AI.conclusion: The combined graph, sequence and contrastive design, with a zero-inflated target head, is presented as a scalable approach for multi-business value prediction.

title: NEIGHBOR: Aligning Service Behaviour and Evidence Use in an LLM Agent for Community Resident Services
summary: Residents who contact a community service desk about a repair or a service charge need answers they can act on, with facts that hold for their case and commitments the desk can keep. In tool-augmented LLM agents, such facts come from documents and records, and the conduct of a service answer is usually specified in a system prompt. We present NEIGHBOR, an LLM agent for community resident services that trains this conduct into the model that drives its tools. NEIGHBOR is deployed on a live resident-service platform for a district of an East Asian city of more than ten million people. It adapts Qwen3-235B-A22B with LoRA on 7,824 supervised fine-tuning examples built from public community-service materials around six service-behaviour targets, among them commitment control and human referral, and the adapted model plans document retrieval and read-only text-to-SQL over the resident's own records. In an offline evaluation with seven configurations, an independent domain expert rated all 350 answers to 50 stratified held-out queries. NEIGHBOR scores 7.74/10 against 5.86 for the same agent running the un-tuned model (+1.88; paired Wilcoxon $p<10^{-8}$; higher on 46 of 50 queries) and improves all six rated dimensions. No tool-augmented answer received a red-line flag (standalone models: 8-14% of answers). An LLM judge ranks the seven configurations much as the expert does (Spearman $\rho=0.93$). Its rubric counts specifics absent from the reference answer as fabricated, so it scores tool-grounded answers 1-2 points lower, enough to change which configuration ranks first. For resident-facing agents, service behaviour is a practical fine-tuning target that raises expert-rated answer quality with the tools held fixed.

AI.tldr: NEIGHBOR is an LLM agent for community resident services, with Qwen3-235B-A22B fine-tuned via LoRA to adopt service-behaviour conduct. In an expert evaluation it scores 7.74/10 against 5.86 for the un-tuned model, with the tools held fixed.
AI.motivation: Residents need answers that are actionable, factually grounded in their case and backed by commitments the desk can keep. In tool-augmented agents the conduct of a service answer is usually specified only in a system prompt.
AI.method: The agent is trained on 7,824 supervised fine-tuning examples built from public community-service materials around six service-behaviour targets, including commitment control and human referral. The adapted model plans document retrieval and read-only text-to-SQL over the resident's own records. It is deployed on a live platform for a district of an East Asian city.
AI.result: In an offline evaluation of seven configurations, a domain expert rated all 350 answers to 50 held-out queries. NEIGHBOR scores 7.74/10 against 5.86 for the un-tuned model (+1.88; paired Wilcoxon p<10^-8), higher on 46 of 50 queries, and improves all six rated dimensions. No tool-augmented answer received a red-line flag, while standalone models received flags in 8-14% of answers. An LLM judge ranks configurations much as the expert does (Spearman rho 0.93), but it penalises tool-grounded specifics by 1-2 points.
AI.conclusion: For resident-facing agents, service behaviour is a practical fine-tuning target that raises expert-rated answer quality with the tools held fixed. LLM judges need care with tool-grounded answers because their rubric can misrank configurations.

title: Intervenable Concept Dynamics for Video Activity Forecasting
summary: Concept bottleneck models route predictions through human-understandable concepts, making their intermediate states inspectable and editable. Extending this model family to forecasting requires modeling how concept activations evolve over time as objects, actions, and their interactions change, yet existing CBMs ground concepts only in observed inputs and do not forecast their future evolution. We study this problem using videos of ongoing activities and forecast future activities through a named-concept state. We propose TRACE-CBM (Temporal Relational Activity Concept Evolution), which first refines observed concept activations with sparse spatio-temporal graphs. It then recursively predicts future concept states, conditioning each transition on the prior activity distribution, and decodes both observed and predicted states with a shared activity classifier. At inference time, the model supports editing concept values, activity activations, and learned edges without parameter updates, exposing the relational spatio-temporal dependencies used for forecasting. Across multiple datasets, TRACE improves observed-activity Top-1 accuracy over concept-based methods by 1.2-8.5 percentage points and attains H3 forecast Top-1 accuracy within 1.9-2.2 points of matched black-box forecasters. Intervention experiments show concept-node edits correct 25.6-34.4% of initially incorrect H3 forecasts without flipping initially correct ones, and concept steering achieves the requested target activity in up to 90.0% of cases.

AI.tldr: TRACE-CBM is a concept bottleneck model for video activity forecasting that predicts future concept states and allows concept, activity and edge edits at inference without parameter updates. It improves observed-activity accuracy over concept-based methods by 1.2-8.5 points and comes within 1.9-2.2 points of black-box forecasters at H3.
AI.motivation: Concept bottleneck models ground concepts only in observed inputs and do not forecast how concept activations evolve as objects, actions and their interactions change.
AI.method: Observed concept activations are refined with sparse spatio-temporal graphs. The model then recursively predicts future concept states, conditioning each transition on the prior activity distribution, and decodes observed and predicted states with a shared activity classifier.
AI.result: Across multiple datasets, TRACE improves observed-activity Top-1 accuracy over concept-based methods by 1.2-8.5 points and reaches H3 forecast Top-1 accuracy within 1.9-2.2 points of matched black-box forecasters. Concept-node edits correct 25.6-34.4% of initially incorrect H3 forecasts without flipping initially correct ones, and concept steering achieves the target activity in up to 90.0% of cases.
AI.conclusion: Forecasting with named, editable concept states is competitive with black-box models and exposes the spatio-temporal dependencies used for prediction, enabling inference-time correction.

title: Diagnosing Prototype Estimation in Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning: Training-Free Geometry Selection and Unlabeled-Query Prototype Rectification
summary: Frozen visual encoders make prototype heads competitive in few-shot class-incremental learning (FSCIL), but it remains unclear how much of the residual head gap is sensitive to noisy novel-class means rather than to the subsequent changes introduced by classifier refitting. On identical features, we construct a retrospective matched counterfactual: first replace each five-shot novel mean with its complete-data counterpart under fixed cosine scoring, then fit a linear probe. Across sixteen strong encoder dataset pairs, mean replacement accounts for the majority of this ordered gap. Shot and classwise diagnostics support a finite-sample mechanism, whereas a weaker base-only encoder does not satisfy the same criterion. This diagnosis motivates ShrinkSel, a support-only selector over prototype radius and covariance shrinkage whose family contains shared LDA as an exact fallback. Across sixteen evaluated pairs, it improves LDA on fifteen by 0.04-1.52 points and selects the exact LDA endpoint on Aircraft. We further introduce Query Prototype Rectification (QPR), a batch-transductive extension that uses gated unlabeled queries to update novel directions while preserving the selected geometry. On CLIP ViT-B/16, QPR adds 1.21-2.03 points; exact query-wise self-exclusion retains the benefit, showing that the gains do not require self-inclusion. The update repairs scarce novel prototypes at a measurable base-class cost and weakens with plentiful supports or very small cohorts. Thus, the evidence available for prototype estimation is a central constraint in frozen-feature FSCIL.

AI.tldr: The paper diagnoses prototype estimation in few-shot class-incremental learning and proposes ShrinkSel, a training-free geometry selector, and QPR, a transductive query-based prototype update. On CLIP ViT-B/16, QPR adds 1.21-2.03 points.
AI.motivation: With frozen encoders, prototype heads are competitive in FSCIL, but it is unclear how much of the remaining gap comes from noisy five-shot novel-class means rather than from classifier refitting.
AI.method: A retrospective matched counterfactual replaces each five-shot novel mean with its complete-data counterpart under fixed cosine scoring, then fits a linear probe. ShrinkSel selects prototype radius and covariance shrinkage from support data, with shared LDA as an exact fallback. QPR uses gated unlabelled queries to update novel directions while preserving the selected geometry.
AI.result: Across sixteen encoder-dataset pairs, mean replacement accounts for the majority of the ordered gap. ShrinkSel improves LDA on fifteen of sixteen pairs by 0.04-1.52 points and selects the exact LDA endpoint on Aircraft. On CLIP ViT-B/16, QPR adds 1.21-2.03 points, and exact query-wise self-exclusion retains the benefit.
AI.conclusion: Evidence available for prototype estimation is a central constraint in frozen-feature FSCIL, and the update helps scarce novel prototypes at a measurable base-class cost.

title: FORCE: Factorized Object Relations for Counterfactual Editing in Video World Models
summary: World models predict how scenes evolve, but they are difficult to interrogate: given a model that forecasts a video, one cannot easily ask what would have happened had a particular interaction between two objects been different. We present Factorized Object Relations for Counterfactual Editing (FORCE), a world model that infers pairwise interactions from raw video without supervision and represents each as an explicit latent per object pair, so that a relation can be removed, changed, transferred or introduced directly. Objects are extracted by slot attention over frozen self-supervised features; a relation encoder infers each pair latent from a short observation window, and an interaction head turns it into a force. The latent is held fixed across the rollout, so an edit persists rather than being recomputed, and every edit acts on the model's own quantities with no mapping to simulator parameters. We evaluate in a simulated environment where the true outcome of an edit is available, scoring the change each edit induces against the change the simulator produces under the same operation. On held-out clips, FORCE's edits made from video agree with the simulator's response at 0.19 to 0.37 on our effect-based score; trained and scored on exact object positions instead, the same architecture reaches 0.57 to 0.85. The gap therefore lies not in the learned relational dynamics but in perception: what bounds an edit is how precisely objects can be located from video, and the precision editing needs lies just beyond what current object-centric perception delivers. Closing that gap is a concrete target for making counterfactual world models work from video.

AI.tldr: FORCE is a video world model that infers an explicit latent for each object pair, so a relation can be removed, changed, transferred or introduced as a counterfactual edit. Edits agree with the simulator at 0.19-0.37 from video, but reach 0.57-0.85 when trained on exact object positions.
AI.motivation: World models forecast video but are hard to interrogate, since it is unclear how a predicted outcome would change if an interaction between two objects were different.
AI.method: Objects are extracted by slot attention over frozen self-supervised features. A relation encoder infers a pair latent from a short observation window, and an interaction head turns it into a force. The latent is held fixed across the rollout so that an edit persists.
AI.result: On held-out clips in a simulated environment, FORCE's edits made from video agree with the simulator's response at 0.19-0.37 on the effect-based score. When trained and scored on exact object positions, the same architecture reaches 0.57-0.85.
AI.conclusion: The gap lies mainly in perception, since object localisation from video limits how precisely edits can be made. Improving object-centric perception is a concrete target for counterfactual video world models.

title: Covariance-aware Scoring: A Geometric Correction for Vision-Language Test-Time Adaptation
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, Under review at ICLR2027
summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) enables vision--language models such as CLIP to adapt to distribution shifts without labels or access to source data. Existing methods adapt through feature caching, prototype estimation, or the online accumulation of feature statistics, but most ultimately score a test feature against a class representative in the ambient embedding space, typically through cosine similarity. We identify this shared decision rule as a limitation under anisotropic feature distributions, which means when a small number of directions account for a large fraction of feature variance, the score can be dominated by high-variance directions that are not necessarily discriminative. In light of this, we propose CARe, a covariance-aware scoring for TTA that replaces the ambient geometry with a Mahalanobis geometry induced by the target feature second moment. Theoretically, we show that under a shared-covariance Gaussian model the covariance-aware decision direction coincides with that of the Bayes-optimal linear discriminant, with ambient-space scoring as the isotropic special case, and establish that the potential benefit of covariance-aware scoring grows with feature anisotropy. Empirically, we show that CARe improves adaptation accuracy over its base cosine scoring on both standard and fine-grained distribution-shift benchmarks across two backbones. Consistent with our analysis, the gains are largest on datasets whose features are most anisotropic and vanish as the features approach isotropy.

AI.tldr: CARe replaces cosine scoring in vision-language test-time adaptation with a covariance-aware Mahalanobis geometry based on the target feature second moment. It improves adaptation accuracy on standard and fine-grained shift benchmarks across two backbones, with the largest gains on the most anisotropic features.
AI.motivation: Most TTA methods score test features against class representatives with cosine similarity in the ambient space. Under anisotropic features, high-variance directions that are not discriminative can dominate the score.
AI.method: The ambient geometry is replaced by a Mahalanobis geometry induced by the target feature second moment. Under a shared-covariance Gaussian model the resulting decision direction coincides with the Bayes-optimal linear discriminant, with ambient scoring as the isotropic special case.
AI.result: CARe improves adaptation accuracy over its base cosine scoring on both standard and fine-grained distribution-shift benchmarks across two backbones. Gains are largest on the most anisotropic datasets and vanish as features approach isotropy.
AI.conclusion: The benefit of covariance-aware scoring grows with feature anisotropy, which supports the geometric correction for CLIP-based test-time adaptation.

title: The Margin Knows the Background: Uneven Abstention in Frozen Vision-Language Models
summary: Selective prediction allows a model to abstain on uncertain inputs, but a single confidence threshold can disproportionately reject examples from particular groups. We study how confidence scores produce this imbalance in frozen vision-language models (OpenAI CLIP, LAION CLIP, SigLIP). We express a family of scores, including the margin and maximum logit, through the average and the difference of the two highest class logits, and ask which carries group information. We show that equal group coverage at every threshold is equivalent to independence between the score and group membership. A randomized margin baseline tests whether a reduction in coverage disparity beats what adding noise achieves. With score choices fixed before testing, the effect of choice depends on the dataset. On Waterbirds, the margin creates coverage gaps 2.5 to 5.5 times larger than maximum logit at 80% coverage, its group signal is in the difference component, and paired background swaps show the background moves it, although maximum logit increases overall error. On NICO++, maximum logit instead increases worst-context error by 5.4 to 6.6 points and offers no improvement over the randomized baseline for OpenAI CLIP. Across both datasets, how far a score pushes a group down its ranking tracks the coverage gap (Spearman 0.88, 0.92) better than plain group identifiability (0.61, 0.65). These results explain why a score that abstains more evenly on one dataset may be less effective on another and motivate judging group coverage and selective risk together against randomized baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how confidence scores cause uneven abstention across groups in frozen CLIP-family models. It shows that the margin and maximum logit differ in group information, and that their effects depend on the dataset.
AI.motivation: A single confidence threshold for selective prediction can reject examples from particular groups disproportionately, and it is unclear how score choice produces this imbalance in frozen vision-language models.
AI.method: A family of scores, including the margin and maximum logit, is expressed through the average and difference of the two highest class logits. Equal group coverage at every threshold is shown to be equivalent to independence between score and group membership. A randomised margin baseline tests whether coverage disparity reduction beats what noise achieves.
AI.result: On Waterbirds, the margin creates coverage gaps 2.5 to 5.5 times larger than maximum logit at 80% coverage, and its group signal lies in the difference component. On NICO++, maximum logit increases worst-context error by 5.4 to 6.6 points and gives no improvement over the randomised baseline for OpenAI CLIP. Across both datasets, how far a score pushes a group down its ranking tracks the coverage gap (Spearman 0.88 and 0.92) better than plain group identifiability (0.61 and 0.65).
AI.conclusion: A score that abstains more evenly on one dataset may be less effective on another, so coverage and selective risk should be judged together against randomised baselines.

title: SFA: A Statistical Physics-Inspired Diffusion Transformer for Efficient and High-Quality Image Generation
summary: Diffusion transformers have achieved remarkable success in image generation, but accelerating attention while preserving generation quality remains a major challenge at high resolutions. Inspired by statistical physics and the widespread occurrence of scale-free laws in nature, we introduce Scale-Free Attention (SFA), which preserves fine local interactions while summarizing distant regions at progressively coarser scales. For $N$ tokens, mean pooling, token-count correction, and a shared softmax over a scale-free spatial hierarchy give SFA $O(N\log N)$ complexity in both forward and backward passes. Our Triton implementation achieves $357.3\times$ forward and $265.6\times$ backward attention speedups over FlashAttention at 262,144 tokens. After 40 epochs of PixelFlow training from scratch on ImageNet at $256\times256$ resolution, SFA achieves the best generation quality among five attention mechanisms, including full attention. Fréchet inception distance evaluated on 50,000 generated samples (FID-50k) improves from 13.25 for full attention to 12.51, and the advantage over full attention persists through 80 epochs. SFA also achieves the best generation quality among the compared efficient-attention methods on Flickr-Faces-HQ (FFHQ). Beyond training from scratch, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium with attention replaced by SFA retains the generation quality of its full-attention counterpart under matched fine-tuning budgets. We obtain similar results when fine-tuning pretrained PixelFlow on ImageNet. SFA establishes scale-free structure as an effective design principle for efficient, high-quality diffusion transformers.

AI.tldr: SFA is a diffusion transformer with Scale-Free Attention that keeps fine local interactions and summarises distant regions at coarser scales, giving O(N log N) complexity. It reports 357.3x forward and 265.6x backward attention speedups over FlashAttention at 262,144 tokens and the best FID-50k among five attention mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Accelerating attention in diffusion transformers while preserving generation quality is a major challenge at high resolution.
AI.method: Mean pooling, token-count correction and a shared softmax over a scale-free spatial hierarchy are used for N tokens, giving O(N log N) complexity in both forward and backward passes. The Triton implementation is trained with PixelFlow from scratch on ImageNet at 256x256, and Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium has its attention replaced by SFA for fine-tuning.
AI.result: At 262,144 tokens, Triton SFA gives 357.3x forward and 265.6x backward attention speedups over FlashAttention. After 40 epochs of PixelFlow training, FID-50k improves from 13.25 for full attention to 12.51, and this advantage persists through 80 epochs. SFA also gives the best quality among the efficient-attention methods compared on FFHQ, and SD 3.5 Medium with SFA retains the quality of its full-attention counterpart under matched fine-tuning budgets.
AI.conclusion: Scale-free structure is presented as an effective design principle for efficient, high-quality diffusion transformers.

title: DiA: Directional Adapter
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Joint first authors with equal contributions. Code - this https URL
summary: Fine-grained action recognition often depends on how an action unfolds over time rather than on appearance alone. Visually similar classes may differ in preparation, execution, or completion phases, making uniformly aggregated temporal context suboptimal. We study this problem under a practical objective: i) improving recognition performance with few tunable parameters, ii) being compute efficient, and iii) using only the readily available video modality. Motivated by this missing temporal observation and the accuracy--compute efficiency--unimodality objective, we propose Directional Adapter (DiA), a parameter-efficient adapter on top of CLIP. DiA formulates temporal specialization into causal and anti-causal directions, allowing past-to-present and future-to-present cues to be modeled differently. To keep this directional modeling parameter- and compute-efficient, both directions use depth-wise temporal convolutions in a compact bottleneck space and are combined through a learnable fusion. DiA achieves state-of-the-art performance among methods using a single video input modality across seven public benchmarks, with only $\sim$3.6M tunable parameters, while also delivering higher throughput and lower inference latency than prior methods. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: DiA is a parameter-efficient CLIP adapter for fine-grained action recognition that models causal and anti-causal temporal directions separately. It reaches state-of-the-art accuracy among single-video-modality methods on seven benchmarks with about 3.6M tunable parameters.
AI.motivation: Visually similar action classes can differ in preparation, execution or completion phases, so uniformly aggregated temporal context is suboptimal. The goal is accuracy with few tunable parameters, compute efficiency and only the video modality.
AI.method: The adapter splits temporal specialisation into causal past-to-present and anti-causal future-to-present directions. Both use depth-wise temporal convolutions in a compact bottleneck and are combined through a learnable fusion.
AI.result: DiA achieves state-of-the-art performance among single-video-modality methods across seven public benchmarks with about 3.6M tunable parameters, and it delivers higher throughput and lower inference latency than prior methods.
AI.conclusion: Directional temporal modelling is an efficient way to add temporal specialisation to CLIP for action recognition using video alone.

title: Monocular Badminton Speed Estimation with Air Drag and Court Geometry
summary: A single camera cannot distinguish between a slowly moving object nearby and a rapidly moving object in the distance without additional information. For a shuttlecock, air drag provides a strong deceleration cue that can be combined with known court geometry. We fit a gravity-and-drag trajectory to smartphone video and compare a free monocular fit with a fit constrained to cross the net plane. Camera calibration uses court lines, and the trajectory is fitted to observed shuttle positions and frame timestamps by robust nonlinear least squares. We evaluated 51 badminton shots from two recording sessions, spanning drop shots, drives, half-smashes and smashes. The net-plane fit reduced the median absolute speed difference from a drag-based stereo reference from 13.3% to 8.6%. A second reference, obtained by differentiating triangulated positions without a drag model, also gave a smaller median difference for the net-plane fit. The results support combining court geometry with flight dynamics for badminton speed estimation from a single camera.

AI.tldr: The paper estimates badminton shuttlecock speed from a single smartphone camera by fitting a gravity-and-drag trajectory, with and without a constraint to cross the net plane. The net-plane fit reduces the median absolute speed difference from a drag-based stereo reference from 13.3% to 8.6%.
AI.motivation: A single camera cannot tell a slow object nearby from a fast object far away without extra information, and for shuttlecocks air drag provides a deceleration cue that can be combined with known court geometry.
AI.method: Camera calibration uses court lines. A gravity-and-drag trajectory is fitted to observed shuttle positions and frame timestamps by robust nonlinear least squares, comparing a free monocular fit with a fit constrained to cross the net plane.
AI.result: On 51 shots from two sessions, spanning drop shots, drives, half-smashes and smashes, the net-plane fit reduces the median absolute speed difference from a drag-based stereo reference from 13.3% to 8.6%. A second reference, from differentiating triangulated positions without a drag model, also gives a smaller median difference for the net-plane fit.
AI.conclusion: Combining court geometry with flight dynamics supports speed estimation for badminton from a single camera.

title: Gaussifier: Fast 2D Gaussian Decomposition
summary: 2D Gaussians render images at thousands of frames per second. However, fitting an image takes seconds of optimization. This confines 2D Gaussians to offline use. Feedforward methods are faster but less accurate without per-image fine-tuning. We present Gaussifier, a lightweight feedforward framework for 2D Gaussian decomposition. We learn a density map of Gaussian centers from per-image fitting data. Equal-mass Voronoi places Gaussians so that each Voronoi cell holds approximately equal density. A stateless, reusable network then refines the output in a few iterations. Gaussifier reaches 40.73/38.61\,dB PSNR on Kodak-24/DIV2K at over 60 FPS. At the same Gaussian count, it exceeds every feedforward baseline by 3.0 to 15.6\,dB in PSNR. With fewer Gaussians than any baseline, it still leads the strongest one by 2.5 to 3.5\,dB. At the same count, baselines with their own per-image fitting need 26 to 326 times longer to reach its PSNR. Gaussifier makes high-fidelity 2D Gaussian images fast and light enough for real-time applications. We release code, weights and a browser-based WebGPU demo at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Gaussifier is a feedforward framework for 2D Gaussian image decomposition that places Gaussians by equal-mass Voronoi partitioning of a learned density map and refines them with a reusable network. It reaches 40.73 dB PSNR on Kodak-24 and 38.61 dB on DIV2K at over 60 FPS.
AI.motivation: 2D Gaussians render images very quickly, but fitting an image takes seconds of optimisation, which confines them to offline use. Existing feedforward methods are faster but less accurate without per-image fine-tuning.
AI.method: A density map of Gaussian centres is learned from per-image fitting data. Equal-mass Voronoi partitioning places Gaussians so that each cell holds approximately equal density. A stateless, reusable network then refines the output over a few iterations.
AI.result: Gaussifier reaches 40.73 dB PSNR on Kodak-24 and 38.61 dB on DIV2K at over 60 FPS. At the same Gaussian count it exceeds every feedforward baseline by 3.0 to 15.6 dB, and with fewer Gaussians it leads the strongest baseline by 2.5 to 3.5 dB. Baselines with per-image fitting need 26 to 326 times longer to reach its PSNR at the same count.
AI.conclusion: The method makes high-fidelity 2D Gaussian images fast and light enough for real-time applications, and code, weights and a WebGPU demo are released.

title: Multimodal Cross-Condition Learning for Temporal Sentence Grounding in Videos
summary: Temporal sentence grounding requires a video representation that preserves query-relevant evidence and a sentence representation that reflects the visual context in which it is interpreted. Prior end-to-end grounding addresses the first requirement through sentence-conditioned visual adaptation, but leaves the language representation independent of the video. This work proposes Multimodal Cross-Condition Learning (MCCL). Its Video Prefix Adapter (VPA) converts pooled visual context into a sequence of continuous tokens that condition a frozen DistilBERT encoder. Combined with the Sentence Conditioned Adapter (SCADA), VPA supports an ordered exchange from vision to language and back to vision. A comprehensive study examines two video backbones, LSTM and Mamba temporal modules, and four conditioning modes on two datasets. Bidirectional conditioning exceeds the stronger one-way mode by 1.6--2.3 mIoU points in all four Charades-STA settings. ActivityNet Captions exhibits a different pattern: bidirectionality helps I3D--Mamba, whereas video-to-text conditioning is stronger with C3D. The study extends one-way visual adaptation into a configurable multimodal framework and reports descriptive gains over the corresponding baselines.

AI.tldr: MCCL is a multimodal cross-condition framework for temporal sentence grounding in which video and language condition each other through a Video Prefix Adapter and a Sentence Conditioned Adapter. Bidirectional conditioning beats the stronger one-way mode by 1.6-2.3 mIoU points in all four Charades-STA settings.
AI.motivation: Prior end-to-end grounding adapts the visual representation to the sentence, but leaves the language representation independent of the video.
AI.method: The Video Prefix Adapter converts pooled visual context into continuous tokens that condition a frozen DistilBERT encoder. Combined with the Sentence Conditioned Adapter, it supports an ordered exchange from vision to language and back to vision. The study compares LSTM and Mamba temporal modules and four conditioning modes on two datasets.
AI.result: Bidirectional conditioning exceeds the stronger one-way mode by 1.6-2.3 mIoU points in all four Charades-STA settings. On ActivityNet Captions the pattern differs: bidirectionality helps I3D with Mamba, whereas video-to-text conditioning is stronger with C3D. The gains over the corresponding baselines are descriptive.
AI.conclusion: The one-way visual adaptation is extended into a configurable multimodal framework, and the best conditioning mode depends on dataset and backbone.

title: A Trustworthy Clinical Decision Support Framework for Brain Tumor MRI Classification: Integrating Attention-Guided Learning, Explainable AI, and Out-of-Distribution Validation
comment: Accepted for presentation at the IC3AI-2026 IEEE conference in Dec 2026. It has been accepted/selected but is not yet published. 6 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables
summary: Deep learning models for brain tumor diagnosis need to do more than achieve high classification accuracy. For practical use, they should also provide understandable predictions, recognize unsuitable inputs, and work within a usable clinical system. This paper presents a framework for classifying brain MRI into four categories: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor. The model uses InceptionResNetV2 with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM), while Grad-CAM provides visual explanations of its predictions. A two-stage out-of-distribution (OOD) mechanism screens unsuitable inputs using an initial grayscale check followed by Mahalanobis distance, softmax confidence, and predictive entropy. These components are brought together in NeuroScan AI, a real-time web application. Evaluated on a Mendeley brain tumor MRI dataset of 12,064 images, the framework achieved 98.70% validation accuracy, 96.73% test accuracy, and a macro-average AUC of 0.9965. The OOD pipeline achieved 99% detection accuracy on a preliminary 100-image benchmark. Grad-CAM visualizations showed qualitative correspondence with clinically established tumor locations across all four classes. Overall, the work brings classification, explainability, input validation, and deployment into one framework, while recognizing that broader clinical and OOD validation is still required.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a brain tumour MRI framework that combines InceptionResNetV2 with CBAM, Grad-CAM explanations and a two-stage out-of-distribution screen, deployed as the NeuroScan AI web application. It reports 96.73% test accuracy and a macro-average AUC of 0.9965 on a 12,064-image dataset.
AI.motivation: Clinical brain tumour diagnosis needs more than accuracy. Predictions should be understandable, unsuitable inputs should be recognised, and the system should be usable in practice.
AI.method: InceptionResNetV2 with a Convolutional Block Attention Module classifies four classes: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumour and no tumour. Grad-CAM gives visual explanations. A two-stage OOD mechanism uses a grayscale check, followed by Mahalanobis distance, softmax confidence and predictive entropy.
AI.result: On a Mendeley brain tumour MRI dataset of 12,064 images, the framework achieves 98.70% validation accuracy, 96.73% test accuracy and a macro-average AUC of 0.9965. The OOD pipeline achieves 99% detection accuracy on a preliminary 100-image benchmark. Grad-CAM maps show qualitative correspondence with clinically established tumour locations across all four classes.
AI.conclusion: Classification, explainability, input validation and deployment are combined in one framework, though the authors state that broader clinical and OOD validation is still required.

title: Selective Positional Allocation for Noise-Robust Query Retrieval in Small-Object Detection
summary: In aerial and remote-sensing imagery, detecting tiny targets is frequently hampered less by the representational capacity of the backbone network than by the manner in which positional priors are distributed across ill-defined foreground and background regions. We introduce SPAR (Selective Positional Allocation and Retrieval), a detection framework that re-conceptualizes positional cues as an allocatable resource: they are intensified at semantically meaningful locations while responses driven by scene clutter are actively attenuated. At the heart of SPAR lies Selective Positional Embedding (SPE), an interpretable embedding mechanism paired with an activation-bar visualization that facilitates direct inspection and hyper-parameter tuning. The encoder branch, termed MOHFE, fuses heatmap-modulated positional signals with category-specific and box-level evidence to yield more compact multi-scale features; the decoder branch, termed HIDQ, employs a foreground gating operation to discard background-dominated candidates prior to query decoding. To cope with the extreme sparsity of small-object evidence, we additionally design DPSConv (Dual-Path Sampling Convolution), which augments retrieval-oriented representations through two geometrically complementary sampling routes. Notably, all heatmap supervision is derived from existing detection objectives and consumed exclusively during training, requiring no auxiliary heatmap annotations and leaving inference as an ordinary forward pass with no additional gradient overhead. Comprehensive evaluations on DOTA, DIOR, VisDrone, PASCAL VOC, NWPU VHR-10, and AITOD demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed design: relative to the baseline, SPAR attains an improvement of up to 9.1 percentage points, shortens the decoder from eight layers to three, and reduces model parameters by 59.4% (66.3M versus 163M).

AI.tldr: SPAR is a small-object detection framework for aerial imagery that reweights positional cues with Selective Positional Embedding, gates background candidates in the decoder and uses DPSConv for sparse small-object evidence. It improves on the baseline by up to 9.1 percentage points and cuts parameters by 59.4%.
AI.motivation: In aerial and remote-sensing imagery, tiny targets are hampered less by backbone capacity than by how positional priors are distributed across ambiguous foreground and background regions.
AI.method: Selective Positional Embedding intensifies positional cues at semantically meaningful locations and attenuates clutter-driven responses. The MOHFE encoder fuses heatmap-modulated positional signals with category and box-level evidence. The HIDQ decoder applies foreground gating to discard background-dominated candidates before query decoding. DPSConv uses two geometrically complementary sampling routes. Heatmap supervision comes from existing detection objectives and is used only in training.
AI.result: Across DOTA, DIOR, VisDrone, PASCAL VOC, NWPU VHR-10 and AITOD, SPAR improves on the baseline by up to 9.1 percentage points, shortens the decoder from eight layers to three, and reduces parameters by 59.4% (66.3M versus 163M).
AI.conclusion: Positional cues treated as an allocatable resource, with gating at the decoder, give accuracy and efficiency gains for small-object detection without extra annotation.

title: From Single-Shot QA to Continuous Perception: Revisiting the Energy Composition and Optimization Boundary of Edge VLMs
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at IEEE International Conference on Data Mining 2026 Teen Research Track
summary: Visual-prefill energy conclusions for edge vision-language models (VLMs) are commonly drawn under single-shot workloads; we revisit them under continuous perception. Profiling nine VLMs across three architecture families on Jetson AGX Thor and Orin (4,508 records, calibrated with a pure-text task), we find two mutually independent energy laws: the per-output-token decode cost grows monotonically with model scale, whereas the visual-prefill (image-encoding) cost is dominated by visual-encoder architectural efficiency, not scale. Under continuous perception ($N{=}10$) with sparse output, visual-prefill energy reaches 92--97\% of total. We derive optimization strategies---visual frame reuse, adaptive output truncation, task-aware routing, and encoder throughput optimization---for edge VLM deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits the energy composition of edge VLMs under continuous perception and finds that visual-prefill energy dominates when output is sparse. Across nine VLMs on Jetson AGX Thor and Orin, prefill cost depends on encoder architecture rather than model scale.
AI.motivation: Conclusions about visual-prefill energy for edge VLMs are usually drawn from single-shot workloads, and the authors question whether they hold under continuous perception.
AI.method: Nine VLMs from three architecture families are profiled on Jetson AGX Thor and Orin, yielding 4,508 records calibrated with a pure-text task. The per-output-token decode cost and the visual-prefill cost are analysed separately under continuous perception with N=10 frames.
AI.result: Two independent energy laws are found. Per-output-token decode cost grows monotonically with model scale, whereas visual-prefill cost is dominated by visual-encoder architectural efficiency rather than scale. Under continuous perception with N=10 and sparse output, visual-prefill energy reaches 92-97% of the total.
AI.conclusion: Optimisation strategies for edge VLM deployment include visual frame reuse, adaptive output truncation, task-aware routing and encoder throughput optimisation.

title: Deep Learning for Detecting Building Setback Rule Violations in Urban Planning: A Case Study on Bangladesh
summary: Dhaka's rapid urban growth has made building setback violations common, narrowing footpaths and blocking emergency access. RAJUK, responsible for building control in the Dhaka Metropolitan Area, enforces setback rules mainly through manual field inspection, which scales poorly. We present a systematic comparison of four machine learning approaches for classifying building setback conditions from street-level photographs: negative (compliant), moderate (borderline), and positive (violation). We built a labeled dataset of 372 geo-tagged images from sixteen Dhaka neighborhoods and expanded it with 5,968 augmented copies for training. We trained and evaluated a multi-layer perceptron (MLP), a Random Forest ensemble on frozen ResNet50 embeddings, a support vector machine on frozen ResNet18 embeddings, and a fine-tuned ResNet18 CNN. On a 1,275-image test set, the fine-tuned CNN achieved 65.4% accuracy (macro-F1 0.50), followed by Random Forest at 59.9% (macro-F1 0.44) and SVM at 58.2% (macro-F1 0.45). All models classify the compliant class reliably but struggle with the borderline moderate class due to visual ambiguity. These results establish reference performance levels for automated setback-compliance screening in a South Asian regulatory setting.

AI.tldr: The paper compares four machine learning approaches for classifying building setback conditions in Dhaka from street-level photographs. The fine-tuned ResNet18 CNN is best at 65.4% accuracy on a 1,275-image test set, and all models struggle with the borderline moderate class.
AI.motivation: RAJUK enforces setback rules mainly through manual field inspection, which scales poorly as Dhaka grows and narrows footpaths and blocks emergency access.
AI.method: The authors built a labelled dataset of 372 geo-tagged images from sixteen Dhaka neighbourhoods, expanded with 5,968 augmented copies for training. They evaluate an MLP, a Random Forest on frozen ResNet50 embeddings, an SVM on frozen ResNet18 embeddings and a fine-tuned ResNet18 CNN, classifying negative, moderate and positive setbacks.
AI.result: On the 1,275-image test set, the fine-tuned CNN achieves 65.4% accuracy (macro-F1 0.50), followed by Random Forest at 59.9% (macro-F1 0.44) and SVM at 58.2% (macro-F1 0.45). All models classify the compliant class reliably but struggle with the borderline moderate class.
AI.conclusion: The results set reference performance levels for automated setback-compliance screening in a South Asian regulatory setting.

title: Beyond Black Boxes: An Ontology Based Vision Framework for Transparent Fruit Disease Detection
summary: Efficiency and reliability in the timely identification of phytopathogens would help minimize crop loss in agricultural sectors but existing deep learning based methods, although accurate, would require a large annotated dataset and are black-boxed in their operation, thus, restricting flexibility and transparency. The current paper presents a hybrid detection framework that is able to overcome these drawbacks through the unified real-time vision with a semantic knowledge base. Web Ontology Language (OWL) was used to develop a comprehensive ontology of the disease of fruits that formally codifies phytopathological knowledge, such as symptom phenotype, spectral phenotype (HSV), and morphological phenotype. Such knowledge-guided configuration guides the image processing pipeline, making it possible to diagnose using this knowledge under expert specified rules without a large training dataset. The ontology underwent a computationally verified test of its structural soundness and commonsensical practical usefulness and scored an overall of 7.4/10. On the public set of MangoFruitDDS, the diagnostic performance was an F1 Score of 85.00%, precision of 85.00%, and a recall of 85.23%. These findings are very competitive and similar to other known deep learning models like the VGG16 that prove that the knowledge-driven approach provides an accurate, transparent, and scalable solution on automated fruit disease diagnosis.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an ontology-based vision framework for fruit disease detection that uses an OWL ontology of phytopathological knowledge to guide image processing without a large training set. On the MangoFruitDDS set it reports an F1 score of 85.00%, close to VGG16-level deep learning results.
AI.motivation: Deep learning detectors for phytopathogens need large annotated datasets and are black boxes, which limits flexibility and transparency.
AI.method: A Web Ontology Language ontology encodes symptom, spectral (HSV) and morphological phenotypes of fruit diseases. This knowledge configures the image-processing pipeline and lets diagnosis follow expert-specified rules. The ontology was checked for structural soundness and practical usefulness and scored 7.4/10.
AI.result: On the public MangoFruitDDS set, the diagnostic performance is an F1 score of 85.00%, precision of 85.00% and recall of 85.23%. The authors describe these as competitive with deep learning models such as VGG16.
AI.conclusion: A knowledge-driven approach can provide accurate, transparent and scalable automated fruit disease diagnosis, according to the authors.

title: Real-Time Obstacle Detection and Distance Estimation on Smartphones for Visually Impaired and Distracted Pedestrians
summary: According to the World Health Organization, at least 2.2 billion people worldwide live with visual impairment, including tens of millions with severe vision loss. Traditional aids such as white canes or guide dogs remain costly, limited in capability, and inaccessible to many. At the same time, smartphone distraction in public spaces has been linked to elevated risks of collisions with vehicles, trips, and falls. These dual challenges motivate lightweight, smartphone-based solutions that combine accessibility with low latency. We present a Kotlin-based Android application that uses a YOLOv8 detector, retrained to recognize eighteen common urban obstacle classes, to deliver real-time obstacle alerts for both user groups. The detector was optimized with pruning, quantization, and early-exit branches, and deployed through the Android Neural Networks API (NNAPI), which can dispatch inference to GPU, NPU, or DSP accelerators when available. On a mid-range smartphone, these optimizations reduced average inference latency from about 3.2 s for the off-the-shelf YOLOv8n to 0.39-0.48 s; the recommended configuration (INT8 quantization with early exit) runs in 0.42-0.48 s while retaining a recall of 0.81. The application combines the optimized detector with ARCore-based or monocular focal-length distance estimation, so it works with a single smartphone camera and requires no LiDAR, depth camera, or other specialized sensor. Multimodal feedback, including Text-to-Speech guidance for visually impaired users and vibration alerts for distracted pedestrians, supports use across different contexts.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a Kotlin Android app that gives real-time obstacle alerts to visually impaired and distracted pedestrians using an optimised YOLOv8 detector and smartphone-only distance estimation. The recommended INT8 with early-exit configuration runs in 0.42-0.48 s with recall 0.81 on a mid-range phone.
AI.motivation: At least 2.2 billion people have visual impairment, aids such as canes and guide dogs are costly or limited, and smartphone distraction in public spaces raises the risk of collisions, trips and falls.
AI.method: A YOLOv8 detector is retrained for eighteen urban obstacle classes and optimised with pruning, quantisation and early-exit branches. It is deployed through the Android NNAPI, which can use GPU, NPU or DSP accelerators. Distance comes from ARCore or monocular focal-length estimation. Feedback is text-to-speech for visually impaired users and vibration for distracted pedestrians.
AI.result: On a mid-range smartphone, the optimisations reduce average inference latency from about 3.2 s for off-the-shelf YOLOv8n to 0.39-0.48 s. The recommended INT8 with early-exit configuration runs in 0.42-0.48 s and retains recall of 0.81.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight single-camera smartphone detection with multimodal feedback is presented as practical for both user groups, without LiDAR or depth sensors.

title: Think Before You Locate: Clinical Chain-of-Though Supervision for Sequential Medical Image Grounding
summary: Clinicians rarely localize a finding from one image alone. They compare current and prior scans, follow structures across slices, and match regions across views or modalities. Yet vision-language models for sequential medical grounding usually learn only from bounding boxes. Boxes show where the target is, but they do not explain why that region in that image answers the question. We study whether explicit, image-grounded reasoning can improve localization, and which tasks benefit from it. We introduce method, whose core is MedChain, a corpus of 182,573 filtered rationales spanning eight sequential grounding tasks and ten imaging modalities. A medical VLM (FlemingVL-38B) first drafts a caption-like rationale, and a multimodal refiner (Qwen3.5-397B-A17B) then re-examines the images, question and annotated box to write a box-conditioned explanation with explicit cross-image reasoning. We fine-tune Qwen3.5 on these rationales with deliberative chain-of-thought supervision (dCoT-SFT). Across 4B, 9B, and 27B models, dCoT-SFT sets a new state of the art on MedSG-Bench. The 27B model reaches 77.24 mIoU and 85.20 Acc@0.5, improving over the strongest prior model by 4.69 and 5.49 points. In a paired comparison using fixed 4B checkpoints, dCoT-SFT improves over answer-only SFT by 3.56 mIoU (95% CI 3.13--4.00). The gains mainly come from change detection and object tracking, while performance drops on three appearance-matching tasks. Replacing a model's own rationale with a rationale from another task reduces mIoU by 12.2 points, showing that localization depends strongly on the reasoning context. Finally, adding GRPO with an IoU reward after dCoT-SFT gives only small and task-dependent gains, which we analyze through controlled multi-seed development experiments.

AI.tldr: MedChain is a corpus of 182,573 box-conditioned rationales used to fine-tune Qwen3.5 with deliberative chain-of-thought supervision for sequential medical image grounding. The 27B model reaches 77.24 mIoU and 85.20 Acc@0.5 on MedSG-Bench, improving on the strongest prior model by 4.69 and 5.49 points.
AI.motivation: Clinicians localise findings by comparing scans over time and across views, but vision-language grounding models learn only from bounding boxes, which show where a target is but not why that region answers the question.
AI.method: A medical VLM drafts caption-like rationales and a multimodal refiner re-examines the images, question and annotated box to write box-conditioned explanations with cross-image reasoning. Qwen3.5 is fine-tuned on these with dCoT-SFT across 4B, 9B and 27B models. GRPO with an IoU reward is added after dCoT-SFT.
AI.result: dCoT-SFT sets a new state of the art on MedSG-Bench. The 27B model reaches 77.24 mIoU and 85.20 Acc@0.5, improving on the strongest prior model by 4.69 and 5.49 points. In a paired comparison with 4B checkpoints, dCoT-SFT improves over answer-only SFT by 3.56 mIoU (95% CI 3.13-4.00). Gains come mainly from change detection and object tracking, while three appearance-matching tasks drop. Replacing a model's own rationale with one from another task reduces mIoU by 12.2 points. GRPO gives only small, task-dependent gains.
AI.conclusion: Explicit image-grounded reasoning improves sequential medical localisation, but its benefit depends on the task and on the reasoning context used.
