title: Diagnosing Zero-Shot Forgetting in CLIP Fine-Tuning: Attention Drift Characterizes Adaptation, Representation Drift Predicts Transfer Degradation
comment: Accepted to the ICDM 2026 Workshops (ICDMW), Teen Research Track
summary: Fine-tuning CLIP on a downstream task typically reduces its zero-shot accuracy on other tasks, and quantifying this loss ordinarily requires a labeled transfer benchmark. We study whether the loss can be anticipated from unlabeled target images that are already available during fine-tuning. Four signals are compared: the entropy of CLS token attention, linear centered kernel alignment (CKA) with the pretrained model, embedding drift, and relative weight change. ViT-B/32 is adapted by full fine-tuning (Full FT) and by LoRA on EuroSAT and Oxford-IIIT Pets over four learning rates and three seeds, with an additional ViT-B/16 grid; DTD and GTSRB are held out as confirmation targets, and forgetting is measured as zero-shot retention on CIFAR-100, Food-101, and ImageNet-R. Within a fixed configuration, the change in attention entropy is strongly associated with forgetting (mean $|\rho|=0.860$). Its sign, however, depends on the dataset, the adaptation method, and the backbone, and the pooled correlation falls to 0.361. A block decomposition shows that this sign is determined almost entirely by blocks 7 to 12. CKA ranks runs by retention at $\rho=0.960$, and the ranking is already established after the first of six epochs ($\rho=0.959$). On the held-out targets, CKA reaches $\rho=0.95$, and the block account correctly predicts the sign of the attention change for both datasets. These results support a simple decision rule: CKA is suited to comparisons across configurations, whereas attention entropy is informative only within a single configuration. The evidence is limited to one model family and short training schedules.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that the change in CLIP's attention entropy during fine-tuning tracks zero-shot forgetting only within one configuration, whereas linear CKA with the pretrained model ranks runs by retention across configurations. The authors recommend CKA for cross-configuration comparison.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning CLIP usually reduces zero-shot accuracy elsewhere, and measuring this loss normally needs a labelled transfer benchmark. The authors ask whether it can be anticipated from unlabelled target images available during fine-tuning.
AI.method: Four signals are compared: CLS attention entropy, linear CKA with the pretrained model, embedding drift and relative weight change. ViT-B/32 is adapted by full fine-tuning and LoRA on EuroSAT and Oxford-IIIT Pets over four learning rates and three seeds, with an extra ViT-B/16 grid. DTD and GTSRB are held-out confirmation targets, and forgetting is measured as zero-shot retention on CIFAR-100, Food-101 and ImageNet-R.
AI.result: Within a fixed configuration, the change in attention entropy is strongly associated with forgetting (mean absolute rho 0.860), but its sign depends on dataset, method and backbone, and the pooled correlation falls to 0.361. The sign is set almost entirely by blocks 7 to 12. CKA ranks runs by retention at rho 0.960, and this is established after the first of six epochs (rho 0.959). On held-out targets CKA reaches rho 0.95, and the block account predicts the sign of attention change for both datasets.
AI.conclusion: CKA suits comparisons across configurations, whereas attention entropy is informative only within a single configuration. The evidence covers one model family and short schedules.

title: Out-of-distribution AI-generated image detection with zero-phase deconvolution for residual whitening
summary: Current AI-generated image detection methods struggle in out-of-distribution testing conditions because detectors are usually not robust when evaluated on generators not included in the training set. This work explores a way to mitigate the forensic bias between sources of images -whether real or generated -by removing generator-specific fingerprints. This new training process can be approximated by pre-processing involving a deconvolution operation designed to remove correlated noise patterns inducing loss of generalization. Indeed, we show that whitening the spatial distribution of the image noise residuals can significantly improve the performance of detectors on images coming from generators unseen during training. In particular, an end-to-end CNN model trained on whitened image residuals improves detection by 12.6% on average compared to a training involving original images.

AI.tldr: The paper whitens image noise residuals with a zero-phase deconvolution before training a CNN detector of AI-generated images. This improves detection on unseen generators by 12.6% on average compared with training on original images.
AI.motivation: AI-generated image detectors often fail on generators not in their training set, because they are not robust to generator-specific fingerprints and correlated noise patterns.
AI.method: A deconvolution operation removes correlated noise patterns from image residuals, approximating a training process that removes generator-specific fingerprints. An end-to-end CNN is trained on the whitened residuals.
AI.result: An end-to-end CNN trained on whitened image residuals improves detection by 12.6% on average on images from generators unseen during training, compared with training on original images.
AI.conclusion: Whitening the spatial distribution of noise residuals is presented as a way to improve out-of-distribution generalisation of AI-generated image detectors.

title: SparseWAM: Driving World-Action Models are Worth 16 Register Tokens
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) transfer scene-dynamics priors to planning by jointly forecasting future scenes and ego trajectories. However, WAMs built on video generators must generate dense future videos at inference, incurring prohibitive latency, while efficient variants discard the world branch at deployment and thus forgo test-time imagination. Even when dense video latents are replaced with patch-level DINO or JEPA features, these representations still involve long token sequences and encode decision-irrelevant information. We therefore propose SparseWAM, which forecasts in a sparse register space of only 16 tokens per frame, compressed from frozen DINOv2 features and shaped by joint planning-and-scoring pretraining to concentrate decision-relevant information. Within this space, SparseWAM employs a modality-decoupled Mixture-of-Transformers with a causal attention mask that lets action tokens condition on imagined future registers, retaining explicit imagine-then-act reasoning at deployment. Its compactness further enables low-cost multimodal sampling. As a result, our SparseWAM achieves 92.6 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and 39.6 on NavHard at only 164 ms latency, roughly 1/5 that of DriveVA, demonstrating the efficiency of the sparse register space. Code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: SparseWAM is a driving world-action model that forecasts future scenes and ego trajectories in a sparse space of 16 register tokens per frame compressed from frozen DINOv2 features. It reaches 92.6 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 at 164 ms latency, about one fifth of DriveVA.
AI.motivation: World action models built on video generators must produce dense future videos at inference, which is slow, while efficient variants drop the world branch and lose test-time imagination. Patch-level DINO or JEPA features still give long token sequences and carry decision-irrelevant information.
AI.method: Features are compressed to 16 register tokens per frame and shaped by joint planning-and-scoring pretraining. A modality-decoupled Mixture-of-Transformers with a causal attention mask lets action tokens condition on imagined future registers, which keeps explicit imagine-then-act reasoning at deployment. The compactness also enables low-cost multimodal sampling.
AI.result: SparseWAM achieves 92.6 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 39.6 on NavHard at 164 ms latency, roughly one fifth of the latency of DriveVA.
AI.conclusion: The sparse register space shows that compact, decision-relevant world-model representations can keep imagine-then-act reasoning while greatly reducing latency. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Faces or Models? Where the Age Gap in Facial Expression Recognition Comes From
summary: Facial expression recognition (FER) systems are increasingly used in elder care, yet their accuracy on older faces is rarely measured. This study evaluated five open-source FER models on the FACES database, which holds 2,052 posed photographs of 171 adults aged 19 to 80. The models cross three architectures (ResNet-18, POSTER++ and QCS) with two training datasets (RAF-DB and AffectNet). All models lost accuracy on older faces by 11.7 to 15.2 percentage points. Older faces were harder for people too: human raters lost 8.6 points, a classifier using only facial geometry lost 8.3, and for anger, fear, and happiness older adults differed more from one another when posing. On specific expressions the models fell much further than people did. AffectNet-trained models misread older neutral faces as sad or angry 62% of the time. RAF-DB-trained models lost fear, disgust, and anger instead. The gap persisted after controlling for architecture, image quality, cropping, and expression intensity. When only the final classification layer was refitted on older faces, the gap shrank from 11 to 21 points to 4 points or less, suggesting that the models' learned features can represent older faces and that the deficit lies in how the final layer was trained.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates five open-source facial expression recognition models on older faces and finds accuracy drops of 11.7-15.2 points. Refitting only the final classification layer on older faces shrinks the gap to 4 points or less, which suggests the deficit lies in training of the final layer rather than in learned features.
AI.motivation: FER systems are increasingly used in elder care, yet their accuracy on older faces is rarely measured.
AI.method: Five models cross three architectures (ResNet-18, POSTER++ and QCS) with two training datasets (RAF-DB and AffectNet), evaluated on the FACES database of 2,052 posed photographs of 171 adults aged 19 to 80. The gap is tested after controlling for architecture, image quality, cropping and expression intensity. Only the final classification layer is refitted on older faces in a follow-up experiment.
AI.result: All models lose 11.7-15.2 points on older faces. Human raters lose 8.6 points and a geometry-only classifier loses 8.3 points. AffectNet-trained models misread older neutral faces as sad or angry 62% of the time, and RAF-DB-trained models lose fear, disgust and anger. When only the final layer is refitted, the gap shrinks from 11-21 points to 4 points or less.
AI.conclusion: The learned features can represent older faces, and the deficit lies largely in how the final layer was trained, so refitting the head is a practical remedy to test.

title: Circumpolar Wall-to-Wall Detection of Retrogressive Thaw Slumps with Scarce Labels and Extreme Class Imbalance
summary: Retrogressive thaw slumps (RTS) are among the most dynamic ground deformations caused by permafrost thaw. Abrupt thaw processes such as RTS could roughly double the contribution of permafrost thaw to climate warming, and already threaten a third of Arctic infrastructure. Circumpolar RTS mapping has advanced quickly, yet released inventories together cover only part of the permafrost region. RTS occupy only 0.1-0.5% of image tiles and labels are costly, so a detector must be designed and evaluated as a rare-target problem. We therefore developed a deep learning system and mapped 20.68 M square kilometres of circumpolar permafrost using 41.6 M tiles of 4.8 m PlanetScope imagery. Training used 22,259 tiles with 2,609 RTS instances in 1,718 of them, and the model was tuned through 172 controlled experiments. A convolutional network matched every alternative tested, including multimodal fusion, foundation-model encoders and masked-autoencoder pretraining, each at far more compute for similar or worse results. Labelled data moved performance most, and a foundation model's advantage appeared only when labels were scarce. Tested once on held-out ecoregions at the real-world prevalence of 0.1-0.5%, the final model achieved an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.812-0.855, an object precision of 0.854 and F1 of 0.644. Deployed wall-to-wall, the model produced a circumpolar map of 19,068 high-confidence detections whose sampled precision ranges from 0.54 to 0.90 by size class. We present an evaluation protocol for rare targets, a controlled account of what governs accuracy under scarce labels, and the circumpolar RTS map the validated model produced.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a deep learning system that maps retrogressive thaw slumps across circumpolar permafrost from 4.8 m PlanetScope imagery and proposes an evaluation protocol for rare targets. On held-out ecoregions at real prevalence, the final model reaches a PR-AUC of 0.812-0.855 and F1 of 0.644.
AI.motivation: Thaw slumps are dynamic permafrost features that could substantially increase permafrost-driven warming, yet released inventories cover only part of the permafrost region. They occupy only 0.1-0.5% of tiles, and labels are costly, so detection is a rare-target problem.
AI.method: A convolutional network is trained on 22,259 tiles containing 2,609 RTS instances, with tuning over 172 controlled experiments. It is compared with multimodal fusion, foundation-model encoders and masked-autoencoder pretraining. Deployment covers 20.68 million square kilometres using 41.6 million tiles.
AI.result: The convolutional network matches every alternative tested, each of which needed far more compute. On held-out ecoregions at 0.1-0.5% prevalence, the final model achieves PR-AUC of 0.812-0.855, object precision of 0.854 and F1 of 0.644. Its wall-to-wall deployment yields 19,068 high-confidence detections, with sampled precision of 0.54-0.90 by size class. A foundation model's advantage appears only when labels are scarce.
AI.conclusion: Labelled data moves performance most, and the paper contributes an evaluation protocol for rare targets, a controlled account of accuracy under scarce labels and a circumpolar RTS map.

title: TopoMix: Continuous Spatial Mixing for Long-Tailed Data Augmentation
comment: Accepted by 2026 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC 2026)
summary: Most mixing-based augmentation methods improve generalization through a simple idea: combine two training samples with a fixed global ratio or a hard spatial replacement. While effective, this design leaves little room for local variation, which becomes a more visible limitation in long-tailed recognition, where minority classes are especially sensitive to the quality of augmented samples. We propose TopoMix, a training-free augmentation method that replaces fixed mixing with continuous spatial mixing. TopoMix constructs a smooth spatially varying mask from a low-resolution random control grid, bicubic interpolation, and stochastic non-linear shaping, and uses this mask for element-wise image mixing and label reweighting. Without introducing trainable parameters or auxiliary networks, TopoMix offers a simple way to make mixing more flexible in the input space. Experiments on standard long-tailed benchmarks show that it consistently improves over representative mixing-based baselines, indicating that smooth spatial mixing is an effective augmentation strategy for long-tailed recognition.

AI.tldr: TopoMix is a training-free data augmentation method that replaces fixed-ratio or hard-replacement mixing with continuous spatial mixing, and it improves over representative mixing baselines on long-tailed benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Mixing-based augmentations use a fixed global ratio or a hard spatial replacement, which leaves little room for local variation; this limitation matters more in long-tailed recognition, where minority classes are sensitive to augmented sample quality.
AI.method: TopoMix builds a smooth spatially varying mask from a low-resolution random control grid, bicubic interpolation and stochastic non-linear shaping, and uses it for element-wise image mixing and label reweighting, with no trainable parameters or auxiliary networks.
AI.result: On standard long-tailed benchmarks, TopoMix consistently improves over representative mixing-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: Smooth spatial mixing is an effective augmentation strategy for long-tailed recognition, and TopoMix offers a simple way to make mixing more flexible in input space.

title: Keyframes First, Motion Second: Revisiting Compressed-Domain Video Captioning under Limited Supervision
summary: Compressed-domain video captioners such as CoCap read the H.264 bitstream directly: a pretrained encoder reads the keyframes (I-frames), while motion and residual encoders, trained from scratch, turn the codec's motion vectors and residuals into action tokens. This motion branch costs decoding time and supervision, both scarce on edge devices. We ask when it pays off under limited supervision. In a controlled study on 2,500 VATEX training clips, we fix a frozen SigLIP 2 keyframe encoder, a GPT-2 caption decoder and the training schedule, vary only the visual tokens the decoder receives (34 configurations), and report held-out test CIDEr with paired bootstrap intervals and three seeds. Motion encoders trained from scratch bring no measurable benefit: CoCap-style action tokens change CIDEr by -0.55 (95% CI [-2.3, +1.2]), and six other uses of motion do not help. Warm-started from a model trained on 48x the caption samples, they add +1.3 CIDEr on average, though not significantly across seeds, and only while the keyframe tokens stay frozen. Reading the keyframes better matters more: fine-tuning SigLIP 2's own attention-pooling head adds 5.4 CIDEr, and one to eight such tokens beat the 16 CoCap-style tokens on every seed while decoding only I-frames (7.3 ms instead of 44-114 ms per clip). The same holds on MSVD's full split in CoCap's own video encoding, where the readout leads by 14.2 CIDEr and action tokens bring no reliable gain, also with clean single-reference motion vectors. Under limited supervision, keyframes come first and motion second.

AI.tldr: In a controlled study on compressed-domain video captioning, motion branches trained from scratch give no measurable benefit under limited supervision, while better keyframe reading (SigLIP 2 attention pooling) gives large CIDEr gains at lower decoding cost.
AI.motivation: Compressed-domain captioners such as CoCap add a motion branch that costs decoding time and supervision, both scarce on edge devices, and it was unclear when this branch pays off under limited supervision.
AI.method: On 2,500 VATEX training clips, the authors fix a frozen SigLIP 2 keyframe encoder and a GPT-2 caption decoder, vary only the visual tokens the decoder receives across 34 configurations, and evaluate held-out test CIDEr with paired bootstrap intervals and three seeds.
AI.result: CoCap-style action tokens change CIDEr by -0.55 (95% CI [-2.3, +1.2]). Motion encoders warm-started from a model trained on 48x more caption samples add +1.3 CIDEr on average, not significant across seeds, and only with keyframe tokens frozen. Fine-tuning SigLIP 2's attention-pooling head adds 5.4 CIDEr, and one to eight such tokens beat the 16 CoCap-style tokens on every seed while decoding only I-frames (7.3 ms instead of 44-114 ms per clip). On MSVD's full split the readout leads by 14.2 CIDEr.
AI.conclusion: Under limited supervision, keyframes come first and motion second: investing in keyframe readout matters more than motion modelling for compressed-domain video captioning.

title: Background Bias Assessment and Mitigation in Plant Disease Detection Using EfficientNet-B0 with Image Processing
comment: 6 pages, accepted and published at 2026 IEEE CSPA
summary: Plant disease detection using deep learning has achieved remarkable accuracies exceeding 99% on benchmark datasets. However, these metrics may mask a critical vulnerability: models may be taking advantage of false background correlations instead of learning real pathological features. This study presents a systematic investigation of background bias in plant disease detection through a two-stage training framework with quantitative validation. We propose a three-condition evaluation protocol testing models on original, leaf-only, and background-only images to directly measure background dependency. Our approach combines standard transfer learning using EfficientNet-B0 and manipulation of background information during optimization. Experimental results on the PlantVillage dataset (20,638 images, 15 disease classes) show that while our model achieves 98.97% accuracy on the original images and maintains 96.62% accuracy on leaf-only images, the performance drops to 23.58% on background-only images. The calculated background bias (BBC) coefficient of 0.762 indicates that a large part of the model's predictive performance depends on leaf-related features rather than background distortions. This research offers clear evidence that even with the most advanced models, environmental shortcuts can be leveraged, and this highlights the importance of bias evaluation. The approach that has been used has laid a foundation for the development of agricultural AI that is ready for deployment. The implementation, models, and evaluation process are all publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that an EfficientNet-B0 plant disease classifier relies heavily on background cues, scoring 98.97% on original images but only 23.58% on background-only images, and it proposes a two-stage training framework and a three-condition evaluation protocol to measure this.
AI.motivation: Benchmark accuracies above 99% for plant disease detection may hide reliance on false background correlations rather than real pathological features.
AI.method: A two-stage training framework uses standard transfer learning with EfficientNet-B0 and manipulation of background information during optimization, evaluated with a three-condition protocol on original, leaf-only and background-only images, plus a background bias coefficient (BBC).
AI.result: On PlantVillage (20,638 images, 15 disease classes), the model reaches 98.97% accuracy on original images, 96.62% on leaf-only images and 23.58% on background-only images, with a BBC of 0.762.
AI.conclusion: Environmental shortcuts can be exploited even by advanced models, so bias evaluation is important; the authors state the approach lays a foundation for deployable agricultural AI, and the implementation, models and evaluation process are publicly available.

title: ReactionBench: A Human-Anchored Benchmark for Modeling Reactions to Video
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Evaluation of Interactive Agents (IAEval). 49 pages (10 main text), 9 figures, 46 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Understanding what happens in a video is not sufficient for socially responsive multimodal systems: such systems also aim to relate what a person observes to how that person responds. Existing video benchmarks largely evaluate events, temporal reasoning, or people depicted in the video, while affective and viewer-response datasets often focus on emotion labels, aggregate responses, or prediction from the stimulus alone. This leaves an underexplored question: can current multimodal models ground an observed viewer reaction in the stimulus context associated with it? We introduce ReactionBench, a human-anchored benchmark for reaction-specific video understanding. Built from a candidate pool of 31,834 synchronized stimulus-reaction clips spanning 433 hours and eight domains, ReactionBench evaluates three complementary abilities: ranking the intensity of a viewer's reactions within a video, matching a reaction to its temporally aligned stimulus, and explaining the concrete stimulus cues linked to that reaction. Human annotation provides 14,894 ratings over 3,257 moments, and the frozen evaluation comprises 250 intensity profiles, 112 matching items, and 200 rationale items with 447 blind-written human references. Across seven multimodal models, reaction-specific grounding remains challenging: the best model reaches 50.9% accuracy on four-way stimulus-reaction matching, while GPT-5 shows no detectable loss under reaction substitution. Performance is also sensitive to evaluation protocol. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: ReactionBench is a human-anchored benchmark for reaction-specific video understanding, and it shows that current multimodal models struggle to ground a viewer's reaction in the stimulus that caused it.
AI.motivation: Existing video benchmarks evaluate events, temporal reasoning or depicted people, while affective datasets focus on emotion labels or aggregate responses, so whether models can link an observed viewer reaction to its stimulus is underexplored.
AI.method: The benchmark is built from 31,834 synchronized stimulus-reaction clips spanning 433 hours and eight domains, and it evaluates three abilities: ranking reaction intensity within a video, matching a reaction to its aligned stimulus, and explaining the stimulus cues linked to the reaction, using 14,894 human ratings over 3,257 moments and 447 blind-written human references.
AI.result: Across seven multimodal models, the best reaches 50.9% accuracy on four-way stimulus-reaction matching, and GPT-5 shows no detectable loss under reaction substitution; performance is also sensitive to evaluation protocol.
AI.conclusion: Reaction-specific grounding remains challenging for current multimodal models, and the benchmark is a frozen evaluation for socially responsive multimodal systems.

title: SIMIT: Self-Improving Vision-Language Models via Imagination at Test-Time
summary: We introduce SIMIT, a test-time self-improvement framework in which a vision-language model creates its own query-specific training data before answering an unlabeled test query. Our goal is to improve performance on a given target test set without annotations or external models. To pursue this goal, some test-time methods improve answers through longer reasoning or repeated sampling but leave the model unchanged. Others update the model using rewards based on majority agreement among multiple candidate answers or the model's own judgments of correctness, but such rewards can reinforce existing mistakes. SIMIT instead imagines similar problems whose solutions it controls: a model need not correctly solve the target query to construct useful practice examples. It synthesizes diverse (question, answer, image) triplets by specifying each answer before realizing its image. To support diverse multimodal tasks, SIMIT combines native image generation with an extensible skill library for structured visuals, including documents, charts, and diagrams. Within this pipeline, multi-stage verification checks that images support their assigned answers, while difficulty filtering retains informative examples. Adaptive budgeting further targets this practice by allocating more samples to queries the model is less confident in answering. The resulting data can improve the model in-context (SIMIT-ICL) or in-weight (SIMIT-FT). Across 17 diverse benchmarks, SIMIT outperforms existing self-improvement methods. Its best configuration achieves a +7.20% mean relative gain over BAGEL-7B, while training-free SIMIT-ICL achieves +6.98%.

AI.tldr: SIMIT is a test-time self-improvement framework in which a vision-language model synthesizes its own query-specific training data, with controlled answers and generated images, and it outperforms existing self-improvement methods across 17 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Test-time methods either improve answers without changing the model or update it using agreement-based or self-judged rewards that can reinforce existing mistakes.
AI.method: For each unlabeled test query, SIMIT specifies an answer before realizing an image to create (question, answer, image) triplets, combining native image generation with a skill library for structured visuals such as documents, charts and diagrams, with multi-stage verification, difficulty filtering and adaptive budgeting that allocates more samples to low-confidence queries; the data is used in-context (SIMIT-ICL) or in-weights (SIMIT-FT).
AI.result: Across 17 diverse benchmarks, SIMIT outperforms existing self-improvement methods; its best configuration achieves a +7.20% mean relative gain over BAGEL-7B, and training-free SIMIT-ICL achieves +6.98%.
AI.conclusion: Self-generated, answer-controlled practice data can improve a vision-language model at test time without annotations or external models, and the training-free variant gives most of the gain.

title: Auditing GeoFM Evaluation for Field-Extent Segmentation: Label Proxies, Baselines, and When Frozen Features Match Fine-tuning
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures. Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (08/2026). OpenReview: this https URL
summary: Geospatial foundation-model (GeoFM) benchmarks for agricultural field-extent segmentation often rely on cropland land-cover proxies and compare against per-pixel spectral baselines. We measure how these choices affect conclusions using identical single-date Sentinel-2 pixels from six countries. Replacing polygon-derived field labels with ESA WorldCover cropland raises random-forest AUROC from 0.55-0.82 to 0.79-0.96, showing that the proxy creates a more spectrally separable task. On the actual field-extent labels, a from-scratch U-Net reaches 0.89-0.98 AUROC and has higher point AUROC than a Prithvi frozen linear probe in five of six regions. We then compare a frozen backbone and full fine-tuning using the same decoder for Prithvi and TerraMind, with ten matched seeds. At $\varepsilon=0.02$ AUROC, 9 of 12 region$\times$model cells are TOST-equivalent. Kenya is the common failure case: positives cover roughly 0.1% of pixels, and full fine-tuning performs better for both models. Cross-region results are less favorable to frozen models. On AUROC and average precision (AP), the U-Net leads the full 30-transfer matrix, while an exploratory analysis excluding Kenya finds that both frozen decoders outperform their fine-tuned counterparts; no AUROC difference is detected between frozen TerraMind and the U-Net in that subset. For Prithvi, a frozen decoder trains about $110\times$ fewer parameters than full fine-tuning. These results argue for auditing labels and baselines before interpreting GeoFM rankings, and for testing a frozen decoder before assuming that full fine-tuning will help. Our conclusions are limited to single-date, per-pixel field-extent segmentation, not parcel-boundary or instance delineation.

AI.tldr: An audit of geospatial foundation-model evaluation for field-extent segmentation finds that label proxies and weak baselines distort conclusions, and that frozen features often match full fine-tuning except in the Kenya failure case.
AI.motivation: GeoFM benchmarks for agricultural field-extent segmentation often rely on cropland land-cover proxies and per-pixel spectral baselines, and the effect of these choices on conclusions is not measured.
AI.method: Using identical single-date Sentinel-2 pixels from six countries, the authors compare random-forest, from-scratch U-Net, Prithvi and TerraMind models, contrast frozen backbones with full fine-tuning using the same decoder over ten matched seeds, and apply TOST equivalence testing at epsilon 0.02 AUROC.
AI.result: Replacing polygon-derived labels with ESA WorldCover cropland raises random-forest AUROC from 0.55-0.82 to 0.79-0.96. The U-Net reaches 0.89-0.98 AUROC and beats a Prithvi frozen probe in five of six regions. Nine of 12 region-by-model cells are TOST-equivalent; Kenya, where positives cover about 0.1% of pixels, is the failure case where full fine-tuning is better for both models. The U-Net leads the full 30-transfer matrix on AUROC and AP, and frozen decoders outperform fine-tuned ones when Kenya is excluded in an exploratory analysis. For Prithvi, a frozen decoder trains about 110 times fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: GeoFM rankings should be interpreted only after auditing labels and baselines, and a frozen decoder should be tested before assuming full fine-tuning will help; the conclusions cover single-date per-pixel field-extent segmentation only, not parcel boundaries or instance delineation.

title: From Clips to Streams: A Unified Framework for Streaming Sign Language Translation
comment: 27 pages, 7 figures, the paper has been accepted to NeurIPS 2026
summary: Sign Language Translation (SLT) research has typically focused on pre-segmented clips, a constraint that disconnects models from the continuous reality of real-world communication. To bridge the gap from clips to streams, we formally define Streaming SLT, a realistic task demanding the joint discovery and translation of linguistic events from continuous, untrimmed video inputs. To address this challenge, we propose StreamSLST, the first end-to-end framework for Streaming Sign Language Segmentation and Translation via Deformable Transformer architecture. Unlike cascaded approaches that suffer from error propagation, StreamSLST employs a parallel decoding strategy to jointly optimize temporal segmentation and translation in a single pass. To enable scalable training on long-form videos, we incorporate a Sentence-aware Sliding Window Sampler that crops continuous streams into trainable units. We further design a Tri-modal Visual-Language Pretraining stage that aligns pose dynamics with textual semantics before joint optimization. To support comprehensive evaluation, we conduct experiments on two real-world streaming datasets, BOBSL and How2Sign, together with two newly constructed synthetic streaming benchmarks, Streaming-Phoenix-2014T and Streaming-CSL-Daily. The results demonstrate that StreamSLST consistently outperforms a matched cascaded segmentation-then-translation pipeline. Interestingly, our analysis reveals that joint optimization learns wider, translation-effective temporal support that simple expansion or rescaling of the annotated spans fails to reproduce. Our work establishes the first robust benchmark for continuous sign language understanding and paves the way for accessible real-world communication interfaces. The source code and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: StreamSLST is an end-to-end framework for streaming sign language segmentation and translation from untrimmed video, and it outperforms a matched cascaded segment-then-translate pipeline on two real and two synthetic streaming benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Sign language translation research has focused on pre-segmented clips, which disconnects models from continuous real-world communication and makes cascaded pipelines suffer from error propagation.
AI.method: StreamSLST uses a Deformable Transformer with parallel decoding to jointly optimize temporal segmentation and translation in one pass, a Sentence-aware Sliding Window Sampler for long-form training, and a Tri-modal Visual-Language Pretraining stage that aligns pose dynamics with text before joint optimization.
AI.result: StreamSLST consistently outperforms a matched cascaded segmentation-then-translation pipeline on BOBSL, How2Sign, Streaming-Phoenix-2014T and Streaming-CSL-Daily; joint optimization learns wider, translation-effective temporal support that simple expansion or rescaling of annotated spans does not reproduce.
AI.conclusion: The work defines the streaming SLT task and offers a first benchmark for continuous sign language understanding, with code and data released.

title: SemaNorm: Stain Normalization via Semantic and Morphology Alignment for Robust Cross-Hospital Computational Pathology
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM) 2026
summary: Stain variability remains a major source of domain shift in computational pathology, yet existing normalization methods largely optimize color consistency without explicitly preserving morphology or diagnostic semantics. We propose SemaNorm, a self-supervised stain canonicalization stain normalizer to recover clean patches from strongly perturbed inputs, avoiding paired transfer, adversarial instability, and identity collapse. It further combines a frozen pathology foundation-model consistency loss with a differentiable nuclei-structure loss to preserve semantic and cellular organization. SemaNorm is evaluated across Camelyon17-WILDS and NCT-CRC-HE-100K using cross-hospital tumor classification, cell-graph morphology metrics, and semantic stability measured with an independent held-out foundation encoder. SemaNorm improves out-of-distribution accuracy by 5.9% over the strongest normalization baseline and by 13.5% over no normalization, while achieving the best morphology preservation. Independent foundation-model and cell-graph analyses further confirm improved semantic and structural stability. These results establish morphology- and semantics-aware optimization as a principled alternative to color-only stain normalization.

AI.tldr: SemaNorm is a self-supervised stain normalizer for computational pathology that combines a frozen pathology foundation-model consistency loss with a nuclei-structure loss, improving out-of-distribution tumor classification across hospitals.
AI.motivation: Existing stain normalization methods optimize color consistency without explicitly preserving morphology or diagnostic semantics, which leaves cross-hospital domain shift unresolved.
AI.method: SemaNorm recovers clean patches from strongly perturbed inputs in a self-supervised way, avoiding paired transfer, adversarial instability and identity collapse, and adds a frozen foundation-model consistency loss and a differentiable nuclei-structure loss.
AI.result: Evaluated on Camelyon17-WILDS and NCT-CRC-HE-100K, SemaNorm improves out-of-distribution accuracy by 5.9% over the strongest normalization baseline and by 13.5% over no normalization, with the best morphology preservation and improved semantic and structural stability.
AI.conclusion: Morphology- and semantics-aware optimization is presented as a principled alternative to color-only stain normalization.

title: CausalPrune: Counterfactual Causal Token Pruning for Efficient Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in multimodal understanding, but their practical deployment is still limited by the substantial computation introduced by excessive visual tokens. Visual token pruning offers an effective solution by removing redundant visual tokens during inference. However, existing methods typically estimate token importance from correlational statistics, which cannot distinguish tokens that causally determine the model output from those spuriously associated with it. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{CausalPrune}, a counterfactual causal token pruning framework for efficient LVLMs. We formulate LVLM inference as a Structural Causal Model and introduce the Causal Token Importance Score (CTIS), which estimates the Average Treatment Effect of intervening on each visual token. To make causal estimation practical, we derive an efficient first-order approximation of CTIS and incorporate backdoor adjustment to mitigate latent cross-modal confounding. Within this causal formulation, layer-wise causal mediation decomposes token importance into direct and indirect effects through intermediate hidden states, enabling progressive pruning across transformer layers in a principled manner. Extensive experiments on various LVLM architectures, such as LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL, demonstrate that CausalPrune maintains comparable or even superior multimodal performance while achieving substantial reductions in FLOPs and prefill latency, consistently outperforming existing pruning methods.

AI.tldr: CausalPrune is a counterfactual causal token pruning framework for large vision-language models that scores visual tokens by their estimated causal effect, reducing FLOPs and prefill latency while keeping comparable or better multimodal performance.
AI.motivation: Existing visual token pruning methods estimate importance from correlational statistics, which cannot separate tokens that causally determine the output from those that are spuriously associated with it.
AI.method: LVLM inference is formulated as a Structural Causal Model, and a Causal Token Importance Score estimates the Average Treatment Effect of intervening on each visual token, using a first-order approximation, backdoor adjustment for cross-modal confounding and layer-wise causal mediation for progressive pruning across layers.
AI.result: Experiments on LLaVA-1.5 and Qwen2.5-VL show that CausalPrune keeps comparable or superior multimodal performance with substantial FLOP and prefill-latency reductions, and outperforms existing pruning methods.
AI.conclusion: Causal importance gives a principled basis for visual token pruning in efficient LVLM inference.

title: Not All Minorities Are Equal: Fairness Outcomes in Private Image Generation
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, Under review for ICASSP 2027
summary: Differential privacy (DP) provides formal guarantees for protecting individuals in artificial intelligence systems, but its consequences for fairness in generative models remain poorly understood. We investigate how privacy-preserving training affects the representation of demographic groups and visual attributes in generative models of human faces. Across two facial image datasets and multiple privacy levels, we find that stronger privacy can disproportionately degrade the quality and utility of some underrepresented groups, suggesting that privacy can amplify existing disparities. However, representation alone does not explain these effects: several well-represented attributes also experience substantial degradation, while some underrepresented attributes remain comparatively robust. These findings show that the impact of privacy-preserving learning cannot be explained solely by data representation and may depend on the characteristics and interactions of the information being learned. Our results highlight the need to consider both privacy and fairness when evaluating generative models.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that differentially private training of face generators can disproportionately degrade some underrepresented groups, but representation alone does not explain the disparities, since some well-represented attributes also degrade.
AI.motivation: The consequences of differential privacy for fairness in generative models are poorly understood, especially for demographic groups and visual attributes in face generation.
AI.method: The authors train generative models of human faces on two facial image datasets across multiple privacy levels and measure the quality and utility of demographic groups and visual attributes.
AI.result: Stronger privacy disproportionately degrades some underrepresented groups, but several well-represented attributes also degrade substantially, while some underrepresented attributes remain comparatively robust.
AI.conclusion: The impact of private learning cannot be explained by data representation alone and depends on the characteristics and interactions of the information learned, so privacy and fairness should be evaluated together for generative models.

title: DDEL: Closed-Loop Mutual Enhancement of Dataset Distillation and Ensemble Learning
summary: Dataset distillation (DD) reduces a training set to a small set of examples, while ensemble learning (EL) combines predictions from several models. When applied in sequence, the distilled set remains fixed as the ensemble learns. We introduce DDEL, a framework that feeds ensemble behavior back into distillation. Each round trains the ensemble, measures loss and prediction disagreement on the source data, and uses these signals to guide the next data update. We implement this loop with distribution matching and a homogeneous three-member ensemble. Preliminary experiments cover skin lesion classification (ISIC 2019), treatment-response prediction (I-SPY1), and binary two-year prognosis classification (NSCLC-Radiomics). With the same images-per-class budget as the open-loop comparison, DDEL reaches balanced accuracy 0.3471 on ISIC and mean ROC-AUC 0.5120 and 0.5597 on I-SPY1 and NSCLC. The I-SPY1 difference is small, and the ISIC trajectory shows that more rounds do not consistently improve performance. These results offer initial evidence for studying DD-EL feedback, with its computational cost and robustness still requiring controlled evaluation.

AI.tldr: DDEL closes the loop between dataset distillation and ensemble learning, feeding ensemble disagreement back into the distilled data, and gives initial evidence of gains on three medical classification tasks.
AI.motivation: In the usual sequence the distilled set stays fixed while the ensemble learns, so ensemble behavior never informs distillation.
AI.method: Each round trains a homogeneous three-member ensemble, measures loss and prediction disagreement on the source data, and uses these signals to guide the next data update, implemented with distribution matching.
AI.result: With the same images-per-class budget as the open-loop comparison, DDEL reaches balanced accuracy 0.3471 on ISIC 2019 and mean ROC-AUC 0.5120 and 0.5597 on I-SPY1 and NSCLC-Radiomics; the I-SPY1 gain is small, and more rounds do not consistently improve ISIC.
AI.conclusion: The results offer initial evidence for studying DD-EL feedback, while computational cost and robustness still need controlled evaluation.

title: CarDiff: Anatomically Aware Dental Caries Synthesis using Diffusion
summary: Synthetic medical image generation can help address limited annotated data in dental imaging, particularly for under-represented caries classes. In this work, we present CarDiff, a semi-supervised framework for dental caries synthesis in panoramic radiographs. The method combines paired mask-image learning with self-supervised generation from augmented masks, while incorporating anatomy-aware conditioning between lesion regions and surrounding structures. Semantic consistency is enforced through segmentation-guided supervision and adversarial anatomical alignment. Experiments on the MLUA-DC1000 dataset show that CarDiff achieves improved synthesis quality compared with existing semantic synthesis baselines, obtaining the best Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) (90.76) and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) (0.48) scores among evaluated methods. We further assess the generated radiographs for downstream segmentation augmentation across seven architectures. Using a 5x augmented training set improves average Dice score by up to 6.5%, with larger gains observed for medium and combined lesion classes. These results suggest that anatomically consistent diffusion synthesis may be useful for dental radiograph augmentation under limited supervision. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: CarDiff is a semi-supervised diffusion framework that synthesizes dental caries in panoramic radiographs with anatomy-aware conditioning, improving synthesis quality and downstream segmentation augmentation.
AI.motivation: Annotated dental imaging data is limited, especially for under-represented caries classes, so synthetic medical images could help.
AI.method: CarDiff combines paired mask-image learning with self-supervised generation from augmented masks, anatomy-aware conditioning between lesion regions and surrounding structures, segmentation-guided supervision and adversarial anatomical alignment.
AI.result: On MLUA-DC1000, CarDiff obtains the best FID (90.76) and LPIPS (0.48) among evaluated methods, and a 5x augmented training set improves average Dice by up to 6.5% across seven segmentation architectures, with larger gains for medium and combined lesion classes.
AI.conclusion: Anatomically consistent diffusion synthesis may be useful for dental radiograph augmentation under limited supervision.

title: Where Generated Floor Plans Stop: Encoding Practice Acceptance Rules to Evaluate Machine Learning Floor Plan Generators
comment: 31 pages, 8 figures. Checker released as floorcheck v0.1.1, this https URL
summary: Machine learning floor plan generators are proposed as aids to design decisions, yet they are judged mainly by how closely a generated plan's room adjacencies match the request, a measure without architectural knowledge. We encode an architecture practice's floor plan acceptance rules, taken from its production layout software, as six checks applied in a fixed order, report each plan at the first check it fails, and calibrate the two room-shape limits, which no building code states, so that each alone rejects 5 per cent of built apartments. A transfer specification records which checks public data can carry. Applied to four published generators and two built corpora, RPLAN and Modified Swiss Dwellings (MSD), the checks stop the generators at different points. A room proportion check alone refuses 33.7 per cent of the House-GAN++ plans the checker can read and build, against 5.0 per cent of RPLAN, a gap that survives three measurement controls. At the 5 per cent rate, MSD apartments pass all six checks 5.5 to 23.5 points more often than House-GAN++, depending on the plans counted. The two generators that score best on the adjacency measure, Compatibility, pass least, because of how they represent plans, and within the two that pass most it barely predicts which plans pass. The checks thus expose what the standard measure misses; the checker is released. Passing is not shown to mean acceptance in practice.

AI.tldr: The paper encodes an architecture practice's floor plan acceptance rules as six checks and shows that these checks expose failures in machine learning floor plan generators that the standard adjacency-based Compatibility measure misses.
AI.motivation: Machine learning floor plan generators are judged mainly by how closely room adjacencies match the request, a measure that has no architectural knowledge.
AI.method: Six checks taken from a practice's production layout software are applied in a fixed order, each plan is reported at the first check it fails, and two room-shape limits are calibrated so that each alone rejects 5% of built apartments; the checks are applied to four published generators and two built corpora, RPLAN and Modified Swiss Dwellings (MSD).
AI.result: A room proportion check alone refuses 33.7% of House-GAN++ plans it can read and build, against 5.0% of RPLAN, a gap that survives three measurement controls. At the 5% rate, MSD apartments pass all six checks 5.5 to 23.5 points more often than House-GAN++. The two generators scoring best on Compatibility pass least, and among the two passing most, Compatibility barely predicts passing.
AI.conclusion: The checks expose what the standard measure misses, and the checker is released; passing the checks is not shown to mean acceptance in practice.

title: OpenMidnight: Closing the Performance Gap Between Open and Proprietary Pathology Foundation Models
summary: Pathology foundation models offer transferable representations for a range of downstream tasks in computational pathology, but reliance on proprietary data, substantial compute requirements, and limited availability of training code and preprocessing pipelines hinder independent validation and further methodological development. We present OpenMidnight 1.1, an open-source replication and refinement of Midnight trained on approximately 12,000 publicly available whole-slide images from The Cancer Genome Atlas. Using an encoder initialized with pretrained DINOv2 weights, OpenMidnight 1.1 uses approximately 320 H100 GPU-hours for pathology pretraining, a 34-fold reduction relative to the compute reported for Midnight. Across 16 classification and four segmentation datasets in THUNDER, OpenMidnight 1.1 achieves the highest mean segmentation Dice (69.7) and ranks fourth among 14 models, ahead of Midnight, with performance that matches or exceeds models trained on substantially larger datasets in several tasks. Our ablation studies additionally examine how initialization, data volume, model size, and tissue composition affect downstream performance, providing empirical evidence to inform the development of future training recipes. Our release of the training code, preprocessing pipeline, and model weights lowers barriers to reproducible research and further development of competitive pathology foundation models.

AI.tldr: OpenMidnight 1.1 is an open-source replication and refinement of the Midnight pathology foundation model, trained on public TCGA slides with about 34 times less compute, and it ranks fourth of 14 models on the THUNDER benchmark.
AI.motivation: Proprietary data, heavy compute and unavailable training code and preprocessing pipelines hinder independent validation and methodological development of pathology foundation models.
AI.method: The encoder is initialized from pretrained DINOv2 weights and pretrained on about 12,000 publicly available TCGA whole-slide images, using about 320 H100 GPU-hours; ablations examine initialization, data volume, model size and tissue composition.
AI.result: Across 16 classification and four segmentation datasets in THUNDER, OpenMidnight 1.1 achieves the highest mean segmentation Dice (69.7) and ranks fourth among 14 models, ahead of Midnight, with performance matching or exceeding models trained on much larger datasets in several tasks.
AI.conclusion: Releasing the training code, preprocessing pipeline and weights lowers barriers to reproducible research on competitive pathology foundation models.

title: BreastXAgent: A lightweight agentic explainability framework for breast density classification
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Published in Proceedings of SPIE, Vol. 14346, Third International Conference on Frontiers of Applied Optics and Computer Engineering (AOCE 2026)
summary: Deep learning models for breast density classification typically return only a label and confidence score. This paper presents BreastXAgent, a lightweight agentic framework that combines a pretrained classifier, Grad-CAM visual explanation, LangGraph-based routing, LLM report generation, and rule-based guardrails to produce controlled, faithful, non-diagnostic reports. On 160 mammography images, uncontrolled LLM reporting produced 75% Grad-CAM overclaims and 62.5% clinical overclaims. Strict prompting and LangGraph routing improved safety but did not eliminate violations. The full BreastXAgent achieved 100% safety pass rate, zero overclaims, and highest utility score. Results demonstrate that agentic guardrails enable safe, structured explanation generation without modifying the underlying classifier.

AI.tldr: BreastXAgent is a lightweight agentic framework that wraps a breast density classifier with Grad-CAM explanations, LangGraph routing, LLM report generation and rule-based guardrails, producing safe non-diagnostic reports with zero overclaims on 160 mammograms.
AI.motivation: Breast density classifiers return only a label and confidence, and uncontrolled LLM report generation produces explanation and clinical overclaims.
AI.method: The framework combines a pretrained classifier, Grad-CAM visual explanation, LangGraph-based routing, LLM report generation and rule-based guardrails, without modifying the underlying classifier.
AI.result: On 160 mammography images, uncontrolled LLM reporting produced 75% Grad-CAM overclaims and 62.5% clinical overclaims; strict prompting and routing reduced but did not eliminate violations, while the full BreastXAgent achieved a 100% safety pass rate, zero overclaims and the highest utility score.
AI.conclusion: Agentic guardrails can enable safe, structured explanation generation without changing the underlying classifier.

title: Comparing Monocular and Multi-View 3D Pedestrian Reconstruction Strategies for Urban Intersection Sensing
summary: Understanding how pedestrians move and interact at urban intersections is central to traffic-safety assessment, mobility planning, and smart-city sensing. Such analyses rely on physically grounded descriptions of motion: 3D body pose, metric trajectories, and pose-derived descriptors such as stature and walking speed. Recovering these from fixed roadside cameras is difficult: viewpoints are oblique and long-range, occlusions are frequent, and neither ground-truth 3D pose nor cross-camera identity labels are typically available. We compare two strategies for deriving pedestrian motion descriptors from a multi-camera intersection dataset: a monocular learned pipeline that combines text-prompted segmentation, tracking, and learned 3D body estimation, and a calibrated multi-view geometric pipeline that combines 2D pose estimation, tracking, cross-camera association, and triangulation. Because 3D ground truth is unavailable, we evaluate both with reference-free criteria relevant to intersection analysis: pedestrian coverage, anthropometric plausibility, walking-speed distributions, computational cost, and failure modes. The two strategies exhibit complementary trade-offs. The learned pipeline is simpler to deploy and covers more pedestrians, but suffers from scale ambiguity and systematic height compression; the geometric pipeline yields metric reconstructions more efficiently, but requires calibration, discards pedestrians seen by only one camera, and can produce severe outliers in dense crowds. We distill these findings into practical guidance for selecting a reconstruction strategy and configuring camera infrastructure according to the target analysis task.

AI.tldr: The paper compares a monocular learned pipeline and a calibrated multi-view geometric pipeline for reconstructing 3D pedestrian motion at urban intersections from roadside cameras, and finds complementary trade-offs without 3D ground truth.
AI.motivation: Pedestrian motion analysis at intersections needs 3D pose and metric trajectories from oblique, long-range, occluded fixed cameras, where neither 3D ground truth nor cross-camera identity labels are typically available.
AI.method: The monocular pipeline combines text-prompted segmentation, tracking and learned 3D body estimation; the multi-view pipeline combines 2D pose estimation, tracking, cross-camera association and triangulation; both are evaluated with reference-free criteria including coverage, anthropometric plausibility, walking-speed distributions, computational cost and failure modes.
AI.result: The learned pipeline is simpler to deploy and covers more pedestrians but suffers from scale ambiguity and systematic height compression; the geometric pipeline gives metric reconstructions more efficiently but requires calibration, discards single-camera pedestrians and can produce severe outliers in dense crowds.
AI.conclusion: The findings give practical guidance for choosing a reconstruction strategy and configuring camera infrastructure for a given intersection analysis task.

title: MedICL: Modality-Anatomy-Aware Visual In-Context Learning for Medical Visual Question Answering
summary: Training-free adaptation of medical vision-language models (LVLMs) is a deployment requirement, yet visual in-context learning (ICL) injects modality- and style-mismatched demonstrations into medical contexts, teaching a frozen model the wrong answering style. We present MedICL, which curates demonstrations instead of retraining the model. MADS selects modality-anatomy aligned demonstrations that cover complementary interpretation dimensions; W2C curates them with weak retrieval signals and a strong verification vote that checks demonstrations rather than the model's own outputs; ECC answers with W anchored demonstration sets, aggregates by abnormality-aware signatures, and re-answers once on conflict. On VQA-RAD, SLAKE, and PathVQA under the LLaVA-Med zero-shot protocol, MedICL improves the strongest zero-shot baseline by +11 - +14 points on open-ended and +7 - +14 on closed questions, recovers 71% of fine-tuned open-ended performance on VQA-RAD at zero training cost, and stays robust to shifted or corrupted demonstration banks.

AI.tldr: MedICL is a training-free visual in-context learning method for medical VQA that curates modality- and anatomy-matched demonstrations instead of retraining, improving the strongest zero-shot baseline on VQA-RAD, SLAKE and PathVQA.
AI.motivation: Visual in-context learning injects modality- and style-mismatched demonstrations into medical contexts, teaching a frozen medical vision-language model the wrong answering style.
AI.method: MedICL uses MADS to select modality-anatomy aligned demonstrations covering complementary interpretation dimensions, W2C to curate them with weak retrieval signals and a strong verification vote over demonstrations, and ECC to answer with anchored demonstration sets, aggregate by abnormality-aware signatures and re-answer once on conflict.
AI.result: Under the LLaVA-Med zero-shot protocol on VQA-RAD, SLAKE and PathVQA, MedICL improves the strongest zero-shot baseline by 11 to 14 points on open-ended and 7 to 14 points on closed questions, recovers 71% of fine-tuned open-ended performance on VQA-RAD at zero training cost, and is robust to shifted or corrupted demonstration banks.
AI.conclusion: Curating demonstrations is a training-free route to better medical VQA adaptation of frozen vision-language models.

title: SAMP: Self-Adaptive Margin Prioritization For Robust Diffusion Watermarking
summary: Diffusion models have made high-fidelity visual generation widely accessible, while also lowering the barrier to producing convincing visual forgeries and complicating content provenance. Existing watermarking methods typically use a fixed embedding strength throughout denoising or treat all watermark dimensions equally. As a result, they may introduce unnecessary distortion when some watermark dimensions are already reliable, while failing to sufficiently reinforce those that are more vulnerable to subsequent perturbations. Therefore, robust watermarking requires adapting both the embedding strength during denoising and the optimization priority across watermark dimensions. To address this problem, we present SAMP, a self-adaptive framework consisting of global margin regulation and vulnerability-sensitive allocation. Global margin regulation adjusts the embedding strength according to the separation between the target codeword and competing codewords, together with the estimated effects of common attacks. Vulnerability-sensitive allocation identifies watermark dimensions that are more easily weakened by local perturbations and gives them higher optimization priority. Experimental results demonstrate that SAMP achieves an average information recovery accuracy of 0.993. Compared with state-of-the-art methods, SAMP improves PSNR by 16.8% and reduces LPIPS by 47.1%. These results validate the effectiveness of SAMP for reliable and high-quality diffusion watermarking.

AI.tldr: SAMP is a self-adaptive diffusion watermarking framework that adjusts embedding strength during denoising and prioritizes vulnerable watermark dimensions, reaching 0.993 average recovery accuracy with better image quality than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Fixed embedding strength and equal treatment of all watermark dimensions add unnecessary distortion for reliable dimensions while under-protecting vulnerable ones against subsequent perturbations.
AI.method: SAMP combines global margin regulation, which adjusts embedding strength by the separation between the target and competing codewords together with estimated effects of common attacks, and vulnerability-sensitive allocation, which gives higher optimization priority to watermark dimensions more easily weakened by local perturbations.
AI.result: SAMP achieves an average information recovery accuracy of 0.993, improves PSNR by 16.8% and reduces LPIPS by 47.1% compared with state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: The results validate SAMP as a method for reliable and high-quality diffusion watermarking.

title: How Reliable Are Object Detection Models Beyond Clear Weather? A Deployment-Oriented Robustness Study for Autonomous Driving
summary: Autonomous driving perception systems must maintain reliable object detection under diverse environmental conditions, not only in clear daytime scenes. However, the cross-weather robustness of modern detectors remains insufficiently characterised under source-only evaluation. This study evaluates representative object detection architectures trained exclusively on clear daytime driving scenes and tested without adaptation under unseen fog, rain, snow, and night conditions. The evaluation covers lightweight and medium-scale one-stage, two-stage, and transformer-based detectors within a unified protocol. Robustness is assessed using performance Drop (%), a Weather Robustness Index (WRI), and class-level sensitivity analysis for critical road participants, including cars, buses, trucks, and persons. Prediction confidence reliability under environmental domain shift is measured using Expected Calibration Error (ECE). Results reveal consistent performance degradation in adverse conditions, reaching 62.90% at night. Buses show the highest sensitivity to environmental variability, while cars remain comparatively stable across weather transitions. Comparisons indicate that YOLO-based detectors exhibit the lowest calibration mismatch, reflecting stronger agreement between predicted confidence and empirical detection correctness. In contrast, DETR achieves the lowest robustness score, with a WRI of 0.6859, indicating greater vulnerability to cross-weather domain shift. These findings offer deployment-oriented insights into detector robustness and confidence reliability for safety-critical intelligent vehicle perception systems.

AI.tldr: A source-only robustness study trains object detectors on clear daytime driving scenes and tests them on fog, rain, snow and night, finding consistent degradation that reaches 62.90% at night, with YOLO-based detectors best calibrated and DETR least robust.
AI.motivation: Autonomous driving perception must remain reliable beyond clear weather, but the cross-weather robustness of modern detectors is insufficiently characterized under source-only evaluation.
AI.method: Lightweight and medium-scale one-stage, two-stage and transformer-based detectors are trained only on clear daytime scenes and tested without adaptation on unseen fog, rain, snow and night conditions, using performance drop, a Weather Robustness Index (WRI), class-level sensitivity for cars, buses, trucks and persons, and Expected Calibration Error (ECE).
AI.result: Performance degrades consistently in adverse conditions, reaching 62.90% at night; buses are the most sensitive class and cars the most stable; YOLO-based detectors show the lowest calibration mismatch, while DETR has the lowest robustness score with a WRI of 0.6859.
AI.conclusion: The findings offer deployment-oriented insight into detector robustness and confidence reliability for safety-critical vehicle perception.

title: CRaFT-XDet: Causal and Robust Fusion Transformer for Dual-Energy X-ray Prohibited Item Detection
summary: Automated prohibited item detection in X-ray security imagery is fundamentally constrained by severe object overlap, scanner-dependent domain shifts, and spurious correlations induced by cluttered baggage composition. Existing detectors largely rely on appearance-driven supervision, limiting their robustness and cross-scanner generalisation. We introduce CRaFT-XDet, a causality-grounded and physics- motivated detection framework that reformulates X-ray threat detection as invariant representation learning under attenuation-driven modality variation. Our approach is grounded in a Scanner-Invariant Causal Detection formalisation (Theorem 1), which establishes that minimising the proposed Causal Invariance Regularisation (CIR) objective across partitioned scanner environments approximates the interventional distribution P (Y | do(Xobj)) under standard identifiability assumptions, providing a principled causal formulation for dual-energy X-ray detection. CRaFT-XDet integrates: (i) causal feature disentanglement to suppress context-induced shortcuts; (ii) physics-motivated regularisation to enforce material-consistent embeddings; and (iii) transformer-based cross-energy interaction modelling for structured reasoning in cluttered scenes. With 29.2 M parameters, 89.5 GFLOPs, and 345 FPS (1.7 ms inference), CRaFT-XDet is real-time deployable. Trained on SIXray with five-fold cross-validation, the framework achieves 0.9389 mAP@0.5 and 0.8021 mAP@0.5:0.95. Without domain adaptation, CRaFT-XDet maintains strong cross- dataset performance on OPIXray and HiXray, indicating robust generalization across heterogeneous scanner distributions. In category-agnostic binary threat detection, the model attains 93.92% recall and 0.9031 mean IoU, highlighting reliability in safety-critical screening where missed detections are costly.

AI.tldr: CRaFT-XDet is a causality-motivated transformer detector for dual-energy X-ray prohibited item detection that learns scanner-invariant representations, reaching 0.9389 mAP@0.5 on SIXray and staying real-time at 345 FPS.
AI.motivation: X-ray prohibited item detection suffers from object overlap, scanner-dependent domain shift and spurious clutter correlations, while existing appearance-driven detectors generalize poorly across scanners.
AI.method: The framework combines causal feature disentanglement to suppress context shortcuts, physics-motivated regularisation for material-consistent embeddings, and transformer-based cross-energy interaction, trained with a Causal Invariance Regularisation objective whose minimization across scanner environments is argued in Theorem 1 to approximate the interventional distribution P(Y | do(Xobj)).
AI.result: With 29.2M parameters, 89.5 GFLOPs and 345 FPS (1.7 ms), the model achieves 0.9389 mAP@0.5 and 0.8021 mAP@0.5:0.95 on SIXray with five-fold cross-validation, maintains strong cross-dataset performance on OPIXray and HiXray without domain adaptation, and reaches 93.92% recall and 0.9031 mean IoU in category-agnostic binary threat detection.
AI.conclusion: The framework is presented as real-time deployable and robust across heterogeneous scanner distributions for safety-critical screening.

title: When Morphs Look Better: Face Image Quality as a Training-Free Signal for Morphing Attack Detection
summary: Face image quality assessment (FIQA) estimates the utility of a face image for automated face recognition and has been proposed as a morphing attack detection (MAD) signal that requires no morph-specific training. We evaluate 17 FIQA methods from all current FIQA categories on 20 morphing attack sets from two datasets, FRLL and FEI, including five diffusion-based attack sets. Each quality score is used directly as a MAD decision score. Unlike prior work, which inverted a quality measure when this lowered its error, we fix the score direction of each method in advance from its definition, so that cases in which morphs receive higher quality than bona fide samples remain visible. On FRLL, DifFIQA(R) achieves a mean D-EER of 11.42%, and together with CLIB-FIQA and eDifFIQA(L) clearly outperforms all other FIQA methods. A strong separation of bona fide and morph scores does not imply good detection performance: on the diffusion-based attacks, up to 11 of 17 methods assign higher quality to morphs than to bona fide samples, and the largest reversed separation in the study coincides with the worst detection result of the study. Performance also depends strongly on the attack: GraFIQs(L), the best detector of DCMorph and Arc2Morph on FRLL, performs poorly on the landmark-based and GAN-based attacks. On FEI, the lowest mean D-EER is 39.75%, and a threshold set on the bona fide data of one dataset does not transfer to the other.

AI.tldr: Evaluating 17 face image quality assessment methods as training-free morphing attack detectors shows that quality scores can be misleading, since on diffusion-based attacks up to 11 of 17 methods rate morphs higher than bona fide samples.
AI.motivation: FIQA has been proposed as a morphing attack detection signal that needs no morph-specific training, but prior work inverted quality scores when this lowered error, hiding cases where morphs receive higher quality.
AI.method: Seventeen FIQA methods across all current categories are evaluated on 20 morphing attack sets from FRLL and FEI, including five diffusion-based sets, with each method's score direction fixed in advance from its definition and used directly as a MAD decision score.
AI.result: On FRLL, DifFIQA(R) achieves a mean D-EER of 11.42%, together with CLIB-FIQA and eDifFIQA(L) clearly outperforming other FIQA methods; up to 11 of 17 methods assign higher quality to diffusion morphs than bona fide samples, and the largest reversed separation coincides with the worst detection result. On FEI the lowest mean D-EER is 39.75%, and a threshold set on one dataset does not transfer to the other.
AI.conclusion: Strong bona fide-morph score separation does not imply good detection, and detector performance depends strongly on the attack type.

title: CRAFT: Corrective and Robust Multi-Agent Framework for Text-to-Parametric CAD
comment: Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on LLM-Aided Design (ICLAD). 11 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Text-to-CAD generation has the potential to make mechanical CAD more accessible, but existing approaches face a trade-off between data dependence and output fidelity. Supervised methods rely on large paired text-model datasets, while zero-shot prompting strategies are often brittle and tend to lose the parametric structure needed for downstream editing and customization. We present CRAFT, a corrective and robust multi-agent framework that produces parametric OpenSCAD programs from natural language without task-specific training. At its core is a JSON intermediate representation that carries symbolic parametric expressions throughout the generation process, so the resulting models remain editable and retain their parametric structure. CRAFT combines semantic understanding, parametric planning, compilation, rendering, self-correction, and component-level verification within a layered recovery process, using multi-view visual feedback to detect and repair geometric errors. Across NopSCADlib, ABC, and Slice-100K, CRAFT is competitive with direct zero-shot baselines in perceptual and geometric quality while exposing substantially more editable parametric structure.

AI.tldr: CRAFT is a training-free multi-agent framework that generates parametric OpenSCAD programs from natural language via a JSON intermediate representation, remaining competitive with zero-shot baselines while exposing more editable parametric structure.
AI.motivation: Supervised text-to-CAD methods depend on large paired datasets, while zero-shot prompting is brittle and often loses the parametric structure needed for editing.
AI.method: CRAFT uses a JSON intermediate representation carrying symbolic parametric expressions through semantic understanding, parametric planning, compilation, rendering, self-correction and component-level verification, with multi-view visual feedback to detect and repair geometric errors.
AI.result: Across NopSCADlib, ABC and Slice-100K, CRAFT is competitive with direct zero-shot baselines in perceptual and geometric quality while exposing substantially more editable parametric structure.
AI.conclusion: Parametric, editable CAD generation is achievable without task-specific training by combining a symbolic intermediate representation with corrective agents.

title: AegisBench: Auditing Aerial Search-and-Rescue Person Detection Under the Conditions It Is Deployed In
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 12 tables. Accepted at the Trustworthy AI for Good (AI4GOOD) workshop at NeurIPS 2026. Code and results: this https URL
summary: Drone-based person detection is being adopted by emergency-management agencies to find missing people faster than ground teams can. The benchmarks behind that adoption were collected in calm, clear daylight, while the missions that trigger deployment happen in floods, wildfires, storms, and at night. AegisBench measures that gap. It applies nine physically motivated corruptions from four disaster families, each at three severities monotone in a declared image statistic or physical quantity, to two aerial search-and-rescue datasets, HERIDAL and SARD. Three architecturally distinct detectors (Faster R-CNN, YOLOv11, RT-DETR) are scored across 168 conditions by one shared evaluator, at confidence thresholds frozen on clean validation data as a fielded system would run. Robustness is highly uneven. Low light is the extreme case: a 4.5-stop exposure loss drives recall to exactly zero for all three detectors on both datasets, a result that holds under threshold-free mAP and across three training seeds, and is mirrored on 300 real night drone images, where 2 of 759 people are found. Surviving detections largely stay on target, so the failure is silent: an empty frame looks the same as one whose occupants the system cannot see. Fine-tuning on milder low-light levels recovers 0.06 to 0.19 recall at the held-out severity, at an architecture-dependent cost on other conditions, and does not transfer to real night imagery. Spatial corruptions rank differently on the two datasets, which we cannot attribute to altitude alone because their parameters scale with frame size rather than person size. We release the corruption engine, evaluation pipeline, and all per-condition results as an audit instrument for anyone evaluating these systems.

AI.tldr: AegisBench audits drone-based person detectors under disaster-like corruptions and finds that low light drives recall to zero for three detectors on two aerial search-and-rescue datasets, a failure that is silent because surviving detections stay on target.
AI.motivation: Drone person detection is being adopted by emergency agencies, but its benchmarks were collected in calm daylight while deployment happens in floods, wildfires, storms and at night.
AI.method: Nine physically motivated corruptions from four disaster families, each at three severities, are applied to HERIDAL and SARD; Faster R-CNN, YOLOv11 and RT-DETR are scored across 168 conditions by one shared evaluator, with thresholds frozen on clean validation data.
AI.result: A 4.5-stop exposure loss drives recall to exactly zero for all three detectors on both datasets, holding under threshold-free mAP and across three training seeds, and mirrored on 300 real night drone images where 2 of 759 people are found; fine-tuning on milder low light recovers 0.06 to 0.19 recall at the held-out severity but does not transfer to real night imagery.
AI.conclusion: Robustness is highly uneven, and the authors release the corruption engine, evaluation pipeline and per-condition results as an audit instrument for these systems.

title: Faithful Where You Look: Anchor-Based Evaluation Hides Text Fabrication in Image-Conditioned Video Generation
